title: Bryce Young Reveals the Mindset That Saved His Panthers Career
full_text:
Bryce Young was getting criticized before he was even a Panther. Carolina traded DJ Moore and a bunch of draft picks to Chicago just to move from No. 9 to No. 1 in the 2023 NFL Draft, and people immediately started wondering if the Panthers had given up too much.
Then Carolina took Young, and the questions only got louder. He was too small. The Panthers should've taken C.J. Stroud. They gave up all of that for the wrong quarterback. The guy hadn't even played an NFL game yet, and people had already made up their minds about him.
I started thinking about all of that again after listening to Young talk to Pat McAfee this week. McAfee asked him about dealing with criticism, and after everything Young has been through in Carolina, I don't know if his answer could've been any more fitting.
I'm not going to sit here and act like all the criticism was unfair, because it wasn't. Young struggled as a rookie, Carolina went 2-15, and Frank Reich didn't even make it through the season. Young finished with 2,877 passing yards, 11 touchdowns, and 10 interceptions, and there were plenty of times when I wondered if the Panthers had made a huge mistake.
Stroud having the rookie season he did in Houston only made it worse. Every time he had another big game, the Young vs. Stroud conversation started all over again. I understood it because, at that point, I was starting to wonder the same thing.
The hope was that Year 2 would look different. Somehow, things got even worse.
Two games into the 2024 season, Dave Canales benched Young for Andy Dalton. I know we've had two years to move past it, but that's still pretty wild when you think about where Young is now. A little more than a year after Carolina gave up everything it did to draft him No. 1, he wasn't even the starting quarterback anymore.
Canales said Dalton gave the Panthers the best chance to win. I don't care who you are, that has to be tough to hear when you're 23 years old and already have people everywhere telling you that your team drafted the wrong guy.
What happened next is probably the biggest reason I look at Young differently now.
Young could've been angry, and I don't think anybody would've blamed him. Carolina had already changed coaches, the offensive line hadn't exactly made his life easy, and there were plenty of other things wrong with the Panthers besides the quarterback.
But Young didn't really go there.
“I'm always going to look in the mirror,” Young said after the benching.
Then he went back to work. Young ran the scout team, stayed ready, and eventually got another chance after Dalton was injured. When he got back on the field, he started playing better, and eventually there wasn't much of a quarterback debate anymore.
That's the part I think gets lost now that we're watching what Young is doing in 2026. He didn't just struggle for a while and then suddenly get better. He actually lost his job and had to work his way back to being Carolina's starting quarterback.
Fast-forward to now, and this whole conversation looks completely different. Young has thrown for 1,268 yards and nine touchdowns through four games. He just threw for 329 yards and two touchdowns against Detroit, and Panthers fans were chanting MVP for him Sunday night.
If you had told me that was coming when Young was sitting behind Dalton, I don't know if I would've believed you.
McAfee asked Young this week how he deals with all the criticism, and his answer made me laugh a little.
“I'm grateful for the engagement,” Young said.
That's such a Bryce Young answer. He's basically saying people care about football, so they're going to have opinions about him, and he understands that. What I found more interesting was what he said about how much those opinions actually mean to him.
“I'm probably not really gonna put anything into it,” Young said.
Now go back through everything that's happened since Carolina traded up to draft him and think about that answer again.
That's where I keep getting stuck with this. What happens if Young actually starts believing everything being said about him?
Maybe the Stroud comparisons get to him. Maybe getting benched for Dalton kills whatever confidence he had left. Maybe Young never plays well enough when he gets another chance, or Carolina decides it has seen enough and starts looking for another quarterback.
We'll never know, and I'm not trying to make this more complicated than it is. Young wasn't good enough early in his career, and some of the criticism was deserved. He had to get better, and he has.
But I also think you have to give him credit for how he handled everything when it looked like his career in Carolina might be falling apart. It's easy to say you don't care what people think when you're throwing for 300 yards, and fans are chanting MVP. Young apparently didn't care all that much when he was sitting on the bench, either.
That's what I kept thinking about after hearing him talk to McAfee. Carolina has changed coaches, changed play-callers, and tried to put better players around Young, and all of that has helped.
But none of it matters if Young doesn't fight his way back from that bench.
Maybe that's one of the biggest reasons the Panthers still have their quarterback.

title: 4 Problems the Panthers Can't Ignore During Their Week 5 Bye
full_text:
I complained about this Week 5 bye as soon as the schedule came out. Four games and then a week off just seemed way too early, especially knowing Carolina would have to play the rest of the season without another break.
I'm starting to look at it a little differently now.
The Panthers are 2-2 and just beat Detroit in a game I didn't think they were going to win. They've also looked a whole lot better over the last three weeks than they did when Chicago put 59 points on them in the opener. But that doesn't mean I've forgotten about some of the things we've seen through four games.
There are still a few things I'd like Carolina to figure out before going to Philadelphia.
I'm not really sure what Carolina can do here because Jaycee Horn and Mike Jackson aren't walking through the door after the bye. Both are on injured reserve, and the Panthers are going to have to make this work without them for a while.
That wasn't exactly easy against Detroit.
Jared Goff threw for 412 yards, and there were times when it felt like Detroit could get whatever it wanted through the air. I know we're talking about a really good Lions offense, and Carolina was asking guys like Will Lee III to do a lot more than anybody probably expected this early.
The good part is they made enough plays when they had to. Lee and Lathan Ransom were there on the fourth-down stop that ended Detroit's final possession, and Carolina found a way to win despite everything going on back there.
But I can't just ignore 412 passing yards because the Panthers won.
Maybe Ejiro Evero changes some things until Horn and Jackson get back. Maybe Carolina uses one of its open roster spots on another corner. Whatever they decide, I don't think they can keep asking this secondary to survive every week and hope it works out.
I feel like every week I'm writing about another Panthers offensive lineman getting hurt.
Taylor Moton has been out. Damien Lewis missed the Detroit game, Monroe Freeling has dealt with an injury, and Corey Bullock had to step in at left guard Sunday night. Bullock settled in, and Carolina still managed to run the ball pretty well, so I'm not complaining about what the backups have done.
I'd just like to stop finding out how many backups they have.
Moton could be getting closer to returning after the bye, and this would be a pretty good time to get him back. Young has thrown for 1,268 yards and nine touchdowns, while Carolina has been moving guys around in front of him.
I've already liked what I've seen from this offense.
Now I'd like to see it with a healthy offensive line.
This is probably the one that bothers me the most.
Carolina gave up 59 points and 552 yards against Chicago, and I came out of that game wondering if the defense was going to be terrible. Then the Panthers held Atlanta to three points and Cleveland to 21, and I started thinking maybe I overreacted.
Then Detroit put up 452 yards.
I don't know what to make of that yet.
I'm not expecting Carolina to hold everybody to three points. I also don't think giving up 452 yards to Detroit is the same as what happened against Chicago because the Lions have a really good offense, and Carolina was missing a bunch of guys.
But at some point, I need to know what this defense is.
Maybe the answer is somewhere in the middle. If that's the case, fine. I just don't want to spend the next three months wondering which version is showing up every Sunday.
I know I've talked about Chuba Hubbard enough already, but I'm going to do it again.
Hubbard ran for 122 yards against Detroit, and Carolina finally had the running game I've been waiting to see. Young still threw for 329 yards and two touchdowns, so it's not like getting Hubbard involved took anything away from him.
I think it actually made things easier.
That's what I don't want Carolina to forget during the bye. Young is playing really good football right now, but that doesn't mean he needs to throw it 40 or 50 times every week. If Hubbard is running the ball like he did Sunday night, give it to him.
I'm probably making this too simple, but I don't think I am.
Make teams worry about Hubbard. Then let Young work off of it.
I'm still not going to say I love having a bye after four games. Ask me again in December, when Carolina hasn't had a week off in two months, and I'll probably be complaining about it again.
But right now, I can see how it helps.
The Panthers aren't 1-3 and trying to figure out how to save their season. They're 2-2, Young is playing the best football of his career, and they just beat a Detroit team I thought was going to come into Charlotte and beat them.
I feel a whole lot different about Carolina than I did after Week 1.
That doesn't mean the Panthers don't have problems. They do, and four games have been enough to show us what some of them are.
Now they have a week to do something about them.

title: Panthers' NFC South Odds Just Took a Turn Nobody Saw Coming
full_text:
If you had told me after Week 1 that the Panthers would have the best odds to win the NFC South a few weeks later, I probably would've asked what you were watching. Carolina had just given up 59 points to Chicago, the defense looked terrible, and the Panthers turned the ball over three times.
I wasn't thinking about winning the division after that game. I was wondering how bad this season might get.
Carolina is now +160 at DraftKings to win the NFC South. The Panthers were +250 at the previous update after opening the season at +350. Atlanta is at +194, New Orleans is +260 and Tampa Bay is all the way down at +1100.
I'm not going to lie, I had to look at those numbers again. We're talking about the same Panthers team that looked completely lost defensively against Chicago, and now they're 2-2, already have a 34-3 win at Atlanta, and just beat Detroit 32-26 on Sunday Night Football.
I've spent the last few weeks trying to figure out what this team is. I'm still not completely sure, but apparently the oddsmakers are starting to believe Carolina might be pretty good.
I know how ridiculous that would've sounded after the Chicago game. I wouldn't have bought it then, either. But look around the NFC South right now and tell me who is running away with this thing.
Carolina and Atlanta are both 2-2, and the Panthers already went to Atlanta and beat the Falcons by 31 points. New Orleans is 1-3, and Tampa Bay is 0-4. Four games isn't much, but it's enough for me to look at this division and think, why not Carolina?
Then there's Bryce Young . I've written enough about how well he's playing, so I'm not going to do the whole thing again here. But 1,268 passing yards and nine touchdowns through four games isn't something I can just ignore, especially after he threw for 329 yards and two touchdowns against Detroit.
And it's not just DraftKings that has started looking at Carolina differently. ESPN's Football Power Index gives the Panthers a 48% chance to win the NFC South, with Atlanta next at 31%.
That's where I started looking at this a little differently myself. One sportsbook moving Carolina after a Sunday night win is one thing. When you start seeing numbers like that in other places, maybe there's actually something here.
Here's what keeps stopping me from going all the way with this. I've changed my mind about the Panthers about three times already, and somehow we're only four games into the season.
They were awful against Chicago. Then they went to Atlanta and won 34-3, and I started thinking maybe Week 1 was just one of those games. Then Carolina lost at Cleveland, and I was right back to wondering what this team was.
So, of course, the Panthers turned around and beat Detroit in a game I picked them to lose.
That's been this season so far. Every time I think I've figured Carolina out, they give me something else to think about.
There are still things I don't trust. The defense has had its moments, but Jared Goff just threw for 412 yards against this secondary. The injuries have also gotten ridiculous, and we don't know exactly who Carolina is getting back after the bye.
But maybe I've been holding that Chicago game against them too much. Since then, Carolina has won two of three, nearly won the Cleveland game, and already has a road win over Atlanta. If this division is still close later in the season, that Atlanta win could end up meaning a whole lot.
Now the Panthers get the bye, and I don't think anybody in that building is complaining about having it this early anymore. After that, we'll get Philadelphia, Tampa Bay, and Green Bay. Ask me what I think about Carolina's chances after those three, and I might have a much better answer.
I'm still not ready to say the Panthers are definitely winning the NFC South. There's too much football left, and this team has already fooled me more than once.
After Week 1, I would've thought that was crazy.
I'm not laughing at it anymore.

title: Bryce Young Just Revealed What's Really Changed for Him in Carolina
full_text:
I've been trying to figure out what's different about Bryce Young this season. I know part of the answer is pretty simple. He's in his fourth year, he's gotten better, and we're finally starting to see some of the things Carolina thought it was getting when it drafted him No. 1 overall.
But I don't think that's all of it.
Young has thrown for 1,268 yards and nine touchdowns through four games, including 329 yards and two touchdowns against Detroit. As good as those numbers are, it's the way he's playing that has stood out to me. He looks comfortable, and I don't know how many times I could've said that during his first few years in Carolina.
Then I listened to Young's interview with Pat McAfee this week, and something he said about offensive coordinator Brad Idzik got my attention.
“He wants my input. He wants all of our input,” Young said.
The more Young talked about Idzik, the more I started wondering if we've been overlooking something pretty important.
Idzik isn't some new coach who came in this year and changed everything. He's been around Young for three years and has already had a big hand in the offense behind the scenes. What's different now is that Dave Canales handed Idzik the play-calling duties.
I think that matters because of the way Young described their relationship. He said they spend the week talking about the game plan, what he likes, and what he feels comfortable with. If Young wants something added or doesn't like something they're working on, they talk about it before Sunday.
Maybe I'm making this too simple, but that sounds like a pretty good way to make your quarterback comfortable.
We've spent years talking about everything Young needed to do better. Get the ball out quicker. Be more aggressive. Handle pressure better. Push the ball downfield. Some of that was absolutely fair, especially for a quarterback Carolina took with the first pick in the draft.
But maybe the Panthers had some figuring out to do, too.
Young said before the season that he had “all the confidence in the world in Brad.” He also called Idzik a big reason for what the offense had already built. I probably wouldn't have thought much about those comments in August, because what else is a quarterback going to say about his offensive coordinator?
Four games into the season, I'm paying a little more attention to them.
This was the part of Young's interview that really got me.
McAfee asked how much information Young wants from his play-caller once he's on the field. I figured Young would talk about wanting as much information as possible before the headset cuts off, but his answer was about as simple as it gets.
“Just give me the play,” Young said.
At first, I kind of laughed at it. Then Young explained why, and it made a lot of sense.
He and Idzik have already talked through everything during the week. Young knows why certain plays are being called and what Idzik is looking for in different situations. Maybe it's third-and-1, and Carolina knows it could go for it on fourth down, or maybe they absolutely need to pick up the first down right there.
Young also talked about knowing when Idzik wants to speed things up or slow them down. Those aren't conversations you can have while the play clock is ticking, and that's where the work they do during the week comes in.
By the time Sunday gets here, Young doesn't need all of that explained again. Idzik gives him the play, and Young already knows what he's looking for.
I don't know if freedom is the right word for it. Trust probably makes more sense.
I'm definitely not saying Idzik took over the play-calling and magically fixed Young. That's not fair to Young, and I don't think it's really what we're seeing anyway.
Young deserves a lot of the credit for this. He's in Year 4 now, and he's been through more than most young quarterbacks have to deal with. There have been coaching changes, bad offensive line play, injuries around him, and even a benching along the way.
The rest of the offense matters, too. Tetairoa McMillan has given Young a legitimate weapon, Chuba Hubbard just ran for 122 yards against Detroit, and Carolina has somehow kept things together up front despite all the injuries. There isn't one thing you can point to and say that's why Young is playing better.
But I keep going back to what Young said about Idzik.
For most of his career, the conversation has been about what Young needed to change. What if Carolina finally figured out that it needed to listen to him a little more, too?
Maybe that's why Young looks so comfortable right now. He has a play-caller who wants to know what he likes, spends the week making sure they're seeing things the same way, and then doesn't try to overload him once the game starts.
I'm not giving Brad Idzik all the credit for what we're seeing from Bryce Young.
But I'm starting to think he deserves a whole lot more than we've been giving him.

title: Bryce Young’s Impressive Start Earns Much-Deserved Praise
full_text:
The brief professional history of the Carolina Panthers’ current starting quarterback has been well-documented. Bryce Young was the first overall pick in the 2023 NFL draft. He suffered through a miserable rookie campaign in which he totaled more turnovers (16) than touchdown passes (11) and was sacked 62 times in 16 games.
Enter new Panthers’ head coach Dave Canales in 2024. After two weeks and a pair of rough outings, the former offensive coordinator of the Tampa Bay Buccaneers benched Young. He would eventually return, started Carolina’s final 10 games and showed that the time off was a bit beneficial.
This past season proved to be somewhat of a breakthrough year for the young quarterback, but it certainly was not without its flaws. Young threw for a career-high 3,011 yards, and his 23 TD passes were also a personal best. However, he did show a knack for late-game heroics.
Still, there were also 15 turnovers in 16 regular-season outings. Young was picked off in the first quarter of the Panthers’ playoff loss to the Rams, but finished the game with 264 yards through the air and one score, plus rushed for a touchdown.
Now it is 2026 and after four games, the reigning NFC South champions own a 2-2 record are coming off an impressive 32-26 prime time triumph over the visiting Detroit Lions. They are tied with the Atlanta Falcons for the best record in the division. Canales’s club is off this week.
🚨 Bryce Young went from being benched in 2024 to leading his team and making ELITE throws like these. He’s getting PAID this offseason. pic.twitter.com/l5C3K1WRgj
NFL writer Mike Jones of The Athletic came up with his “quarter-season superlatives” for the 2026 season. When it came to a player or a team making what he referred to as the “biggest leap,” he singled out Carolina’s rising signal-caller.
“After a rocky first two seasons, Bryce Young displayed promise down the stretch of last season and helped Carolina end its playoff drought. He ranked No. 21 in passing (3,011 yards) and No. 27 in passer rating (87.8), but comfort in coach Dave Canales’s offense has translated into strong results this season.”
It’s been quite the start for the 25-year-old performer. He leads the NFL with 1,268 yards through the air, and currently ranks 10th in the league in passer rating (100.0). Young has hit on 62.3 percent of his throws, connecting for nine scores compared to only two interceptions. He has not fumbled this season, despite being sacked 10 times, and does have one rushing touchdown.
Josh Sweat unblocked gotta be terrifying for Bryce Young pic.twitter.com/lcFhewvdwy
For comparison, let’s take a look at how the 2025 season started out for the 2021 Heisman Trophy winner. The team lost its first two games and actually got off to a 1-3 start. Young was connecting on just 60.4 of his attempts for only 753 yards. There were 5 touchdown passes, three interceptions, and a pair of lost fumbles (1 retuned for a touchdown). He was sacked just six times, and his 77.1 passer rating ranked a dismal 27th in the league.
Talk about improvement? Instead of leap, it’s more like leaps and bounds for the Panthers’ quarterback. He and his teammates return to action on October 18. It will be fascinating to see if Canales’s club can build off that impressive win over the Lions, and Young can pick up where he left off after a strong four-game performance.

title: Khalil Mack to Bears Trade Buzz Picks Up Steam Thanks to NFL Insider's Report
full_text:
There is nothing Chicago Bears fans would love more than a reunion between the team and edge rusher Khalil Mack.
Of course, the Bears acquired Mack in a blockbuster trade with the Raiders in 2018 and he became a fan-favorite over four seasons before Chicago traded him to the Los Angeles Chargers .
But with the Chargers at 0-4 and going nowhere, and with the Bears possibly in the market for an edge rusher, many have wondered if a reunion could be in the cards .
And that thought is now picking up steam thanks to an NFL insider.
According to The Athletic's Jonathan Jones , sources he talks to around the NFL believe Mack to the Bears "makes the most sense."
"I mentioned several names in last week’s column as potential trade candidates," he stated. "Again, it is still early, and I always caution against matching any player to any particular team a month before the deadline."
"But Khalil Mack to Chicago is something multiple league sources told me makes the most sense if both teams continue on their respective trajectories," Jones added.
Jones goes on to note that the belief is Mack could cost as little as a fifth-round pick. Sign us up.
With the Chargers sitting at 0-4, they are up against it when it comes to their chances of making the postseason, as only the 1992 San Diego Chargers have done so after an 0-4 start.
If things don't turn around by the Nov. 10 deadline, Los Angeles could (and should) be a seller and there is no more prime trade candidate than Mack.
The 35-year-old has already said he has contemplated retirement before, and it's likely his chances of calling it quits have increased since then. Knowing that he could ride off into the sunset for nothing in 2027, the Chargers would be wise to move him if postseason play isn't in their future.
If Mack wants to be moved and his top choice is the Bears, we can see the Chargers obliging his request out of respect for the future Hall of Famer.
When Mack was traded, it's wasn't because he wanted to leave. Instead, the Bears were in the midst of a rebuild and wanted to pick up some draft capital. Mack wanted to stay in Chicago and called the trade "bittersweet" at the time.
Based on comments he made on the "Bussin' With The Boys" podcast last month, it's clear Mack views his time in Chicago fondly.
“Looking back on it, you realize how important those moments are,” he said of his time with the Bears . “You definitely shouldn’t take those moments, and those teams that you got (for granted). That (2018) defense we had was very special… Just having everybody all at once, at the same time, playing at the level we were playing at, and having those creative minds behind us — it was a special time.”
If the Bears continue looking like the contender they have looked like over the first four games, that would only increase the likelihood that Mack would be interested in a reunion.
Chicago's edge rushers room has been a pleasant surprise over the first four games of the season, with Dayo Odeyingbo, Austin Booker and Montez Sweat posting seven of the team's 10 sacks.
The spotlight was extra bright on Odeyingbo and Booker before the start of the season because they were unknowns, but both have answered the bell thus far .
That leaves the Bears in a good spot where they aren't desperate, but we know things can change on a dime, and especially in the lead up to the trade deadline, which is a month away.
The truth is, the Bears should not be content at any position and should continue to look for help everywhere, including at one of the most important spots on defense at edge rusher.
And that's especially true given the fact that Odeyingbo has been playing a lot of snaps inside, which gives the Bears a slightly elevated need for more depth along the edge.
Mack would be just what the doctor ordered there. The veteran is still an impact player, as evidenced by his three sacks in four games, and we know about his leadership, also.
If Mack is available at the trade deadline, the Bears bringing him back is the very definition of a no-brainer move, especially with the belief Mack will only cost a fifth-round pick.

title: Bears OT Theo Benedet Can Earn His Place or Fall on His Face Against Packers
full_text:
The Chicago Bears have a healthy offensive line for their Week 5 matchup at Lambeau Field against the Green Bay Packers, with Joe Thuney, Darnell Wright, and Jonah Jackson all avoiding the Week 5 injury report.
Well, healthy among the active players.
Left tackles Braxton Jones and Ozzy Trapilo are on the IR. Trapilo has been out all season, while Jones is week-to-week after a right knee injury suffered against the Philadelphia Eagles during a Week 3 Bears win.
Theo Benedet is the next man up, and was last week during Chicago's 23-12 win over the New York Jets as well.
Green Bay is a weight class up from New York in Week 4. While Benedet graded out well versus the Jets against the run (77.4 via PFF), he struggled against the pass rush and finished with a far-below average pass-protection grade (55.2).
That is not the statistical alignment you want against the Packers' defense.
Benedet will be stuck with Packers edge-rushers Lukas Van Ness and Rashan Gary for a good number of snaps on Sunday afternoon.
That could be a very problematic assignment for the undrafted Canadian.
The two have 5.5 sacks this season, while Van Ness had 1.5 sacks and four quarterback hits by himself during a win against the Jets in Week 2.
Green Bay doesn't rank particularly well in Team Pass Rush Win Rate (No. 19), but the Packers are able to convert pressures into sacks. Green Bay has 10 sacks, tied for No. 8 in the NFL.
The Packers are a much better team defending the pass than the run, but the Bears are missing running back Kyle Monangai and could have a far-less-than-100% D'Andre Swift splitting carries with Roschon Johnson.
Tyson Bagent will need a reliable blindside to get the passing game going if the running game isn't producing.
Benedet will almost certainly have his hands full, even if he's able to be that.
Benedet is on the final season as an Exclusive Rights Free Agent after three straight one-year deals in Chicago.
His next step is either a restricted free agency with competitive offers or an uncertain future away from the Bears as an unrestricted free agent.
Games like this could decide his fate.
If Benedet holds his own, the team will feel confident with him on the left side and not rush Jones or Trapilo back. If he is a liability in protection at all, he could see his immediate and future opportunities vanish.
Sunday is the biggest test of Benedet's career. He can either help further Chicago's NFC North divisional crown hopes or set them back behind the Pack and tied for last place in the division, assuming the Detroit Lions dispatch of the Arizona Cardinals as expected.
Earn his place or fall on his face. We'll see what path Benedet takes.

title: Ben Johnson Acknowledges the Lasting Bears Legacy Set by Mike Ditka
full_text:
The new coach paid his respects to Da Coach on Friday at Halas Hall.
Ben Johnson is easily the most popular Bears coach since the late Mike Ditka, who has passed away at age 86. Ditka's record is a bar even for Johnson to take aim at so many years later.
"I just want to start off extending my condolences to the Ditka family," Johnson said. "Sad news here this morning, obviously. As far as I'm concerned, coach Ditka is a gold standard in terms of this place. I mean, he's a legend around here as a player, as a coach. His impact is still being felt to this day. And as the head coach of the Bears I feel humbled to be in that same chair that he was once in.
"It's a sad day to hear that he's passed on. He's in our thoughts and prayers."
The NFL is deeply saddened by the passing of Hall of Fame coach and tight end, Mike Ditka. Our thoughts are with his family and loved ones. ❤️ pic.twitter.com/H9cMGPc8ln
Johnson is the ninth Bears head coach since Ditka, counting interim coach Thomas Brown in 2024. Johnson said he never had the opportunity to meet Ditka but the ways his presence is still felt at Halas Hall is as obvious as the trophy case in the main entrance to Halas Hall, housing the only Lombardi Trophy the franchise has ever won.
"Well, I mean, certainly his picture is all over the place," Johnson said. "I don’t know if there’s been a head coach with that much — other than, obviously, George Halas — but that much success just for, I think it was 11 years, and the number of winning seasons, the win/loss record, obviously a Super Bowl winner.
Mike Ditka, taking Bears fans to task after a game they won: “Wanna see fans? Get on a bus and drive to CLEVELAND. I’ll show you some fans. They start when you are warming up, they start when they break the pop bottles open gang.” RIP Legend pic.twitter.com/XOZRqNmaGs
"As a head coach, it’s been hard to replicate that since his time, certainly as a player as well. It means a lot to the McCaskey family. I don’t want to put words in their mouths but he’s one of those big names when you walk into the player entrance, he’s one of those big names for a reason."
Ditka was fired after 11 seasons, seven of those with winning records/playoff berths.
. @JBigCatWilliams recalls the "most nervous" he ever was in his NFL career. It involved him, Richard Dent and Steve McMichael going out drinking after curfew in Platteville. Williams went to the bar to pay for the beer pitchers and the bartender said the tab was picked up… pic.twitter.com/NS1yqJSVbr
He won six division titles and a Super Bowl in putting together a 106-62 record (.631). In the 34 seasons since they fired him, the Bears are 242-283 (.461) with six division titles and two more wild card playoff berths.
Ditka's teams won six postseason games, three in their Super Bowl year and one each in 1984, 1988 and 1990. Since his 1993 firing, the Bears have won five postseason games total.

title: Three Factors That Will Decide Bears Week 5 Matchup Against Green Bay
full_text:
One of the league's most storied rivalries will be on display when the Bears travel to Lambeau Field to take on their rivals to the north on Sunday.
Even without Caleb Williams in the lineup, both teams seem to be going in opposite directions. Ben Johnson's Chicago Bears are humming on both sides of the ball. They sit at 3-1 and have won with two different backup QBs under center over the past two weeks.
Tyson Bagent will start against Green Bay , and he'll be eager to build on last week's performance, where he completed 25 of 34 attempts for 268 yards in the Bears' 23-12 win over the Jets.
Meanwhile, the Packers will try to fend off speculation about their demise after stumbling out of the gates. They're currently 2-2, but they barely survived in their two victories and were blown out in their two losses. It's been a disappointing season for Green Bay faithful thus far.
According to DraftKings Sportsbook , the Bears are 2.5-point favorites heading into the divisional clash. The vast majority of the experts are also putting their chips in on them .
Sunday's contest marks the first time in 20 years that the Bears are favored on the Packers' home turf. That game went extremely well for Chicago , and they'll be eager to repeat history.
What will they need to accomplish in order to get that done?
The Packers' defense looked formidable in every category for much of last season. However, they haven't been the same ever since edge rusher Micah Parsons tore his ACL in the team's Week 15 matchup against Denver. He's the engine that makes that defense go, and they've been stuck in neutral (or, more specifically, reverse) without him.
Green Bay has given up the fifth-most rushing yards (139.3 yards per game) over the first month of the season. The Falcons ran them over for 242 yards in their Week 3 clash. The Bears will try to recreate that blueprint on Sunday, and it should be easier after linebacker Edgerrin Cooper ruptured his Achilles tendon last week.
Bagent stood in the pocket and made some strong throws all over the field against the Jets. Aside from the turnover-worthy plays, it was an impressive performance in his first regular-season action in more than three years. He would still greatly benefit from a strong running game, though. They don't want to put the game on his shoulders.
Unfortunately, Kyle Monangai will be sidelined with a turf toe injury . They'll be depending on D'Andre Swift and Roshon Johnson (and potentially Salvon Ahmed being called up from the practice squad) to carry the load. If they can run the ball efficiently, Bagent should reap the benefits in the play-action game.
While the sky over Green Bay has seemingly been falling to begin this season, they have gotten some positive returns from their pass-catching unit.
Christian Watson is on pace for a 1,400-yard campaign and has scored a touchdown in three of four games. Matthew Golden appears to have shed the bust label, as he's on pace for over 1,100 yards and has two receiving TDs of his own. Tucker Kraft might not have picked up where he left off last season, but he's also one of the league's top young tight ends.
The Bears have done a great job holding their opponents in check on defense through the first month of the season. They have given up the third-fewest passing yards in the league (179.8 yards per game).
The Packers have a potent collection of weapons, though. This will undoubtedly be Chicago's toughest test thus far. Chicago's pass defense will need to bring their A-game to avoid a potential shootout.
The Packers' makeshift offensive line has been one of the league's most susceptible units. They added three veterans to the line (Kevin Zeitler, Laken Tomlinson, and Mekhi Becton) after their Week 3 blowout loss against Atlanta, but they didn't have much more success up front against the Buccaneers last week.
Quarterback Jordan Love has only been sacked eight times, but he's been under constant duress. The struggles up front have led him to complete only 56.5% of his passes through the first four games.
Meanwhile, the Bears have done a great job of getting consistent pressure on opposing QBs. If they can continue that trend on Sunday, then they should come out with a win in the unfriendly confines of Lambeau Field.

title: How Bears Injuries Alter Ben Johnson's Gameplan Against Packers
full_text:
Chicago Bears head coach Ben Johnson has been able to navigate through the early timeline without starting quarterback Caleb Williams, following his hamstring injury in Week 2 , to win two straight over the Philadelphia Eagles and New York Jets.
Johnson is going to be tested in an even bigger way this Sunday against the Green Bay Packers, though, with Kyle Monangai officially ruled out with toe and thumb injuries and D'Andre Swift being way less than 100% if he even suits up with a hip issue.
Schematically, it would've been nice for Johnson to have his primary rushing duo against a Packers defense that is more vulnerable to the run.
Green Bay's defense owns a 139.2 yards per game average through four games, good for a No. 28 rank league-wide.
The Packers are much better against the pass, allowing just 185 passing yards per game. That's good for the No. 4 rank in the league through the first month.
Tyson Bagent may have to rise up and play an even bigger role this week to lead the Bears to victory in a key divisional/rivalry matchup.
Roschon Johnson could be due for a major workload if Swift isn't up for it, with a practice squad running back potentially needing to string the offense along as well.
That combination may put Bagent under the gun. If the run game isn't a strength like it typically is, he may have to do more than game-manage.
Bagent was bailed out by penalties a week ago against the Jets, having three interceptions called back. One pick he threw actually did stand.
That level of play against this Green Bay squad may not be salvaged the same way.
While Bagent had turnover issues that stopped short of being anything more than theoretical, he was still able to keep the offense on schedule and throw for 268 yards. Bagent is proving he could be a serviceable backup during the weeks Williams isn't healthy.
This opportunity against the Packers could lift Bagent to notoriety as a potential starter somewhere ahead of the trade deadline. A dud could do the opposite.
Johnson's coaching chops will be put to the test versus a rival he has been successful against more often than not, and in major-stakes games to boot.
Luckily, he's been in similar situations before, lacking his top two backs as a play-caller a few seasons back.
With the Detroit Lions in 2023, Johnson leaned on reserve Craig Reynolds after injuries to Jahmyr Gibbs and David Montgomery to nab wins over the Carolina Panthers and Tampa Bay Buccaneers in consecutive weeks.
Doing something similar against Green Bay with Roschon Johnson playing the Reynolds role would only further convince Bears fans that they have the right guy leading the franchise on the field.
A loss would simply maintain the status quo. There are luckily more chances for Chicago to embarrass the Pack this Sunday than vice versa.
Still, the NFC North has been extremely competitive in 2026, so a win would only increase the odds of a bye week this postseason.

title: Salvon Ahmed May Be Due For Big Bears Opportunity With Kyle Monangai Ruled Out
full_text:
The Chicago Bears have ruled running back Kyle Monangai out for their Week 5 matchup with the Green Bay Packers at Lambeau Field. The news of the team's 324-yard leader creates intriguing opportunities all over the running back room.
Bears head coach Ben Johnson shared uncertainty about how long Monangai will remain out. Reports peg Monangai as a potential several-week absence from Chicago's offense. He's been seen in a walking boot.
"Bears RB Kyle Monangai is dealing with a turf toe injury, placing uncertainty around his availability over the next 1-2 weeks, per sources, though he’s hoping to play through it and the team/player are still managing the situation," ESPN's Jeremy Fowler said.
Roschon Johnson could be due for significant reps against Green Bay with the Monangai injury news. No one stands to gain the most in terms of raw carries and breakout potential than Johnson. Injuries held Johnson back in 2025, but he could greatly benefit for one or more on Sunday afternoon.
Whether D'Andre Swift's hip and knee injuries hold him back from being a factor during the NFC North Divisional clash is another major question. Johnson said Swift "should" be able to go, but how durable he'll be remains a mystery.
That might open up the possibility of a practice squad gameday elevation for running back Salvon Ahmed to serve as a depth piece behind Swift and/or Johnson against the Packers.
Zavier Scott, the other option, has spent less time with the organization and doesn't have the built-in advantages Ahmed does.
Ahmed hasn't gotten an NFL regular season snap since 2023. Ahmed was a member of the Miami Dolphins and averaged 2.8 yards per carry on 22 carries that year. He was able to find the end zone once.
Ahmed spoke to fulfilling his purpose on the Bears after Chicago's 34-10 win over the Cleveland Browns in the preseason.
"It’s just God’s favor and God’s blessings. Coming out here, I just want to progress every single day. That was just the first game, we’ve got a lot more to go. I’m just happy to be here and I just want to fulfill my purpose for myself and this team," Ahmed said after a two-carry, 17-yard performance.
Now, Ahmed could have the chance to fulfill his purpose of being an emergency body who stayed ready for this chance.
After two seasons on the Indianapolis Colts' practice squad and on the IR, Ahmed's chance could be transformational to his career.
Ahmed has spoken to the connection he has with Bears running backs coach Eric Studesville, who was with Ahmed in Miami Gardens during his most productive professional campaigns.
Specifically, Ahmed spoke to the confidence Studesville has helped instill in him.
"I spent a big portion of my career with [Bears running backs coach], so just being out here with him, he gives me a lot of confidence," Ahmed said.
That familiarity is an ace in the hole for Ahmed to get any potential leftover backup opportunities over Scott in Week 5.
Whether or not that translates to a substantial role on Sunday, or an eventual promotion off the PS, with possibly two backs ahead of him in the pecking order still remains to be seen.
Ahmed is in a better position than he's been, though, with Monangai ruled out.

title: Caleb Williams, D'Andre Swift Progress and More From Bears' Final Week 5 Injury Report
full_text:
Big news coming out of the Chicago Bears final injury report of the week, as quarterback Caleb Williams has made some progress in his return from a hamstring injury.
But first, the bad news: it was revealed earlier in the day that Kyle Monangai has been ruled out with his toe and thumb injuries, with the toe injury being the bigger concern currently.
For some good news, D'Andre Swift is off the injury report entirely, so Chicago will have the services of one of their two top backs.
Now, a look at the full injury report and more from Friday.
Williams was able to log a limited practice Friday, which amounts to the first practice participation he's had since his hamstring injury in Week 2 .
Not only that, he is officially listed as questionable to play, so there's a chance he could go, although we're very skeptical Chicago will send him out there off one limited practice.
If not, this at least opens the door for Williams to make it back in Week 6. Head coach Ben Johnson detailed some of the progress Williams has made recently.
"We got him progressively increasing the amount of running that's going on, and of course the throwing aspect of it is a big part of his position as well," Johnson explained . "Our guys have a good plan in place and we're just going step by step with that right now."
Along with Williams, the three PUP guys, Kyler Gordon, Shemar Turner and Noah Sewell, are all questionable after finishing the week off with full practices.
Johnson said it is "highly likely one of the PUP players would be activated this week, but didn't say who, according to ESPN's Courtney Cronin .
As for Swift, he turned in a full practice to end the week and does not have a designation, so he's good to go. Swift should see an increased workload with Monangai sidelined, and we'll also be seeing some Roschon Johnson and maybe Salvon Ahmed.
Monangai is sporting a walking boot due to his turf toe injury, and ESPN's Courtney Cronin labeled him as week-to-week.
The good news is, Monangai is not considered a candidate to go on injured reserve, so that means the Bears don't expect more than a two or three week absence.

title: Mike Ditka Feuded With Players, Fans and Rivals, and Chicago Loved Da Coach for All of It
full_text:
George Halas was the founder and coach of the Bears, but Mike Ditka was a real Bear.
The colorful coach and Chicago tight end who embodied the toughness and gritty attitude for which the franchise became known, died at the age of 86 on Friday.
Perhaps it is ironic and fitting that Ditka would pass away only days before the Bears renew their rivalry against their biggest rival, the Green Bay Packers, a team Ditka loved to beat. The exact same scenario happened when the franchise's best player, Walter Payton, died in 1999.
Da Coach, as he became known to all, played for the team as a Hall of Fame tight end from 1961-66 under Halas, then led them to their only Super Bowl after returning to Chicago following a stint as a Cowboys assistant coach under Tom Landry. Ditka was fired by team president Michael McCaskey in January of 1993 after a run that included a record of 106-62, NFC Central championships in 1984, '85, '86, '87, '88, '90 and another playoff berth in 1991 as a wild card. Of course, this included the fabled 1985 run to Super Bowl XX, when the Bears went 18-1 and crushed New England 46-10 for the title.
Just an absolute legend. Video via @SixPointSports pic.twitter.com/fKiYBnrtFw
Ditka's return to the team he played for as head coach in 1982 was controversial, as defensive coordinator Buddy Ryan had been the coach many players supported for the job. But Halas kept Ryan on under Ditka at the players' urging and a real tension ensued between the two throughout the four seasons they were together. Although, after both retired and had been out of the game the respect they had for each other was also made known.
Ditka was Da Coach from the moment he walked in the door.
"Give me three years, and if you walk with me, we'll get to the dance," Ditka was said to have promised players when he arrived. He also told them at the same time most of them would not be with the team when they would win the Super Bowl.
Mike Ditka End Around in the Super Bowl🎯 pic.twitter.com/AznMFjwiSy
Ditka made good on his pledge after restoring discipline and the work ethic required. At the same time, he brought along an ego and it rubbed plenty the wrong way. He feuded with the media, and often his own players. Sometimes it was good-natured, other times not so much. He hollered at Packers fans during a press conference, threw a big wad of gum at 49ers fans, and was loved by Bears fans. His argument with "Neal of Northlake" on WSCR was played regularly over and over in Chicago for years.
Maybe Ditka's best quote ever about his relationship with anyone was about eccentric quarterback Jim McMahon, who he always seemed at odds with but whose skillset was essential.
There won't be another Ditka - he was the main event on an 85 Bears team full of charismatic personalities. You got the feeling that he meant everything he said - even directed at fans calling into coach's radio show! Rest easy to an NFL legend. pic.twitter.com/r46i9ca8St
"We have a strange and wonderful relationship," Ditka once said. "He's strange and I'm wonderful."
Ditka was born in Carnegie, Pennsylvania, on Oct. 18, 1939, as Michael Keller Dyczko, and the family later changed their name to Ditka. As he grew up in Aliquippa, Pa., a hotbed of football, Ditka stood out in several sports, went to Pitt and played two ways as an end and defensive end. He basically pioneered the position of tight end with the Bears as Halas loved his blocking and receiving ability and wanted to see both utilized with flanker Johnny Morris' receiving skills. Ditka made the Pro Bowl five straight years to start his career, caught 56 passes for 1,076 yards and 12 touchdowns as a rookie and helped lead them to the 1963 NFL championship.
RIP Coach Ditka. Legend. Straight shooter—he set the standard for truth in press conferences. If you asked a dumb question, it was coming back at you hard. As a Chicagoan these moments are seared in my brain. pic.twitter.com/0ietUkBck5
They traded him to Philadelphia after a dispute over money and production. He famously said Halas "threw nickels around like manhole covers." And at that point in his career he has admitted he had a drinking problem, as well. Ditka later played for the Cowboys in a Super Bowl. He finished with 427 catches for 5,812 yards and 43 TDs. He won a Super Bowl ring with Dallas in the 1971 season and played in another in the 1970 season.
When Halas brought Ditka back to Chicago, he handled such a wide array of personalities that his job almost seemed more like a warden than a coach. Ditka's view of Walter Payton, though, was a bit above the rest and he considered Payton a special talent.
"When God said he would make a halfback or fullback, he might have said Gale Sayers or he might have said Jim Brown," Ditka said of Payton. "But when he said he would make the best football player who ever lived, he probably said two men: Jim Thorpe and Walter Payton."
Much of the talk leading up to Super Bowl XX was about @JimMcMahon rear end. When a 🚁 was buzzing the practice field he “let ‘em know where it hurt” 🌙😂 pic.twitter.com/x7mpQVCZzx
Ditka was known as "Iron Mike," for good reason, and not all of it because of his powerful playing style. He coached them to a win a little over a week after he had a heart attack in 1988.
He often was accused of bullying other teams, coaches and even some of his own players in a sport where it was not necessarily a negative. He had a running feud with Packers coach Forrest Gregg from the time Gregg arrived as coach in 1984. Gregg was actually a former Cowboys teammate of his.
There was always something a little heartwarming about the gentle way Mike Ditka imparted life wisdom to his players ... pic.twitter.com/5WRrd1Gs44
Ditka went 7-1 against Gregg's Packers, including one of his great tactical moves: The birth of William "The Refrigerator" Perry.
The 300-pound defensive lineman wasn't getting played much by Ryan, who rarely found use for any rookie. So Ditka, angered that 49ers coach Bill Walsh had used a guard as fullback against the Bears in the 1984 NFC championship game, decided to do the same with Perry in 1985 at the end of the Bears' convincing 26-10 win at San Francisco. The next week, he took his feud with Gregg to another level and unleashed the Fridge as a ball carrier against the Packers in a 23-7 win and later as a receiver in Green Bay for a TD catch in a 16-10 win. Finally, he had Perry carry for a TD in the Super Bowl, but Payton didn't get to score a TD after a long career of servitude as the only shining light for plenty of losing Bears teams. Ditka later admitted he made a big mistake there.
"I didn't even think of it," he said about getting Payton a TD.
Rest in peace to a Pittsburgh legend. Mike Ditka and Will Ferrell in kicking and screaming will always  be the best #mikeditka pic.twitter.com/wvtQnHtVyT
The moody Ditka was the ideal person to coach a group of divergent personalities because of his own personality. McMahon once nicknamed him Sybil, after a book about a woman with multiple personality traits.
“It was more than a team,” Ditka said about his Bears. “It was a team of characters that had character that played for a crazy man, who let him be crazy and had fun doing it and don’t apologize for it ever."
After his firing in Chicago, Ditka went into media and then took over as Saints coach. There, he inherited a terrible franchise and helped make it worse by trading away his entire draft class for running back Ricky Williams.   Ditka had been 106-62 as Bears coach but with the Saints he was 15-33 and lasted three seasons until Tom Benson fired him.
Ditka used his celebrity status well after football, going into movies, television and also sportscasting. He was a longtime contributor on ESPN's pregame.
The Bears honored Ditka by retiring his jersey No. 89 in 2013. He is survived by his wife Diana and their children, Mark, Matt, Mike and Megan.

title: Mike Ditka's Greatest Bears Victories as Player and Coach Go Well Beyond Super Bowl XX
full_text:
The NFL world lost a legend Friday. Former head coach of the Chicago Bears and winner of Super Bowl XX Mike Ditka died at the age of 86 , according to a statement from his family.
Ditka was a larger-than-life figure with a personality that could fill Soldier Field on its own. Even to this day, over 40 years since he delivered Chicago its first and only Super Bowl title, hundreds of fans dress up like him on game day. His iconic sweater vest, aviator sunglasses and epic mustache are seen everywhere at Soldier Field on Sundays, and I don't doubt that we'll continue to see these lookalikes for many more decades to come.
Even among a franchise as storied as the Chicago Bears, a team that dates back to the very start of the NFL and has featured some of the all-time greatest players and coaches, Ditka stands out as a true legend of the game, and not just for his Super Bowl triumph. As we remember an all-time great player, head coach, and person, let's relive a few of Ditka's greatest victories.
The story of the NFL simply cannot be told without Ditka, who displayed greatness from the very beginning of his career. In 1961, Ditka set an NFL record for the most receiving yards (1,076) in a season by a rookie tight end, a record that stood for 63 years until Brock Bowers broke it in 2024 . An asterisk is needed, however, since Ditka did it in 14 games rather than 17 like Bowers.
Additionally, Ditka caught 12 touchdown passes in his rookie season, and that record still stands to this day. Sam LaPorta and Rob Gronkowski are tied for second place with 10 touchdowns in their rookie seasons, 2023 and 2010, respectively. Again it must be noted that Ditka did this in only 14 games.
While Ditka's career as head coach of the Bears didn't start well, he brought the team back to relevancy in just his third season by picking up the Bears' first playoff win of the Super Bowl era. In the divisional round of the 1984 NFL playoffs, the Bears defeated the defending NFC champions, the Washington Redskins, at RFK Stadium. Ditka's team took a 10-3 lead into halftime and turned it into a 16-3 lead on the second play of the third quarter. Washington did trim the lead to six, but they couldn't complete the comeback.
For the Bears fans who weren't alive to witness that game, they got a taste of how important that win was to the franchise after watching the Bears' miraculous wild-card win over the Green Bay Packers last season. That win ended a drought of 15 years without a playoff win, and it came in dramatic fashion, to boot.
While the Bears' 1985 season is best remembered for their 46-10 shellacking of the New England Patriots in Super Bowl XX, it was their previous game that was potentially even more impressive. Facing the Los Angeles Rams in the NFC Championship , the Bears won 24-0, holding Rams quarterback Dieter Brock to just 10 completions on 31 pass attempts. Even more impressive, they held future Hall of Fame running back Eric Dickerson to only 46 rushing yards on 17 carries.
Holding any NFL team to zero points is an incredible feat. Doing it in back-to-back games, in the playoffs against very good teams, no less, is the stuff of legends. And that's exactly who Mike Ditka was.
Going back to 1957, when the AP NFL Coach of the Year award was first created, only 14 coaches have won it more than once, and Ditka joined this exclusive club in 1988. Ditka led the Bears to a 12-4 record that year, their fifth straight NFC Central division championship, and he did it all despite suffering a heart attack during the season.
The Bears' season that year ended with a brutal 28-3 loss in the NFC Championship game to the eventual Super Bowl champion San Francisco 49ers. However, that did not diminish Ditka's great accomplishments that season, and he earned his second AP NFL Coach of the Year award, just three years after winning his first one.

title: Kyle Monangai Injury Update From Ben Johnson Confirms Bears RB's Week 5 Status
full_text:
We have been monitoring the status of Chicago Bears running back Kyle Monangai all week.
Monangai was on the injury report to begin the week with toe and thumb issues and did not practice on Wednesday or Thursday .
Head coach Ben Johnson initially said there was no concern about Monangai's thumb , but at the time we didn't know the running back had a toe issue, also.
On Friday before practice, Johnson revealed that Monangai will not play in Week 5 against the Green Bay Packers, according to Sean Hammond of The Chicago Tribune , who added that Monangai is wearing a walking boot.
"We'll see how long that injury sidelines him," Johnson said.
It was reported on Thursday that Monangai is dealing with a turf toe that has the potential to sideline him multiple weeks.
"Bears RB Kyle Monangai is dealing with a turf toe injury, placing uncertainty around his availability over the next 1-2 weeks, per sources, though he’s hoping to play through it and the team/player are still managing the situation," ESPN's Jeremy Fowler said.
ESPN's Courtney Cronin confirmed Monangai's week-to-week status but said he is not a candidate for injured reserve, so the expectation is he won't be out longer than three weeks.
Monangai isn't the only injury concern the Bears have at running back, as D'Andre Swift is dealing with hip and knee injuries . However, Swift did get back to practice on Thursday after no participation Wednesday, so he's trending in the right direction.
NFL Network's Ian Rapoport reported that Swift is expected to play, so that's good news for Chicago's ailing backfield.
"D'Andre Swift, good news here, did return to practice yesterday. He's dealing with a hip injury and a knee injury that has been lingering. The belief is that he should be able to go."
With Monangai ruled out, Roschon Johnson will be the next man up to get some of his carries. We'd also expect Swift to get more work for Chicago on top of his typical workload.
The Bears will have to call someone up from the practice squad, and the choice will be between Salvon Ahmed, who has been in Chicago since the offseason, and Zavier Scott, who was added to the Bears' practice squad after cutdown day.
We suspect Ahmed will be the one who gets the elevation, and he could see some work behind Swift, also, after he proved to be a more effective runner than Johnson during the offseason.
That said, Johnson is likely to be more involved than Ahmed, as he better fits the profile of the power back Johnson wants to combine with Swift.

title: How and Why the Bengals Can Crush the Dolphins in Miami
full_text:
After dropping two games that could've landed in their favor at the end, the Cincinnati Bengals catch a break in week five.
The winless Miami Dolphins are heading down the path that many projected for them coming into the season and the Bengals need a rebound.
Normally, I'd happily point out the flaws in the opponent’s game and maybe land a joke or two along the way, but this week feels like punching down and we've seen Bengals teams play down to their opponents before.
Yes, the 0-4 Miami Dolphins are currently a bad football team, but they have many rookies on their roster that I personally liked during draft season. Those guys can play, but they are rookies; you'll have your chances to welcome them to the NFL.
Instead, let's start at quarterback where Malik Willis needs to show enough to keep this franchise from drafting a QB with that likely top five selection in 2027.
Through four games, Willis hasn't exactly made a strong case for himself.
He owns the 30th ranked PFF grade for all quarterbacks and Willis is completing just 56% of his passes.
He's under a ton of pressure so far also. Willis is holding the ball and inviting some of it himself, but this offensive line ranks 27th in Pass Block Efficiency (PFF) and 24th in ESPN’s Pass Block Win Rate. Whoever is at fault, being under pressure on 46.9% of dropbacks is an unsustainable number.
Even when he's not under duress, Willis is completing the lowest rate of passes in the entire league. So he can't just blame the bodies around his feet.
To be fair, Willis is throwing the football down field at a very high rate. His 10.5 Average Depth of Target (ADoT) leads the league.
He's going to push that ball down field and if it isn't open, Willis can and will run. His 10.9% scramble rate is the highest of all QBs in the league. He's even had some nice runs called back due to penalties around him.
Largely, this passing offense just isn't working so far. Their 36% Success Rate is the worst in the league as the skill players are struggling to get open. Their average separation at the catch point is 27th in the league at 3.1 yards per attempt.
It's not just the passing game, the Dolphins run game lost budding star Devon Achane for the season and now they're 31st in Running Success Rate (32.3%).
Miami likes to run with a lead blocker in fullback DJ Herman, but the results have been poor so far as he owns the lowest run blocking grade from PFF of all backs in the NFL.
They're currently using 21-personnel at the third highest rate in the league, but getting a -0.12 EPA result with a 26% success rate when running the ball. Like the Bengals, Miami may have to re-think their fullback usage (Erick All) as they're averaging just 0.74 yards BEFORE contact when they run the football. That ranks 27th in the league.
Run or pass, this Dolphins offense owns the worst success rate in the entire NFL.
How about the defense? It's also trash.
Overall, Miami’s defense ranks 29th in EPA per play but almost all of that ranking is being sunk by their 31st ranked passing defense. Their 9th best run defense is formidable but has an area to attack.
Let's start with a familiar issue. The Dolphins are struggling to cover opposing tight ends. Good thing National Tight End day isn't for another couple of weeks. We don't need this getting any uglier.
So far this season, Miami has allowed 29 catches for 333 yards and two touchdowns to tight ends. Only the Bengals and Detroit Lions have allowed more yardage to the position.
And that's 29 catches on just 31 targets. So opposing QBs are completing 94% of their throws to tight ends. For the Dolphins, that's an average of 7 catches for 83 yards allowed per game to opposing tight ends.
Last week, Vikings’ TJ Hockenson went off. He saw 13 targets and caught 13 balls for 119 yards.
Hello, Mike Gesicki! Gesicki is currently on pace for 47 catches, 659 yards and 13 TDs this season.
And also maybe this is the week for Erick All Jr. to catch a pass?
Leaving themselves open and vulnerable in the middle of the field makes sense as Miami is second in the league for Cover-6 rate (22%). Using this coverage, Miami has already allowed 285 yards on 20 completions.
You can exploit Cover-6 over the intermediate part of the field and that's where the Bengals have had a ton of success this season with a second-best 122 passing yards per game and a fifth-best +0.73 EPA per pass.
Miami owns the 25th ranked EPA per play defense against Shotgun offenses. They are allowing a 50% success rate and completion percentage of 81.1 to opposing offenses. You may have guessed it, but that's the worst in the league.
On 3rd Downs, it doesn't get better for them as they're the 30th ranked defenses in EPA per play. Opposing offenses see their success rates rise to 54.5% and their completion percentage go up to 83.9% –  both bottom of the league numbers.
So what's the issue if the Miami run defense is good but their pass defense stinks?
Unlike the Bengals, who defend the run well with less defenders in the box, the Dolphins do it with extra defenders in the box at the sixth-highest rate in the NFL.
This leaves the Miami defense exposed on the back half and they cannot generate enough pressure to hide the coverage on the back end. Miami is 27th in pressure rate and 28th in sack rate on defense.
Defensive tackle Zach Sieler used to be a very good player in Miami but at 31-years old now, maybe he's starting to see a decline in play.
His 30.0 PFF run defense grades ranks him 74th amongst all interior defensive linemen through four weeks.
Teams are attacking him right now in the run game and without Kenneth Grant as their anchor inside, Miami has an exploitable weakness in run defense.
Amongst the rookies starting for the Dolphins is 5th rounder Michael Taaffe at safety. His PFF grade of 35.4 ranks him 69th of 70 starting safeties and his 25% missed tackle rate makes Jordan Battle look like prime John Lynch.
The Bengals are heavily favored in this game and it's easy to see why, but after two straight losses and nightmares of Mike White still lingering in my mind, I'm just going to sit and watch and try not to approach this game with too much excitement.
Go take care of business, Bengals.

title: Bengals Injury Update: Star Game Statuses Revealed by Zac Taylor Leading Into Dolphins Road Trip
full_text:
The Bengals wrapped up the latest week of practice with plenty of injury questions for head coach Zac Taylor to answer. Cincinnati faces Miami this weekend, hoping a bunch of players can fight through minor issues.
Taylor noted names like Ja'Marr Chase (concussion), Bryan Cook (ankle), and Colbie Young (knee) are going to be questionable for the game, same with Tee Higgins (groin). Kyle Dugger (quad) is out on Sunday. Chase and Cook logged full Friday practices.
Higgins also practiced fully in the lighter Friday session after two days of not practicing. Taylor stated Chase is still in the concussion protocol and "we'll see" on him officially playing Sunday.
Dexter Lawrence (wrist/rest) sounds ready to roll for the action. Taylor did not mention him among the injured group, while noting Dalton Risner (knee) is playing.
Cincinnati is going to need a few players to step up amidst these statuses, including Young and safety PJ Jules.
Miami is 0-4 and power-rated as one of the (if not the worst) teams in the league by major betting markets, but anyone can be beaten in the NFL. The Dallas Cowboys learned that the hard way on Thursday night, losing as big favorites against the 0-4 Buccaneers.
"It's early in the season, so you can't pay attention to the record. These guys, they got a new head coach that's kind of playing really hard. They got a really good coaching staff," Taylor said this week. "They've got some really good cornerstones of the team that they're building around right now. You're absolutely right in that there are just some things in those games that have kind of shot themselves in the foot a little bit, similar to our losses, that you could be in a totally different record right now, and that conversation about you is different.
"But they're good, and if we're not on top of it, they're a team that can get after you when you go down there. And so our players understand that, we've watched the tape, so all you gotta do is watch the tape, and you see what's there, and you can see what they're building, and so they've got our attention."
It's already a massively important game for Cincinnati's long-term goals. According to RotoWire , no team in the past 10 seasons has started 2-3 and made the Super Bowl, let alone won it.
The Bengals battle the Dolphins at 1 p.m. ET on Sunday.

title: Bengals Rising Star Eager For Increased Role, Highlights Importance of Ja'Marr Chase Practicing
full_text:
After showcasing solid chemistry with Joe Burrow last week against the Jaguars, Dohnte Meyers has another opportunity this week when the Bengals travel to face the Dolphins.
After practice, Meyers told reporters that he is eager to compete at a high level again this week. He also clarified the chemistry he and Joe Burrow have built, saying their shared drive to improve every day is the foundation of that trust.
"I'm honestly just looking forward to competing that's something I always look forward to, enjoying the sport we play," Meyers said. "Work, work and practicing reps, that's something we both take serious and we take pride in, that's something he recognizes and continues to work at," Meyers said on his relationship with Burrow.
Meyers revealed that his mentality changed last week after Chase went down with his concussion. The change for Meyers shifted to competing in Chase's honor on the field last week.
"The mentality changed a little bit just for going out there and competing for your brother," Meyers said. "In that instance you just like 'dang my brother went down, now I gotta make sure I go out there and fight for him and do what he wanna do which is go out and win.'"
He commented on his happiness about having Chase back at practice on Thursday, saying he immediately began joking with Chase as they got back to work.
"I was out there joking with him about it, Meyers said. "I was glad to have him back out there working and grinding, especially doing what he loves to do best.”
Chase's status for Sunday remains up in the air. If he misses this week's game, however, Meyers appears ready as ever to step up and lead an injury-riddled receiver room.
Colbie Young appears on track to return this week, as he practiced in full on Thursday, meaning both Bengals training camp standouts could start at receiver this Sunday.

title: Bengals Young Receiver Gets Closer to Return From Injury
full_text:
Questions still remain about whether the Bengals will have Ja'Marr Chase on Sunday against the Dolphins even after he returned to practice on a limited basis on Thursday. However, it increasingly looks like they will get Colbie Young back from a knee injury much sooner than expected.
After a limited practice on Wednesday, Young practiced in full on Thursday and looks poised to return to the field when the Bengals offense needs him most. Young said he felt better physically and that while the injury felt worst when it first happened, X-rays showed otherwise. He also said he tried to return to the game against the Steelers after sustaining the injury, but wide receivers coach Troy Walters held him out.
"Just being out there honestly, knowing I can physically move around and run around, knowing I definitely have a shot for Sunday," Young said at his locker. "When the play happened it definitely felt like it could have been something way worse, but after we got the X-rays and did our treatment and training, our trainers have done an amazing job to get me back out there as fast as possible.
"I told Troy 'I'm trying to go back in' and then he kinda held me out, and then we got re-evaluated and it just probably wasn't the best idea to go back in that game."
Another sign that Young could be healthy enough to play Sunday is the fact that he spent time catching passes from Joe Burrow after practice.
He said, after getting back to the locker room, that Burrow is like a human JUGS machine. He then emphasized how valuable the extra reps with Burrow are for his development on the field.
"He's a human JUGS machine, as much time as we can see the ball in the air from his arm it's always amazing to get work," Young said. "Everyone has a different arm angle, its not the same as the JUGS so seeing him throw it different ways, it's gonna be easier for the game."
If healthy enough in time for Sunday, Young should bring a solid level of play to a receiver room reeling from injuries to Chase, Tee Higgins, and Andrei Iosivas.

title: Bengals Safety 'Very Hopeful' to Play Sunday at Dolphins
full_text:
The Bengals' secondary could get back one of its most important players on Sunday against the Dolphins. Bryan Cook practiced in a limited capacity Thursday, an improvement from Wednesday, when he did not practice at all.
Cook confirmed after practice that, while recovering from his ankle injury has been frustrating, he is very hopeful he will be back on the field against the Dolphins this week.
"Kind of frustrating, but I'm trying to figure it out," Cook said at his locker. "Very hopeful, I'm trying to do everything I can to be out there."
Cook followed this up by emphasizing how much the defense depends on him in certain areas. He also said that he could have corrected mistakes before they happened.
"They depend on me in certain aspects, some things that on the field like 'this person made a mistake' but I feel like me not being out there can hurt," Cook said. "I can help to a certain extent like certain plays that may have been a mistake, I feel like I could have been out there and said something to correct it before that play even happened."
Cook emphasized that while he badly wants to get back on the field, he will make sure he is healthy first to avoid hurting his teammates and harming the defense's performance.
“You know how much I love my teammates, and I want to be playing but I can’t be selfish in that aspect, But at the same time, I feel if I'm not being who they need me to be on the team, on the field, I'm hurting my teammates," Cook said. "So I never let that happen. It's always team first at the end of the day. So if I can be what I need to be for my team, I'll be out there, and if I feel like I'm giving them less than myself, I’ll never let that happen. It’s always team-first at the end of the day.”
Last week, the team elevated Russ Yeast from the practice squad to rotate with PJ Jules at safety, opposite Jordan Battle.
Both played admirably, and we could see them again this week. Cook practicing is a great sign for his immediate availability; however, with the bye week looming, Zac Taylor and the coaches could choose to let him continue healing this week.

title: Bengals Safety Jordan Battle Knows Actions, Not Words Will Answer Questions About His Tackling
full_text:
Cincinnati Bengals safety Jordan Battle heard the comments, and he doesn’t fully agree.
Not the shipload of comments on social media about his missed tackle Sunday against the Jacksonville Jaguars.
“No,” Battle said. “I almost cussed. But no, I don’t pay attention to none of that on social media.”
The comments Battle was challenging were the ones made by defensive coordinator Al Golden on Wednesday when he was asked about Battle’s missed tackle of Jaguars tight end Brenton Strange on third and 18.
Strange added 12 more yards after the miss for a 23-yard gain that gave the Jaguars a first down, eventually leading to a field goal in the first quarter of the Bengals’ 22-17 loss.
“If I'm being completely honest, I don't think the criticism on that one – we've always got to make a tackle; we understand that – but he needs friends on that one,” Golden said. “We've got to gang-tackle that. We have to have our cleats in the ground, vision, we've got to know the down and distance, we've got to know the sticks.
“There should be guys breaking on either side of Jordan,” Golden added. “It shouldn’t be just a one-man show. He knows he's got to be better on that play. I know I have to coach everybody else better to get them where they need to be when that ball is thrown on third and 18.”
Battle appreciated Golden defending him but said regardless of what else was happening on the field, he needs to make that tackle.
“I hold myself to a high pedestal, and my expectation for myself is very high,” he said. “If I’m one on one with the guys, I expect to make the tackle. Yeah, we want more guys around the ball, but if I happen to be the only guy around the ball, I for sure have to make the tackle.”
Missed tackles has been an ongoing theme since Golden took over as defensive coordinator last year.
SportRadar had Battle with 21 missed tackles last season, third most in the league behind then-teammate Geno Stone (26) and Colts linebacker Zaire Franklin (23).
To show how subjective a stat such as missed tackles can be, ProFootballFocus had Battle with 17 missed tackles last year, which was tied for 23rd in the league.
This season, the two stat sites are more aligned, as both show Battle with five. That ranks tied for ninth on SportRadar and 18th on PFF.
Battle offered his theory on why he has struggled with missed tackles.
“I feel like sometimes I just tend to just go full speed,  don't break down, just try to run through a guy,” he said. “Later on that drive, I did a better job of coming to, gathering and then getting them on the ground.
“So I gotta work on controlling my speed and just work on getting to a gather and just finish a guy and try to be chest to chest,” he added.
Bengals head coach Zac Taylor also came to Battle’s defense earlier in week.
Taylor wasn’t taking issue with the validity of the missed tackle numbers. He just said he feels as though Battle is making a lot of good plays that are overshadowed because the glare is so bright on the misses.
“I think there’s a lot of great examples of Jordan Battle tackling,” he said. “The (third-and-18) one coming out of the post is the one we got to get on the ground. There are a bunch of other examples where he does come out of the post and get people down with some tough tackles on the sidelines.
“He has to be a standard setter for us in that way,” Taylor added. “It’s a disappointing one for us, the one that got out. But there are some great examples of him doing an excellent job of it.”
Battle suffered a hamstring injury in the Week 3 game at Pittsburgh and has fighting through it given the state of the safety room with fellow safety Bryan Cook dealing with an ankle injury that forced him to miss the Jacksonville game and might keep him out Sunday against Miami as well.
“It was fine,” Battle said of his hamstring. “The second half got a little tight, but it was nothing I couldn’t play through.
“I feel much better right now,” he added. “It’s definitely loosened up, and I feel ready to go.”
The Bengals listed Battle as limited on Wednesday’s injury report, but he was a full participant Thursday.
While Battle doesn’t read the social media comments about his tackling, he does get hear repeated questions about from reporters. And he said he’s fine with that.
“I'm not gonna say it gets annoying because it's what we expect,” he said. “Playing the game of football, we gotta give you guys the answer. You guys are gonna ask the questions, and that’s fine with us. We signed up for this.
“Go out there and be better on the field and make tackles, and we can avoid those questions.”
