title: Packers-Bears Final Injury Report: Green Bay Gets Season-Changing Opportunities
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – As they muddle through their sputtering start to the season, the Green Bay Packers have been given a two-headed monster of opportunities for Sunday’s game against the so-called Monsters of the Midway, the Chicago Bears.
First, star quarterback Caleb Williams suffered a hamstring injury a few weeks ago. It was interesting, at least, that he returned to practice on Friday and was listed as questionable on the final injury report, but he is expected to be inactive for a third consecutive week. The Packers knew that and have been preparing for backup Tyson Bagent.
Now, the Bears will line up without their best running back, Kyle Monangai. He entered Week 5 ranked seventh in the NFL with 324 rushing yards and sixth with a 5.4-yard average. So, the Packers will have a better chance to stop the pass without Williams and now they will have a better chance to stop the run without Monangai.
Running back Chris Brooks, who started against Tampa Bay last week, is out with an ankle injury. The Packers promoted running back Pierre Strong from the practice squad on Thursday and he’s ready to play in his first game since the 2024 finale for the Browns.
“I always train like I’m ready to play,” he said. “Especially being on P-squad, you never know really when you’re going to be called up, so I always prepare and train like I’m ready to play.”
Savion Williams, who was designated for return from injured reserve this week after missing the start of the season with an ankle injury, is out, as well.
“He’s done well in limited action,” LaFleur said of Williams. “We’re just trying to ramp him up, give him a little bit more each and every day.”
The former starting guards, Aaron Banks (knee/toe) and Jacob Monk (quad), are doubtful. Banks, who played the first half of the Week 2 game against the Jets, did not practice on Wednesday and Thursday but was limited on Friday. Monk, who was injured late in the Week 3 game against Atlanta, returned to practice as limited participation on Friday, as well.
Kevin Zeitler wasn’t about to spill any beans, but he might be ready to make his Packers debut at right guard following last week’s ramp-up. He said he feels “much better” now compared to this time last week.
“Just going to keep attacking 'til game day gets here and we'll see what the best option is for that day,” he said after Friday’s practice.
He said he got “a couple” team reps this week as he learns the offense on the fly.
“Still a lot to process coming in already into season,” he said.
Defensive tackles Javon Hargrave and Anthony Campbell and guard/center Jager Burton are questionable. Hargrave was added to the injury report after being limited on Friday.
When Kyle Monangai didn’t practice on Wednesday, coach Ben Johnson hinted it was more of a rest day after he got 30 carries against the Jets. However, Monangai didn’t practice this week and was in a walking boot at the end of the week.
“We were certainly conscious of the thumb, and it turns out the toe is a bigger deal than we initially anticipated,” he told reporters on Friday morning. “He'll be out this week. He won't be participating in this game, and we'll see how long that injury sidelines him. We got him with a specialist, and we'll work through that.”
So, the Packers, who are 2-2 and dealing with tens of millions of dollars of injuries , will face backup quarterback, Tyson Bagent, along with the running back tandem of D’Andre Swift and Roschon Johnson. It will still be a lightning-and-thunder tandem, with Swift the slasher and Johnson a burly 227 pounds.
Coming off a season of 1,087 rushing yards and three consecutive seasons of more than 1,250 total yards, Swift entered the week ranked eighth with 311 rushing yards, highlighted by 124 yards and three touchdowns in the blowout win over Carolina in Week 1. He’s averaging 4.5 yards per carry but got in the doghouse last week after fumbling twice against the Jets.
Johnson, a fourth-round pick in 2023, had two carries in seven games last season and four carries in seven games this year. He did rush for 352 yards with 34 catches as a rookie and ran for six touchdowns in 2024.
“They’ve got a great duo, one of the best duos in the league,” safety Evan Williams said this week of the Monangai-Swift pairing. “I feel like what they do really well is fall forward. Swift is a probably a little more of a finesse back, but still a guy that can lower his shoulder and deliver a punch when you know when he’s coming through a hole. Monangai, he’s a little less of the finesse and more of your true, downhill-type running back.”
However, three starting linemen who did not practice on Wednesday are ready to go for Sunday.
Three players who the Bears have designated for return from injured reserve, nickel Kyler Gordon, defensive tackle Shemar Turner and linebacker Noah Sewell, were full participation all week and are questionable.

title: Packers Friday Update From Practice: Huge RB News and Mike Ditka Tribute
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – Just a couple days before the 214th meeting between the Green Bay Packers and Chicago Bears, a legend of the rivalry, Mike Dikta, died at the age of 86 .
Before fielding any questions before Friday’s practice, Packers coach Matt LaFleur, who will be coaching against the Bears for the 16th time on Sunday, paid tribute to the Hall of Famer.
“Before we begin, I always want to embrace this rivalry,” LaFleur said. “Sometimes in life, there are things that happen that are more important than football, so I just wanted to offer my condolences to the Bears and to the Ditka family in memory of Mike Ditka – obviously a true legend of the game as a player, as a coach. Just wanted to throw that out there.”
A statement from the Green Bay Packers pic.twitter.com/xIRijncS4i
In a game in 1961 that the Packers won 31-28, Ditka caught nine passes for 190 yards and three touchdowns.
“One of the fiercest competitors in NFL history, Mike helped define the intensity and tradition of the Packers-Bears rivalry, the oldest in professional football,” the Packers said in a statement. He embodied the toughness and passion that have made the rivalry one of the most storied in all of sports.”
As for Sunday’s game, only two players did not practice on Friday: running back Chris Brooks (ankle) and left guard Aaron Banks (knee/toe). The Packers will go with MarShawn Lloyd, Kaleb Johnson and Pierre Strong, who was signed from the practice squad on Thursday .
Jacob Monk (62) is back. Only Chris Brooks and Aaron Banks not going through the opening warmup. pic.twitter.com/4Q1yulO10H
Jacob Monk, who started the first three games at right guard, returned to practice. He was inactive for last week’s win at Tampa Bay and didn’t practice on Wednesday or Thursday this week because of an injured quad sustained at the end of the Week 3 loss to Atlanta.
Travis Glover played well in Monk’s absence last week, but the team more than likely will go with veteran Kevin Zeitler against Chicago.
“We’ll see,” LaFleur said. “He’s been practicing the last two days. He’ll be out there today. A lot of it is just how comfortable he is, and we’ll go from there.”
Meanwhile, in what almost certainly will be the biggest news of the day, Bears running back Kyle Monangai will not play. That means the Bears will be without their starting quarterback, Caleb Williams (hamstring), as well as Monangai (toe).
Monangai entered Week 5 ranked seventh with 324 rushing yards and sixth with 5.40 yards per carry. His absence will mean a bigger role for D’Andre Swift, who entered the week ranked eighth with 311 rushing yards with a 4.51-yard average.
Regardless of who’s in the backfield, the Packers will be challenged through the combination of Chicago’s formidable offensive line and Green Bay’s loss of star linebacker Edgerrin Cooper.
As coach, Ditka led the Bears to victory in Super Bowl XX. It’s one of the most legendary teams in NFL history, with the Bears rolling to an 18-1 final record. The 1985 Bears defense is universally regarded as one of the greatest defenses of all-time.
As a player, Ditka was a Hall of Fame tight end. He was a Pro Bowler as a rookie in 1961 and a first- or second-team All-Pro from 1962 through 1967. He caught 427 passes for 5,812 yards and 43 touchdowns in 12 seasons with the Bears, Eagles and Cowboys.
“The things that he accomplished in this game are legendary,” LaFleur said.
The teams will release their final injury reports of the week after Friday’s practices. For now, here are the injury reports from Thursday.

title: Why Are Packers Struggling? You Won’t Believe How Much Money Has Gone Down Drain
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – You get what you pay for, as the saying goes.
The NFL salary cap for this season inched past $300 million for the first time. Of the $301.2 million cap, the Packers have $59.9 million cap dollars on either injured reserve, the physically unable to perform list or the exempt list.
Toss in the $48.2 million cap dollars in dead money clogging the franchise arteries, the Packers have almost 36 percent of the salary cap consumed by players who will not be on the field for Sunday’s pivotal NFC North showdown against the Chicago Bears.
Looked at through another prism, the Packers have $95.1 million in average annual salary on injury lists, according to OverTheCap.com . When Josh Jacobs’ contract is added, that increases to $107.1 million. That’s almost $20 million more than the runner-up Panthers and about $3 million more than the rest of the NFC North combined.
And those figures don’t even include Aaron Banks’ grotesque four-year, $77 million contract. The injured guard’s deal is worth $19.25 million per season with a 2026 cap charge of just a bit more than $12.0 million.
It’s obscene, really. This isn’t necessarily a blame-somebody story, though some suspect roster decisions are part of it. Really, it’s just the harsh reality confronting the Packers’ painful start to the season.
The Packers have 10 players on their roster with average annual salaries of at least $12 million. Here’s the list.
QB Jordan Love ($55.0 million): Love has started every game and played every snap despite taking a beating the first three games behind a porous offensive line. Due in part to surrounding issues, he ranks 25th out of 27 qualifying quarterbacks in completion percentage and 16th in passer rating.
Edge Micah Parsons ($46.5 million): Parsons had an All-Pro debut season before last year’s torn ACL. He has not started practicing and will miss the circle-them-on-the-calendar home games against the Bears and Cowboys.
WR Christian Watson ($23.0 million): After an injury-plagued start to his career, general manager Brian Gutekunst appears to have placed a winning bet on Watson, who is on pace for 1,400 receiving yards. He’s 10th in the league with 331 yards, ninth with a 16.6-yard average and tied for third with four touchdowns.
RT Zach Bako-Bewele ($22.0 million): After establishing himself as one of the best right tackles in the game, Bako-Bewele signed a big contract extension last year. He missed the end of last season with a partially torn patellar tendon and will wind up playing in essentially one game this season after a full tear.
LG Aaron Banks ($19.25 million): Banks was a dubious signing in free agency in 2025 but was decent when he played. This year, he’s played 22 snaps in four games and almost certainly will not play against the Bears due to knee and toe injuries.
TE Tucker Kraft ($18.75 million): Kraft got a huge contract extension before Week 1. He made an impressive return from last year’s torn ACL but hasn’t found his stinger in his comeback season. His 16.7 percent drop rate is the second-worst among tight ends.
DT Devonte Wyatt ($18.3 million): Wyatt got a contract extension this offseason and the team is looking for some payoff. In four games, he has 11 tackles with no sacks, quarterback hits or tackles for losses and, according to Pro Football Focus, only two pressures. His 2.8 percent pass-rush win rate is tied with teammate Jonathan Ford for 106th out of 123 defensive tackles with at least 37 pass-rushing opportunities, according to PFF.
S Xavier McKinney ($16.75 million): McKinney was first-team All-Pro in 2024 and second-team All-Pro in 2025. He has one interception this season and has played every snap.
WR Jayden Reed ($16.75 million): After missing only one game during his first two seasons, when he caught 109 passes and scored 14 touchdowns, he will have missed 25 games the last two seasons following a broken collarbone in 2025 and a neck injury in 2026.
RB Josh Jacobs ($12.0 million): Jacobs had a combined 2,882 rushing and receiving yards and 30 touchdowns during his first two seasons but remains on the exempt list serving what’s essentially a paid, indefinite suspension. Without him, the run game is the worst in the NFL.
Of those 10 players, only five are on the field. Of those five, Kraft and Wyatt have not played to expectations following season-ending injuries.
It’s not all Gutekunst’s fault. He didn’t make a blockbuster trade for Parsons knowing that he’d suffer a torn ACL. He didn’t give Bako-Bewele a huge contract extension knowing that he’d suffer career-changing knee injuries. He didn’t know that Reed would take a shot that would result in neck surgery. He didn’t know that Jacobs would get in an altercation with a woman.
Teams pay their best players top dollar because field-tilting players, as Ron Wolf would tell you, win games. Instead, Barryn Sorrell is starting for Parsons. Skyy Moore is starting for Reed. They took a flier on Kaleb Johnson in hopes of overcome the absence of Jacobs.
That doesn’t absolve Gutekunst of all blame, obviously. The next men up that he procured haven’t been nearly good enough. It would be impossible to replace Parsons, obviously, but the Packers invested a second-round pick in Anthony Belton and a third-round pick in MarShawn Lloyd, who haven’t been close to good enough in replacing Bako-Bewele and Jacobs, respectively. His mismanagement of the offensive line meant having to take a shot on 34-year-old Laken Tomlinson to replace Banks, who was a dubious signing at the time .
Dead money on the salary cap is the price of doing business at times. About 16 percent of Green Bay’s salary cap is invested on players no longer on the roster. The bulk of that, a little more than $17 million apiece, is tied up in Rashan Gary, who the Packers were happy to dump on the Cowboys after his contract extension didn’t pan out, and Kenny Clark, who was traded to Dallas as part of the Parsons trade.
So, because they’re playing with one hand tied behind their back , the Packers are 2-2 and haven’t played anything resembling a complete game this season.
Not that Sunday’s opponent, the reigning NFC North champion Bears, is the paragon of roster management, but they have a total of $54.9 million cap dollars tied up in dead money or reserve lists. The Packers have about double that at $108.2 million.
Are the Bears better than the Packers? Maybe, maybe not. Is the roster the Bears will field on Sunday better than the one that will be fielded by the Packers? Probably.
If Green Bay loses, the season will be in danger of being dragged down to the bottom of the bay by the tons of talent that’s on the sideline.

title: Jordan Love Excels In This Phase, So Why Aren’t Packers Leaning Into It?
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – The Green Bay Packers’ offense is, in a word, bad.
Or substitute any of these other words: disappointing, feeble, impotent. They all apply to a team that will enter Sunday’s rivalry showdown against the Chicago Bears ranked 28th in scoring.
One of their strengths through four games has been the Jordan Love-operated play-action passing attack. That phase of the game is excellent.
According to Pro Football Focus, 31 quarterbacks have dropped back to pass at least 50 times through the first four games of the season. Overall, Love ranks 29th in completion percentage (56.5), 20th in yards per attempt (6.8) and 19th in passer rating (86.5).
In standard dropbacks, Love is 30th with a completion rate of 53.8 percent, a decent 18th with 6.5 yards per attempt and 25th with a 74.0 passer rating.
It’s a completely different story when Love gets to use play-action. From that same group of 31 quarterbacks, Love ranks seventh in completion percentage (70.6), 15th in yards per attempt (7.7) and third in passer rating (132.8).
Doing a little math, Love’s completion percentage is plus-18.1, his yards per attempt is plus-1.2 and his passer rating is a staggering plus-58.8.
The numbers suggest Love should be using play-action early and often. The reality? Love is 27th in play-action usage at 20.7 percent of his dropbacks. He was somewhere just above or just below the league average the last three seasons with 25.4 percent in 2025, 25.7 percent in 2024 and 25.4 percent in 2023.
Which begs one question: Why don’t the Packers use more play-action passes? Considering it’s the one thing they’re doing well, the limited usage doesn’t make any sense.
But first, let’s get into something that really doesn’t make any sense. How can you have a productive play-action passing game when you have an unproductive running game?
It is weird to believe any defense would be suckered by a fake handoff to MarShawn Lloyd, who is averaging 2.7 yards per carry. But, oddly, it works.
“It does go against your first inclination, there’s no question about that,” Aaron Schatz of FTN Fantasy told Packers On SI on Thursday. He was the founder of Football Outsiders; FO’s research brought to light the counterintuitive nature of play-action passing.
“But all the research that's been done says that's the case. You don't have to establish the run in order to make play-action work because the linebackers have been taught their whole life that when the quarterback does the handoff, that’s a run. Go get it.”
“What I like to say is that you don't have to establish the run because the run was established in Pop Warner,” Schatz said.
“These guys have been playing their whole lives with the quarterback making that move, right? Especially at a younger age, it was more often a run, not a play-action fake, so they're just conditioned to believe that the run is coming.”
Schatz pointed to last season’s top six teams in terms of the difference in efficiency between using play action and not using play action. The first four, as you might expect, were run-centric offenses: the Seahawks, Bills, Ravens and Falcons. The next two were the Titans, who finished 30th in rushing, and the Commanders, with Jacory Croskey-Merritt and Chris Rodriguez atop the depth chart.
“So, you don't need to be able to run the ball in order to make the play action work,” Schatz said. “If you look at the opposite, teams that were not as good on play action as they were otherwise, it includes Jacksonville, which was a good running team for a lot of the year, and Cincinnati, where Chase Brown had a really good year, and San Francisco, where Christian McCaffrey didn't have a good year but he's Christian McCaffrey!”
Green Bay’s rushing attack is the worst in the NFL by a considerable margin. Since the success or failure of the run game shouldn’t matter in terms of play-action effectiveness, why doesn’t Packers coach Matt LaFleur lean into the strength that has been Jordan Love’s play-action passing?
“I think you have to stay in manageable situations,” LaFleur explained. “If it’s second-and-20 and you run a play-action, it’s probably not going to be as effective as if it’s even second-and-7. I think that [not needing an effective run game to have an effective play-action game] could hold true for some of the first-down situations, but it’s more when you’re in get-back-on-track then I think it’s less effective.”
Schatz agreed with LaFleur on that one. The Packers are 30th in the league with a 3.6-yard average on first down. Of 31 quarterbacks who’ve thrown at least 20 passes on first down, Love is 28th in completion percentage. Of 53 dropbacks, 26 have produced incompletions or sacks. That means a lot of second-and-10 situations. The run game, meanwhile, is averaging 2.8 yards per carry.
That’s meant a lot of second-and-long and third-and-long plays, where even linebackers with a stop-the-run mentality will shrug their shoulders at a play-action fake.
When Love has been up for success, the play-action game has been dynamic. Why has it been so good, even when the team’s horrendous run game should limit the effectiveness?
“I think it works well when we’re running the football,” LaFleur said. “Everything plays off one another and, like I just mentioned, you’ve got to stay in some of those situational calls. And then like many teams do, a lot of times with play-action you’re looking for premier looks, and it gets a little bit harder if teams are going to play off and soft to get some of the premier looks that you’re looking for. I would say coverage dictates some of that, as well.”
Added together, this is another case where the fate of the Packers’ offense doesn’t necessarily fall on LaFleur’s play-calling or Love’s accuracy. It will be up to the new offensive line to set the offense up for success and allow LaFleur to put Love in position to use play action as a major weapon.

title: With Chris Brooks Sidelined, Packers Add ‘Dawg’ to Running Backs
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – The Green Bay Packers took a 52-man roster (one less than the limit) and an 18-man practice squad (one over the limit) out to the practice field on Thursday.
The Packers on Thursday afternoon promoted running back Pierre Strong from the practice squad, where he will take the place of last week’s starter, Chris Brooks, on the roster against the Chicago Bears on Sunday. They also made official the signing of linebacker Jack Dingle to the practice squad.
With Kristian Welch taking Edgerrin Cooper's place on the roster, the Packers filled Welch's spot on the practice squad with a high-RAS linebacker. https://t.co/9HI2a5cg4A
Brooks suffered an ankle injury during last week’s win at Tampa Bay.
“We’re going to give him another day, see where he’s at tomorrow and then, obviously, make a decision after that,” coach Matt LaFleur said before practice .
As it turns out, the Packers moved quickly rather than waiting until Friday or even Saturday, when they usually make their final roster moves before gameday.
That Brooks presumably won’t be available against Chicago is no surprise. The Packers re-signed Damon Bankston to the practice squad earlier in the week, a sign that Strong would be needed in the game and someone would be needed for the scout team.
With a keen eye for cutback lanes and above-average acceleration, Strong was the team’s most productive running back during training camp.
“The cutback, pass pro, hands out the backfield, anything on special teams,” Strong said after the final preseason game. “I consider myself a dawg. I can do it all.”
It appeared he had put himself in position to make the roster through a combination of his performance and Josh Jacobs landing on the exempt list. Instead, during final roster cuts, the Packers acquired Kaleb Johnson from the Steelers and released Strong.
Strong was a fourth-round pick by the Patriots in 2022. After spending his rookie year with New England and the 2023 and 2024 seasons with Cleveland, he failed to make the Browns’ roster in 2025. The Packers signed him to the practice squad, and that’s where he spent the entire season without playing in a game.
“I’m hungry. I’m always going to be hungry,” he said. “Practice squad, 53-man roster. I’m still hungry, but I’m very hungry now. So, I want to get back to where I’ve been.”
He might get his chance against the Bears. The other healthy backs on the roster are MarShawn Lloyd and Johnson. Lloyd, a third-round pick in 2024, has carried the ball 30 times for a team-high 81 yards – a paltry 2.7-yard average. Johnson has carried the ball 20 times or 80 yards, a 4.0-yard average highlighted by a 31-yard run against the Bucs.
Both players fumbled in the game, though. LaFleur’s patience had worn thin, raising the possibility of benching players who put the ball on the ground.
Strong has carried the ball 99 times in three seasons with a 5.0-yard average. Plus, he contributed 17 tackles on special teams. This preseason, he carried the ball 15 times for 58 yards (3.9 average) and had a 68-yard kickoff return at Denver.
“Obviously he made some big plays not only in the kicking game but did a nice job running the ball,” offensive coordinator Adam Stenavich said a few days later. “We’ve got to get him going a little bit more in protections on third down, things like that, get him the ball in his hands in the passing game just to see how he does there, but he’s done a nice job so I’ve very encouraged by what I’ve seen from him so far.”
Strong hasn’t played in a game since the 2024 finale at Miami. Asked what it would mean to make the roster, Strong at the end of the preseason said, “The world, you know? It ain’t even about me no more. I just brought my little girl in the world, so everything I do is for her. So, it’s just like, I want her to grow up and watch her father play football. So, like I said, it’d mean the world to me. Where I’m at right now, millions of kids wish they were here. So, I’m just staying. I’m going to stay and grind.”

title: Packers-Bears Thursday Injury Report: Chicago Star Out Again
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – With Sunday’s rivalry showdown between the Green Bay Packers and Chicago Bears looming, both teams’ offensive lines are coming together.
The question is who they’ll be blocking for.
For a second consecutive day, Bears running back Kyle Monangai did not practice on Thursday due to thumb and toe injuries. He carried the ball 30 times during last week’s pounding of the Jets, so another day of rest should do him some good.
For the Packers, running back Chris Brooks – the starter last week against Tampa Bay – did not practice for a second consecutive day due to an ankle injury.
“We’re going to give him another day, see where he’s at tomorrow and then, obviously, make a decision after that,” coach Matt LaFleur said before practice .
If Brooks is out, the Packers will ride with MarShawn Lloyd, Kaleb Johnson and practice-squad back Pierre Strong.
Whoever is in the backfield, chances are they’ll be running behind what the Packers hope will be the No. 1 line for the rest of the season. During the media portion of practice, Kevin Zeitler was the right guard. He got repeated snaps in combo-blocking drills alongside starting center Sean Rhyan or starting right tackle Anthony Belton.
“He’s progressing good,” LaFleur said of Zeitler. “He’s getting a little bit more each and every day. Again, we’re trying to ramp him up to where he feels comfortable to go out there and play winning football.”
Along with Brooks, former starting left guard Aaron Banks (knee and toe) and former starting right guard Jacob Monk (quad) were the three players who did not practice.
Rookie center/guard Jager Burton, who did not play against Tampa Bay due to a groin injury, returned to practice on Thursday. He sat out Wednesday due to back spasms.
“I had a little tweak from lifting, but I’m feeling a lot better now,” he said. “It’s more of a day-to-day thing, but it’s just kind of weird with backs. It’s something you’ve got to protect a little bit.”
Receiver Savion Williams, who was designated for return from injured reserve this week following a preseason ankle injury, practiced for a second consecutive day as limited participation.
“It’s great,” quarterback Jordan Love said on Wednesday. “Say has missed a good amount of time right now, been on IR. He’s a key part to our offense. He’ll definitely be able to step in and make plays when he gets back and, obviously, it’s just about getting him back, ramping him up like you said, but he’s a key part of our offense. So, we’ll need him out there and it’s good to see him back.”
Burton’s progress to limited was the only change to Green Bay’s injury report.
The big development in Chicago came on the offensive line. After playing about 90 snaps against the Jets, left guard Joe Thuney, right guard Jonah Jackson and right tackle Darnell Wright did not practice on Wednesday. All three progressed to limited participation on Thursday.
Their presence will be huge, obviously, because they are the driving force behind the NFL’s top-ranked running game. Plus, starting left tackle Braxton Jones was placed on injured reserve on Saturday with a knee injury.
Also for Chicago, the team’s other top running back, D’Andre Swift, progressed to limited participation as he rebounds from hip and knee injuries.
Monangai is seventh in the NFL with 324 rushing yards and Swift is eighth with 311 rushing yards. The Packers have 232 rushing yards as a team.
Quarterback Tyson Bagent, who will start again in place of injured Caleb Williams (hamstring), downplayed the impact of the injuries.
“We're having a ton of meetings throughout the day,” he told reporters in Chicago. “Those guys will hit the field at some point this week. I’ve really just got to be a pro, get the base plan down and really nothing changes.
“Every week, you see big boys taking a couple days off here and there, especially when you get 90 plays. We wouldn't expect all 11 to be out there firing on all cylinders after a game like that. So, really just doing what we need to do right now. Recovery is at a premium in order to get everybody feeling fresh. I think that's more important than having guys beat up out there, going through half-effort reps on the practice field.”

title: Is Packers Coach Matt LaFleur on Thin Ice? Here Are Latest Hot-Seat Rankings
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – Is Green Bay Packers coach Matt LaFleur on the hot seat?
A team that’s built to win a Super Bowl is about the ugliest 2-2 imaginable and facing a Week 5 showdown against the rival Chicago Bears, whose coach, Ben Johnson, would love to push LaFleur off the hot seat and into the boiling cauldron.
On the other hand, while the NFL is a bottom-line business, there needs to be some nuance to the conversation about LaFleur’s future.
“LaFleur’s roster right now is a nightmare,” noted Sports Illustrated’s Conor Orr, who put LaFleur at No. 4 in his latest hot-seat rankings .
LaFleur’s calling card is his creativity as an offensive play-designer and play-caller. The offense, however, ranks just 27th in points scored.
Is that LaFleur’s fault? Or is that the fault of a combination of misfortune, with season-ending injuries to receiver Jayden Reed and Zach Bako-Bewele, and poor roster construction by general manager Brian Gutekunst, who was guilty of overrating the talent on the offensive line?
On paper, running back Josh Jacobs, tight end Tucker Kraft and receivers Christian Watson, Matthew Golden and Jayden Reed would be a formidable quintet.
But Jacobs is, essentially, serving an indefinite suspension, Kraft is coming off a torn ACL and Reed is out following a neck injury. Those five players didn’t play a single snap together last season and they won’t this season.
Without Jacobs and with that had been a subpar offensive line, the running game has been terrible.
NFL rushing leaders pic.twitter.com/WWuESV5ffs
The defense, meanwhile, is starting the season without its best player, Micah Parsons, and just lost arguably its second-best player, Edgerrin Cooper, to a torn Achilles.
“Green Bay has something like 30 percent of its total salary cap either on injured reserve or the commissioner exempt list,” Orr noted.
Then again, the Packers hold the dubious NFL leads for penalty yards, dropped passes and fumbles. LaFleur isn’t guilty of false starts and drops, but those continued mistakes reflect poorly on the coach and his staff.
Discipline-Related Penalties 1. PHI, LV & IND 1 ... 30. LAR & GB 8 32. SEA 32 Penalties included: Unnecessary Roughness, Unsportsmanlike Conduct, Taunting, ... (see footnote for full list) pic.twitter.com/LhnPPpgEYP
“Green Bay had a string of high-improbability losses last season and already saw a divisional game against the Vikings turn violently on the heels of a strange fourth-down decision,” Orr concluded as part of a much more extensive and thoughtful breakdown.
“But LaFleur has also been making tuna salad out of a dreadful situation in 2026. Jordan Love’s hit total went way down on Sunday, and the Packers’ rushing game looked like it improved marginally. He deserves credit for that.”
LaFleur is No. 5 in Fox Sports’ hot-seat rankings , with Ralph Vacchiano placing him between the Eagles’ Nick Sirianni and the Chargers’ Jim Harbaugh.
The contract extension that LaFleur was given after last season’s flameout could be his saving grace this time around, with Vacchiano wondering if the team’s board of directors would be willing to eat the remainder of a contract that is believed to be worth in the neighborhood of $15 million per year.
“However,” he continued, “the Packers also can’t ignore what’s happening to his team. They are regressing offensively even though they have an outstanding young quarterback in Jordan Love and an array of good receivers. And the defense has taken a huge step back after the loss of DC Jeff Hafley.”
Those last two points aren’t exactly accurate. Watson and Golden aren’t exactly an “array” of receivers, and the defense hasn’t taken a “huge step back” under new defensive coordinator Jonathan Gannon.
Regardless, Vacchiano is correct that the Packers “are at risk of being buried in a very dangerous division.” That’s part of what makes this such a huge game for the Packers.
At CBS , LaFleur ranks only ninth and the hot seat is actually “cool.” Bryan DeArdo also pointed to the contract, though it’s important to note the Packers would be off the hook (at least partially) if LaFleur were to land on his feet in the next coaching cycle.
“Because of his contract, the only way LeFleur's job would actually be in jeopardy at season's end is if the Packers have an epic collapse and there are rumblings that he's lost the locker room,” DeArdo wrote (while misspelling LaFleur’s name).
In the prediction markets, LaFleur’s seat has cooled considerably since the night of the blowout loss to the Falcons. At Kalshi , for instance, his odds to be “out before March” were as high as 90 percent. It was at 20 percent on Thursday morning but bounced up to 28 percent while this story was being written.
This, obviously, is a huge game for the Packers. They are 2-2, with their two wins coming against teams with a combined 1-7 record. With a win, they’d be in second place in the division and right in the thick of everything that they set out to accomplish this season. With a loss, they’d be in last place in the division and in deep trouble.
LaFleur, for his part, is keeping the messaging as normal as possible this week. It’s not about him. It’s not about Ben Johnson. It’s about winning this game.
“I do think, it’s an NFC North opponent and they’re the defending champion,” he said on Wednesday. “So, there’s always an added importance in divisional games. And they’re one of the premier teams in the National Football League. I think our guys will be ready to roll, but it’s more important that we focus on the day to day, making sure our process is right and making sure our preparation’s on point.”

title: Packers Thursday Update From Practice: A Strong Possibility
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – Green Bay Packers running back Chris Brooks missed a second consecutive practice on Thursday with the ankle injury sustained last week at Tampa Bay.
“We’re going to give him another day, see where he’s at tomorrow and then, obviously, make a decision after that,” coach Matt LaFleur said before practice, the second of the week before Sunday’s huge rivalry showdown against the Chicago Bears.
Brooks was one of three players who didn’t practice on Thursday.
If Brooks isn’t able to play this week, the Packers almost certainly would add Pierre Strong from the practice squad. While the Packers have an empty spot on their 53-man roster, they probably would elevate him rather than promote him.
With 15 carries for 58 yards (3.9 average), Strong was one of the team’s more productive running backs during the preseason but lost out on his bid to make the 53-man roster after the team traded for Kaleb Johnson.
“I feel like God puts everybody through a test. So, I'm hungry,” he said after the final preseason game. “I'm always going to be hungry. Practice squad, 53-man roster. I'm still hungry, but I'm very hungry now. So, I want to get back to where I've been.”
The Packers have the worst rushing attack in the NFL this season and are on pace for the worst rushing attack in NFL history .
Could Strong help? A fourth-round pick by the Patriots in 2022, he totaled 499 rushing yards and averaged 5.0 yards per carry with New England in 2022 and Cleveland in 2023 and 2024. He added 26 receptions, averaged 23.8 yards per kickoff return and even contributed 17 tackles.
Jager Burton is back after dealing with back spasms yesterday. Three players aren’t practicing: Chris Brooks, Jacob Monk and Aaron Banks. Here’s a little of QB1. pic.twitter.com/MainZbIEsT
Four players did not practice for the Packers on Wednesday. Along with Brooks, the others were Aaron Banks (knee/toe), who was supposed to be the starting left guard, Jacob Monk (quad), who had been the starting right guard, and rookie interior lineman Jager Burton (back).
Banks and Monk didn’t practice on Thursday, either, though they were doing rehab work on the field. Burton, who didn’t play at Tampa Bay after being listed as questionable with a groin injury last week, was dealing with back spasms on Wednesday but returned on Thursday.
Right tackle Anthony Belton, who was limited participation on Wednesday with a knee injury, practiced again on Thursday. LaFleur said he didn’t have any concerns about his availability for Sunday.
The team doesn’t do any 11-on-11 drills in front of reporters. During the opening segment of the media viewing period, there is a five-man line working with quarterback Jordan Love on cadence and adjustments.
Kevin Zeitler for the second consecutive day was the right guard.
“He’s progressing good,” LaFleur said. “He’s getting a little bit more each and every day. Again, we’re trying to ramp him up to where he feels comfortable to go out there and play winning football.”
The Packers’ new No. 1 line of left tackle Jordan Morgan, left guard Laken Tomlinson, center Sean Rhyan, Zeitler and right tackle Anthony Belton could make its debut on Sunday.
“I’m real excited, just based off last game, just how much better that felt coming out of it,” Rhyan said. “I think the whole unit wants to feel that way. And we played pretty well, but I think that we can play even better.
“And that’s real exciting because if we’re playing really well, then the whole team is going to play well and I know we as O-line take pride in that, so f*** it, we’re excited. We’re going to keep getting better, they’re going to throw the best five out there, and we’re going to keep going.”
The teams will produce fresh injury reports after Thursday’s practice. For now, here are the reports from Wednesday.

title: With Bad Run Game, Packers Should Trade for One More Veteran to Fill Hole
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – The Green Bay Packers’ big-ticket left guard, Aaron Banks, is injured. Because of ineffective play from the backups, they signed 34-year-old Laken Tomlinson. Because of ineffective play from young right guard Jacob Monk, they signed 36-year-old Kevin Zeitler.
With Luke Musgrave injured, they signed 31-year-old tight end Jonnu Smith. To strengthen their defense after offseason attrition, they signed 31-year-old tackle Javon Hargrave and traded for 30-year-old linebacker Zaire Franklin.
Suddenly, the youngest-in-the-league Packers have hit middle age.
So, with general manager Brian Gutekunst setting aside youth for seasoning, maybe there’s one more oldie-but-goodie roster move to be made.
Trading for Cardinals running back James Conner.
It’s a possibility we’ve mentioned a few times, both before and after Josh Jacobs was arrested.
Conner, 31, is on injured reserve following a foot injury that sidelined him for most of last season. He was limited to individual drills during training camp but was placed on IR for the start of the season. He is expected to be ready to go in a few weeks, at which point maybe there will be some clarity on Jacobs’ future.
At 6-foot-1 and 233 pounds, Conner fits the big-guy mold the Packers have typically preferred. Jacobs is one of the best dirty-work runners in the NFL. Block a play for 2 yards, Jacobs is going to fight for 2 or 3 more.
Conner is that same style of player. In 2024, Jacobs during his blockbuster debut season in Green Bay ranked eighth out of 46 backs who had at least 100 rushing attempts with 3.45 yards after contact per carry, according to Pro Football Focus. Conner was 13th with 3.30. He was 14th in rushing attempts but fourth with 62 forced missed tackles.
“Conner, he’s a beast,” Packers coach Matt LaFleur said before the 2024 matchup against Arizona. “He’s a big, physical back that is more elusive than he leads on just in terms of (being) a bigger guy.”
Conner is a proven workhorse. In 2023, he rushed for a career-high 1,040 yards even while being limited to 13 games. In 2024, he topped that with 1,094 yards in 16 games.
Jacobs is an adept receiver. So is Conner. Drafted in 2017, Conner from 2018 through 2024 averaged 40.1 receptions per season. He caught a career-high 55 passes in 2018 and averaged a career-high 10.1 yards per catch in 2021. In 2024, he caught 47 passes for 414 yards (8.8 average) and one touchdown.
When healthy and assuming he’s still got some spring in his step, Conner would be leaps-and-bounds better than Chris Brooks, MarShawn Lloyd and Kaleb Johnson.
Brooks is an incredibly valuable role player but doesn’t bring a lot of juice as a runner. Lloyd, the 2024 third-round pick, has some juice but hasn’t shown the speed to turn the corner, as he would prefer to do, or the power to gain yards after contact. Johnson has power but lacks the acceleration.
Moreover, Lloyd and Johnson fumbled last week against Tampa Bay, with LaFleur clearly exasperated after the game. Conner fumbled four times out of 283 touches in 2024 but had zero in 235 touches in 2023.
Just like Tomlinson brought stability and performance to the line in his debut against Tampa Bay, Conner could do the same thing for a rushing attack that ranks last in the NFL with 58.0 yards per game and is on pace to finish with the fewest rushing yards since the 1970 merger , when teams played only 14-game seasons.
Again, working under the assumption he comes back in something close to vintage form and hasn’t been tackled by Father Time, Conner’s size, power and proven production would give the Packers the balance they’ve been lacking all year. That, in turn, would do two things for the offense.
One, it would be in better down-and-distance situations. Green Bay is last in the NFL in third-down conversions due in large part to its average third-down play requiring 8.1 yards. That’s the fourth-longest distance required, with three teams averaging 8.2.
Two, it would have a real play-action threat. Love’s play-action passer ratings were 113.7 in 2023, 104.4 in 2024 and 100.3 in 2025. This year, it’s a whopping 132.8, but LaFleur hasn’t leaned on it much because he hasn’t been able to lean on his running game at all.
Josh Jacobs was one of the Packers’ team leaders. He was voted a captain in 2024 and 2025 and probably would have again if not for the off-the-field incident that has meant what’s essentially a paid, indefinite suspension.
“You want positive energy around you whether you’re talking (to people) or not,” Cardinals coach Mike LaFleur told reporters recently . “You know when you walk in a room or walk into someone’s house and you can just feel that the energy’s right? That’s what you feel – at least me, and I know the offense and the team, when you walk by him or when he’s in the room. He doesn’t have to say much to get his point across.”
Yes, age is a number that can’t be ignored with a running back, though three 30-something backs – Baltimore’s Derrick Henry, Minnesota’s Aaron Jones and San Francisco’s Christian McCaffrey – all have more than 340 combined rushing-receiving yards. Among running backs, they are in the top 14 in the league.
With first-round pick Jeremiyah Love and free-agent Tyler Allgeier atop the depth chart and their season going nowhere fast, the Cardinals might be interested in trading one of their more popular players. With Jacobs’ status in limbo, the Packers might be interested.
The financial price wouldn’t be exorbitant; Conner’s base salary is $2.355 million; the Packers would only have to pay a prorated portion of that. There also are per-game roster bonuses. The price to make the trade would be low, too, considering that Conner is 31 and coming off an injury that limited him to three games last season.
To be sure, the Packers will need some sort of assurance that Conner is healthy and can be a factor, whether that’s the Cardinals getting Conner some game reps once he’s healthy or simply an honest conversation between the coaching brothers.
“I always go back to return to play, return to performance, and both those guys are smart enough to know that they want to be back when they can actually perform at the level that they're capable of,” Mike LaFleur said of Conner and tight end Tip Reiman.
By the time Conner is ready, the Packers might have some certainty on the status of Jacobs and the ability of the others to provide a real, honest-to-goodness running threat. Those timelines, and the trade deadline being Nov. 10, could be in a convenient alignment.
The Packers for the better part of two decades had shown almost zero interest in 30-something players. It’s different this year, with general manager Brian Gutekkusnt frantically trying to maximize the Jordan Love-Micah Parsons window.
Thus, for a team that hasn’t just bent from its usual roster-building philosophy but run from it with its veteran-centric additions, a healthy Conner would make a lot of sense in perhaps providing the running game the Packers have lacked through four games.

title: Texans-Titans Week 5 Injury Report: Updates on Tank Dell, Azeez Al-Shaair
full_text:
The Houston Texans and Tennessee Titans have released their final injury reports for their Week 5 matchup after wrapping up the events of Friday's practice session.
And for both sides, things are looking relatively clean. That's especially so for the Texans, considering they've only officially ruled out one player heading into this weekend's divisional matchup in Nashville.
Let's sort through the latest on the injury front for both sides heading into Week 5, and what it might mean for a defining matchup between two 0-4 teams in the AFC South :
WR Tank Dell: OUT (knee) S M.J. Stewart: QUESTIONABLE (quad) OT Blake Fisher: QUESTIONABLE (illness) OT Braden Smith: QUESTIONABLE (foot) OG Ed Ingram: QUESTIONABLE (illness) OT Aireontae Ersery: QUESTIONABLE (illness) DT Kayden McDonald: QUESTIONABLE (ankle)
The only name the Texans have ruled out days ahead of Sunday's matchup is wide receiver Tank Dell. It was the largely outcome to be expected for Houston's fan favorite pass-catcher for Week 5, who's gradually been returning from his severe knee injury that's left him sidelined since December 2024.
Dell's status seems to be progressing pretty well since the Texans activated his 21-day window to return from injured reserve earlier this week. He was a limited participant in practice on both Wednesday and Thursday, yet was left as a DNP for their third session.
So Dell will be out for Week 5, but will be worth watching over the next couple of weeks. He could be activated from the IR at any time between now and Wednesday of Houston's Week 8 bye.
Another piece of good news for the Texans: their starting middle linebacker and green-dot signal caller Azeez Al-Shaair was completely removed from the injury report, and is officially good to go for this weekend.
The Pro Bowl linebacker missed last weekend against the Dallas Cowboys with a groin injury he suffered the week prior, but his full participation at practice on Friday was the last domino that needed to fall before he'd been deemed active for Week 5.
That means for Al-Shaair, he'll be slotting back into his regular starting slot in the middle of the field as Houston's top linebacker, and will start next to either Jake Hansen or Kenneth Murray.
Outside of the two big names that the Texans saw take a step forward in this week's practice, Houston has listed six players as questionable for this weekend.
Three offensive linemen contracted a new illness as of Thursday's practice, which left them as DNP, but all of Blake Fisher, Ed Ingram, and Aireontae Ersery were back to participating on Friday. All three should be expected to play.
Then Houston has three returnees from IR that could make their season debut this weekend: safety M.J. Stewart, offensive tackle Braden Smith, and rookie defensive tackle Kayden McDonald . All three appear to be trending in a good direction, and could all inevitably be activated for Sunday, barring any surprises.
S Amani Hooker: OUT (concussion) TE David Martin Robinson: QUESTIONABLE (hamstring) WR Carnell Tate: QUESTIONABLE (back) CB Joshua Williams: QUESTIONABLE (pec)
The Titans' side of things also looks relatively clean as the Texans' injury report appeared. But two names do tend to stick out a bit more than most.
One is veteran safety Amani Hooker, who will officially be missing this week with a concussion he suffered in Week 4 against the Baltimore Ravens, and leaves the Titans' secondary a little more depleted than usual.
Then, No. 4 rookie wide receiver Carnell Tate also appears to be dealing with a new back injury suffered in this week's team practice. However, Titans head coach Robert Saleh did note that Tate would be "good to go" for Sunday, easing any worries from their end wondering if he'd be ready to play.
Kickoff between the Texans and Titans lands on 12 p.m. MT in Nissan Stadium, where one team will inevitably check off their long-awaited first win of the season by the end of the action.

title: Texans' Most Disappointing Players at Quarter Mark of the Season
full_text:
There's no question about it: through the first four weeks of the 2026 NFL season, the Houston Texans have been among one of, if not the most disappointing team across the league due to their gloomy 0-4 start.
From entering this season with sky-high Super Bowl expectations to now being one of four remaining teams in the NFL without a win on their record before Sunday's slate of Week 5 games , things really haven't gone the way the Texans had envisioned through this point in the year.
But when looking deeper into the Texans' early-season woes, who on the roster has disappointed the most of all en route to their 0-4 record? Not everyone in Houston has had an individually poor start to the year, yet for a select few, it's hard to argue against it.
Let's take a look at five players for the Texans on both sides of the ball to determine who's had a similarly poor individual start to the year as Houston has as a collective at 0-4:
While the first game of Montgomery's tenure in a Texans uniform was wildly positive due to his three-touchdown day, the veteran runner hs yet to reach anywhere close to those same highs in the games that have followed.
From Weeks 2 through 4, Montgomery has recorded less than 70 rushing yards on 27 carries, is averaging 2.4 yards per attempt, and has yet to hit the end zone again since his first game against the Buffalo Bills in Week 1.
The offensive line hasn't helped his case much at all. Yet, even when factoring in those run-blocking woes, Montgomery himself has not been explosive, efficient, and has gradually seen Woody Marks get more and more involved as the season progresses.
In reality, Marlin Klein can't be knocked too harshly for his lack of production through the first quarter of the season. Because the Texans have done him no favors when it comes to getting their second-round pick involved in the offensive game plan early.
Klein has seen less than 25 offensive snaps through the three games he's been active in this season. He's only gotten one reception in those appearances, coming off of a 16-yard catch in Week 1 against the Bills. This weekend, the Texans decided to make Klein a healthy scratch for the first time this year.
It's far from the ideal start any team has in mind for one of their premier day-two picks. If the Texans staff fails to get him more involved soon, this situation will look even uglier than it does right now.
Upon Braden Smith's foot injury suffered during training camp that led him to hit the injured reserve list for the first four weeks of the season, it's been veteran Trent Brown who's claimed his role as starting right tackle for the time being. And it's hard to say things have gone positively for him in that timeframe.
The stats aren't exactly the prettiest: in 184 pass-blocking snaps, Brown has allowed 12 pressures, two sacks, and one hit. More frustratingly, Brown has five penalties to his name in four games as the most experienced starting lineman. And we all know how this offensive line's run-blocking has fared thus far.
This week, Smith returned to practice from his foot injury and could be seeing a return to the Texans' lineup in the very near future. Whenever he is healthy, it'd be far from surprising to see him plug in on the right side over Brown in hopes of some type of improvement.
The name on the Texans' defense who's probably seen the highest dose of criticism for his start to the 2026 season has been third-year cornerback Kamari Lassiter; someone who entered this season viewed largely as the best No. 2 corner in the NFL , to now being a primary cause of Houston's defensive lapses in two of their four games on the season.
In Week 1 against the Bills, Lassiter allowed five receptions on seven targets for over 100 yards and a touchdown. Last weekend against the Dallas Cowboys, he had an even worse performance, where he allowed eight catches on 11 targets for 136 yards— most of which came from star wideout CeeDee Lamb.
This Texans' defense can't be nearly as lockdown as it was last season if Lassiter isn't able to carry his weight on the opposite side of Derek Stingley Jr. Four games into the new year, and he simply hasn't met expectations.
The past couple of weeks have admittedly been a step forward for Texans veteran safety Reed Blankenship. He went from allowing nearly 150 yards and two touchdowns in Weeks 1 and 2 to a much more stable past couple of performances of allowing a combined 71.
However, when mixing together not only his slow start to the year, but also the maneuvering this secondary has made to try and incorporate his zone-heavy play style into their own scheme, things have gone far from as anticipated for the former Philadelphia Eagles captain , based on what the Texans invested in him this offseason.
So while this secondary shouldn't blame all of their issues on Blankenship and his fit within this defense, he certainly hasn't helped much outside of his interception on Daniel Jones in Week 3. With M.J. Stewart returning from his quad injury this week, it'll be interesting to see how Blankenship's usage may change because of it.

title: Texans QB C.J. Stroud Credits Surprising Factor for His Recent Success
full_text:
The Houston Texans' 0-4 record hasn't made for much of a positive start to the season for many players on this roster.
However, it's fair to say that even in the Texans' winless first four games, quarterback C.J. Stroud has done his part in commanding this offense to some pretty decent results considering the circumstances he's been put in.
He's taken care of the ball pretty well by throwing a 5:0 TD-INT ratio in four games, has thrown for more yards per game than his Offensive Rookie of the Year season in 2023 (285.3 yards/game), and even has a higher passer rating than he's seen through the past two seasons (95.9).
So what's been the secret to Stroud turning things around for a solid start on his behalf? Some fans might be surprised at where the quarterback himself handed the credit.
For Stroud, two aspects of the Texans' offense that have been largely criticized either early this season or even dating back to last year have stuck out to him as a positive: that's his pass protection and his receivers creating separation.
"I think just the way we've been protecting. I thought the pass protection has been really good on early downs," Stroud said on what's led to . "I think the way we're running routes, and we've been seeing a lot of man coverage, so just trying to pick that apart for guys. Creating separation is big in that too."
"But yeah, I would say those are really important things: creating separation, protecting, doing the little things the right way, the fundamental things. So, we've been able to do that, and we've got to keep that going."
Especially with wide receiver Nico Collins back in Stroud's arsenal this past weekend, the Texans' passing offense really began to turn a positive corner .
Houston had 30 points for the first time in a game this season (something they did just three times last regular season), Stroud had another 300-plus-yard outing with two touchdowns, and the offense finally gained some sense of potency that wasn't as available without Collins in Weeks 2 and 3.
However, even with Stroud carrying his weight through the start of this season, it hasn't led to the team success everyone in the building would've hoped for.
﻿ The run game has remained a non-factor . The Texans' defense has been far from the state they proved to be in 2025. And now, this team finds itself in a deeper hole record-wise than where they were this time last year.
That's all a pretty tough break for Stroud, who's been able to put the pieces together for a solid individual campaign on his part, yet hasn't seen his work develop into any real success as a collective.
Despite the unfavorable circumstances for Stroud, he's still finding himself looking in the mirror to determine what he can do better moving forward, in hopes he and the Texans can flip the script, which comes down to working better on third down and in the red zone.
"It's all about winning," Stroud continued. "So, looking at myself in the mirror like, what else can I do to be better to make us better on third down, to keep us on the field? To control the game maybe a little more."
"But I think our offensive line's protecting well in the pass game. Thought [Nick Caley] called a good game last game, just letting us be aggressive. But I feel in rhythm. I feel like I'm putting the ball where I need to put it, but also I just want to be better on third down and in the red zone."
"Those critical situations that you look back like, damn, we would've got this first down or if I would've did this, we could've stayed on the field. So, always things you can correct."
If Stroud keeps up at his current pace, and the defense can dial in to look closer to the form that led them to 12 wins in 2025, seeing Houston turn around in the weeks ahead isn't impossible to imagine.
We've seen just as recently as last year that this team is more than capable of rattling off many wins in a row once they start building up some momentum.
But things have to turn around fast. A loss in Week 5 against their AFC South rival Tennessee Titans for an 0-5 record could be the nail in the coffin for any dreams of a late-season comeback. So expect Stroud to keep focused as ever, and hope to inspire his defense to follow suit.

title: Why Texans Made a Subtle Change to QB Davis Mills' Contract
full_text:
The Houston Texans have made a small, but potentially meaningful change, to the contract of backup quarterback Davis Mills.
According to KPRC2 's Aaron Wilson , the Texans have converted $3.7 million of Mills' contract in signing bonus from salary, while also adding four void years from 2027 to 2030 for proration purposes.
The move isn't an extension on Mills' contract. He's still slated to be an unrestricted free agent after the 2026 season, as he was when entering the year.
However, the move does have some other notable implications that matter, both for the sake of the Texans' current salary cap situation and perhaps for the future of Mills in Houston.
The Texans' move to change Mills' contract probably isn't any adjustment that would put the quarterback's roster spot in jeopardy this season. Houston clearly likes what their QB2 brings to the table as a reliable plug-and-play signal-caller if and when his services are ever needed.
So no, he's not going to be put on the trade block anytime soon . What this move does do, though, is offer the Texans some immediate cap relief by transitioning Mills' salary to a signing bonus, and creates further flexibility around their roster as a whole.
Now, the Texans are able to stretch their overall salary cap number to over $6.2 million, which tends to matter for the sake of any pending or upcoming roster additions, or even players on injured reserve.
Houston needed more operating space to work with, and by making a minor tweak to their QB2's expiring contract, they're able to do just that without rocking the boat much at all.
As previously noted, the Texans will still be faced with the implications of Mills' expiring contract after this season, even with the restructure.
However, the move on Mills' contract does leave a good bit of dead money on the books for the Texans––only in the event that the veteran quarterback isn't extended on a new deal before he hits the open market.
According to @TexansCap on X , the Texans will be due to pay $2.977 in dead money on Mills' deal if he is not extended by February 14th— two days after this season's Super Bowl.
Houston Texans and Davis Mills completed a contract restructure, creating $2.707 million in cap savings for 2026. Four (4) void years were added for salary cap purposes, leaving a $2.977 million dead money charge in 2027 if Mills is not extended by Feb 16, 2027.
So while it might not truly cement that Mills could inevitably be around for longer than this season, willingly attaching potential dead money to the end of his deal feels like a bit of a hint that the Texans could extend their backup to a new deal , rather than letting him become a free agent in 2027.
The Texans proved before the 2025 season started when giving Mills a one-year, $8 million extension that they valued Mills as a fixture of their quarterback room, and there's nothing in that deal that would indicate Houston is feeling differently now.
If anything, Mills became even further cemented into his spot as the Texans' QB2 after his three-game starting stretch from last year, where he was able to be a more than serviceable option under center and rattle off a perfect 3-0 record that sparked Houston's late-season comeback en route to 12 wins.
So perhaps in due time, you could expect the Texans and Mills to agree to terms on a new extension ––whether that be during the season or after. But for now, it's a simple restructure that provides Houston a tad bit more flexibility on the books for this year.

title: 3 Biggest Texans Concerns That Could Cost Them Again in Week 5
full_text:
The Houston Texans have looked far from perfect through the start of their 2026 campaign, which has inevitably left them with a deep 0-4 hole to climb out of moving forward.
This week, the Texans have a date with their AFC South rival Tennessee Titans on tap , which could offer a great opportnity for Houston to get back on track. The Titans are one of four teams in the NFL still left with a winless record at this point in the year, and have a combined record of 6-32 dating back to 2024.
However, for the Texans to right the ship in Week 5 in Nashville, there's a select few concerns this team will have to iron out to flip the script from their past four weeks. And if those aren't solved, maybe a Titans upset wouldn't be crazy to imagine.
Let's sort through three of the biggest concerns the Texans need to address heading into Week 5 with hopes they can spark their first win of the new season:
The Texans' run game has been among the worst in the NFL through four games.
While the Texans' five rushing touchdowns place them within the top 10 teams in the league for the stat, their total rushing yards (335) and yards per carry (3.4) rank in the bottom five.
David Montgomery hasn't seen the same highs he reached in Week 1 with his hat trick of touchdowns, and while Woody Marks has looked a bit better than his rookie campaign, his upside of explosiveness and pass-catching ability still hasn't been able to save Houston's gloomy results on the ground.
Everyone in the building knows the run game has to take a step forward this week. DeMeco Ryans has made it an emphasis heading into this weekend, C.J. Stroud made it clear that he wants to see better success following Week 4's loss, and could lead to the running backs being more involved this Sunday.
If those blocks upfront continue not to hold up, though, or the running backs can't find any sense of efficiency in the opportunities they get, it'll once again be tough sledding for this offense to really build the necessary momentum to be the balanced group they want to be.
Head coach DeMeco Ryans returning to his post as the Texans' defensive play-caller might be able to inspire the change Houston needs on their defense. But what Houston really needs to get right on the defensive side of the ball is their secondary––because things have been rough four games in.
The Texans are one of six teams in the NFL to have allowed over 1,000 yards through four weeks of action. Keep in mind, this Houston defense has what many considered to be the best secondary unit on paper heading into the season, but now has numbers that rank them near the bottom of the pack.
Kamari Lassiter has been underwhelming by allowing over 100 yards in two of his four games. Reed Blankenship's fit in the secondary hasn't been as seamless as many had imagined, and leaves this defense with a huge problem to solve in order to lift back to their elite status of 2025.
Houston will have a much-easier task on their hands this week against a Tennessee passing offense, who's ranked in the bottom five of the league for total passing yards and passing touchdowns. So if this game can't offer a get-right opportunity for the Texans' secondary, it's hard to find a game on the schedule that will.
On one hand, the Texans' offense has done a great job of controlling the ball and limiting giveaways pretty effectively through the past four games.
Particularly in the case of C.J. Stroud, while he did give up two fumbles in game one against the Buffalo Bills , he has yet to throw an interception in any of his four starts thus far. That's a big win for the Texans' quarterback.
Yet, at the same time, the Texans' defense hasn't been able to complement Stroud's play with many giveaways coming their way.
Houston has gone without recording a turnover in three of their four games thus far, with their only takeaways coming in Week 3 against turnover-prone Daniel Jones and the Indianapolis Colts, and even those couldn't help get a win on the board.
Coming out in Nashville to claim at least one turnover–– if not more–– will be key for the Texans to play to their full potential. If not, it puts more weight on Stroud's shoulders to carry the load offensively, and that doesn't tend to be as great of a formula for success as a dominant defensive day would be.

title: Texans' Poor 0-4 Start Isn't Fooling Titans' Cam Ward, Robert Saleh
full_text:
The Houston Texans have their second AFC South game of the year on tap for this weekend as they'll be traveling to Nashville for a date with the Tennessee Titans .
And it's a massive game for both sides. Each side has suffered from four straight losses to open the new year, is hungry to flip the script this weekend, and avoid extending that streak to build some momentum in their race to climb up the division standings, and the AFC as a whole.
So one of these 0-4 teams is leaving this weekend with a win. And it seems like, even with such a gloomy record, the Titans certainly won't be overlooking the talent this Texans roster will bring to the table for Week 5 .
It's clear those in the Titans' building have been talking up what the Texans will be bringing to the table throughout this week––because there are a select few who haven't been shy to express how Houston's talent goes beyond what their record on the season says.
Titans quarterback Cam Ward was among those in Tennessee to applaud the type of talent the Texans have, as he would call them one of the best 0-4 teams in the NFL while previewing the Week 5 matchup on Wednesday.
"Every division game is a rivalry. That's one thing we want to do, is own the South," Ward said this week. "We've got a great opportunity versus them, and they gonna be excited. They look at us the the same exact way as we look at them: we're both 0-4 teams. We're both searching for a win this year. And it could really get us going the right direction."
"But it's going to be an exciting game. They're one of the best 0-4 teams out there in the NFL, and they're going to have their hands full when they come play us as well."
Yet it's not just Ward who's keeping all hands on deck for the challenge the Texans will bring this weekend. Titans head coach Robert Saleh was even more complimentary about Houston's roster, touting them as maybe "the greatest 0-4 team in the history of football."
"Might be the greatest 0-4 team in the history of football," Saleh said of the Texans. "Their defense is, obviously, one of the top-five units in all of football. They've lost four games to four really, really good football teams... They've been in a lot of really, really tight games. I think they've all come down to the last second, with the exception of maybe Cincinnati."
"But, overall, well coached. A lot of respect for DeMeco and his staff. Playmakers all over the place on defense. Nico Collins is there. C.J. Stroud plays at a high level. They're putting up a lot of points and yards on offense. And it's going to be a tremendous challenge."
Of course, all of that praise from a divisional opponent is certainly nice for the Texans to hear heading into their matchup after facing a bundle of criticism through the past several weeks. But at the end of the day, talk is cheap.
A loss against Tennessee might just end up being the dagger for any dream of a 2025-esque comeback for Houston. So DeMeco Ryans and his crew are going to have to ensure they have all of their operations tightened up to land their first win of the year against a divisional opponent they've frequently taken care of in recent memory.
Houston has won six of their last seven games against Tennessee dating back to 2022. Time will tell if they can add to that win total this weekend and prove those in the Titans' building right that this is indeed one of the best 0-4 teams in the league.

title: What Texans' Will Anderson Jr. Said About DeMeco Ryans Calling Plays
full_text:
The Houston Texans' defense will be making some changes heading into their Week 5 game against the Tennessee Titans .
Rather than Texans' defensive coordinator Matt Burke continuing to be the team's lead defensive play-caller, head coach DeMeco Ryans announced on Wednesday that he could be reclaiming the role as defensive play-caller this weekend against Tennessee.
The move effectively places Ryans back in the same role that he was in when he first arrived in Houston back in 2023. He had been the Texans' defensive play-caller for two years, and had relative success in the process, though decided to make a pivot in those operations last season.
After the Texans' 0-3 start in 2025, it was Burke who would take those duties over from Ryans en route to their 12-win season. And now, the two will be reverting back to their previous ways in hopes they can spark a similar change from their even-worse 0-4 start.
It's a move that many have suggested could be a possibility for the Texans to try out in hopes of getting their defense back on track from the up-and-down start they've had to the season.
Ryans noted upon his announcement that being the play-caller is no slight on Burke's abilities, yet allowed for the communication process to be a bit more streamlined on that side of the ball–– which has seemingly been an issue through four games of the season.
But how do the players on the Texans' defense feel about the shift?
In Will Anderson's mind, Ryans brings a different style of coaching: one that's more direct, but also allows for a bit of grace.
"I think what DeMeco brings–– that style of coaching where he's going to call you out. He's going to make sure that you know exactly what you're going to do, what you need to do and what you didn't do," Anderson said.
"I think he gives grace, but he's also going to hold people accountable. He's going to come in the meeting because he played this game, and he knows, like, 'Hey, man, you ain't repping our style right here."
So from Anderson's perspective, it feels like a positive change. The Texans' can get a more direct style of coaching, more direct communication, and hope to lead to better results on the defensive end.
Through four games this season, the Texans have allowed the 26th-most points scored and the 20th-most yards in the NFL on top of their brutal 0-4 start .
For a defense that many expected to be at the top of the league in terms of effectiveness, something had to change. And now, Ryans will be the one leading the ship defensively, and hope to turn things around in the process.
"I think it comes a little differently when it comes from DeMeco," Anderson continued. "When DeMeco's up there, you sit up a little bit more. You're more on your P's and Q's. Nothing against Burke. Burke's done a good job, but when the head coach is up there, it's kind of different."
"We have a ton of respect for him. He's going to get a lot of guys going with the energy that he brings. So, I'm excited for that."
Getting the right play-caller for this defense would be a big step for this Texans' defense to get back on track. That process becomes even easier when you've got the buy-in of one of the best defenders in the NFL . So perhaps this is the week where Houston flips the script for their first win of the new year.

title: Texans Sign Former Titans WR to Roster Just Before Week 5 Matchup
full_text:
The Houston Texans have added a depth piece to their wide receiver room just a few days ahead of their Week 5 matchup against the Tennessee Titans ––doing so by adding a pass-catcher who played in Tennessee a little less than two months ago.
According to an announcement from the Texans, the team has signed wide receiver Bryce Oliver to the 53-man roster.
Oliver is actually a recent part of the Texans' practice squad as well, considering he was in the facility for a two-week stretch in September . Houston added him as a part of the practice squad following his release from the Titans on cutdown day, yet the Texans would also release him on September 30th.
Fast forward to right ahead of Week 5, and the Texans seemingly wanted to bring Oliver back onboard, thus offering another layer of depth at the position, and even someone who was a part of the opposition for the past couple of years.
Oliver, 26, is a 6-foot-1, 214-pound wideout in his third year pro, and was a pretty regular piece of the Titans' receiver room for two years from 2024 to 2025.
An undrafted product out of Youngstown State, Oliver has played in 13 games throughout his NFL career thus far, all of those coming in Tennessee.
He's played in over 200 combined offensive and special teams snaps from his two years stationed there, and has hauled in seven receptions on 10 targets for 103 yards. He's also recorded three kick returns for 113 yards in 2024.
So he's not exactly the most experienced pass-catcher at the NFL level just yet. Most of his offensive production stems from his college days at Youngstown State. However, the Texans saw some value in him to bring him back aboard to their main roster, and clearly have a role in mind for him.
Oliver's signing now makes for the Texans' second practice squad reunion of the week, considering the front office opted to bring back quarterback Mark Gronkowski on Wednesday, thus giving this depth chart a third signal caller to lean on.
Heading into the Texans' Week 5 game against Tennessee, they had five wide receivers on their active roster before bringing in Oliver. Now, that total rises to six, and feels like a sign that the former Titans wideout will be primarily commanding special teams duties.
The Texans already have a solid dose of receivers on the roster due for their respective reps on the offensive side: Nico Collins, Xavier Hutchinson, Jaylin Noel, and Kayshon Boutte easily rise above him, and maybe even Jared Wayne.
There's also Tank Dell, who's presence on the team simply can't be ignored at this point in the season . He's officially seen his 21-day return window activated from injured reserve, hinting at Houston's wide receiver room will likely have another target to roster here in the coming weeks.
So for Oliver to make an impact, that gravity will have to come from outside of the offensive side of the ball and onto the special teams side. Or, he'll simply have to be moved up the depth chart in the event of any injury above him, which has yet to be reported within the wide receiver room as of Wednesday's injury report.
His first opportunity to do so will also come against the team he started his career with in Tennessee on Sunday at 12 PM MT, if he is indeed activated for game day.
