title: What Kellen Moore, Saints Players Said After Embarrassing Loss to Falcons
full_text:
The New Orleans Saints gave the city little reason to celebrate after their crushing 45-24 loss to the Atlanta Falcons on Monday evening.
On a night commemorating the 20th anniversary of the Domecoming , Atlanta spoiled the occasion by jumping on New Orleans early and never relinquishing control. The Falcons rushed for 205 yards, produced several explosive plays and sent the Saints to 1-3.
Afterward, head coach Kellen Moore and several Saints players addressed the slow start, defensive breakdowns, turnovers and the disappointment of falling flat on such a meaningful night.
On his opening thoughts after the loss:
“Really disappointing game for us. Obviously, I thought the Dome was an incredible night, incredible energy. We obviously did a poor job just preparing our football team. We really, in all three phases, did not do enough to win this game. Atlanta came in and played a lot better than us.
“I didn't coach well enough, play well enough, so obviously, it wasn't good enough. We're at where we're at. We're a 1-3 football team with some good moments, but not enough consistent football to be where we ultimately want to be. We have a lot of work to do. There's a path for us, but it's going to take a lot of work to get there. We've got to keep going.”
On the Saints' continued slow starts:
“It is just disappointing. Obviously, not coaching it well enough, not executing well enough. They came out, went right down the field and scored. We went three-and-out and didn't score until the second quarter.”
On whether the Saints have tried changing things to start faster:
“We have tried a number of different things. Obviously, we have to solve this. We have to find a way.”
On the team's preparation:
“I just think, at the end of the day, they executed better than us. They played faster than us. They, obviously, ran the ball really well, created some explosive plays in the pass game. On our side of it, we weren't able to run the ball well enough. We turned the ball over, and that's a challenging formula.”
On the struggles running the football:
“We weren't able to run well, and we weren't able to put ourselves in position to have the opportunities to continue to run it and find that ability to finally get it going. When you fall behind, you play in some different circumstances. Obviously, you are going to have to adjust the plan.”
On the significance of the Domecoming game:
“We talked about it at the beginning of the week. The guys were fired up. I thought there was good energy. We just didn't execute well enough in the beginning, and they got going.”
On whether preparation was an issue:
“I don't think there's a lack of preparation. I think there's a lack of execution on some of it. We were prepared. I think the turnover early killed us, and we've got to be able to put some of those early drives together and score more points early on to get it going.
“As an offense, we knew exactly what went wrong and what went right. We just have to clean up those little things and take responsibility for that. I have to be able to put us in the right position to go out and do that. There's a lot to learn from. It obviously sucks, but we're going to keep going.”
On his left hand getting hit in the first quarter:
“Yeah, I took a helmet or something to it. I think it was just bruised up, so it should be good. I was able to play the rest of the game.”
On whether the injury affected his grip or throwing:
“No. It was just part of it. It didn't affect my right hand, obviously, so it was just something to deal with.”
On the disappointment considering the significance of the game:
“It is extremely disappointing. It is embarrassing. You can't say enough good things about the fans showing up and the entire process, what this game meant, and we fell short as a team to not get that win. That was our mission. That was my message, and we did not win.
“It was a team loss. We've got to do better on all fronts. As an offense, we have to start faster when we are going against another really good offense and be able to do our part. We've got to do a lot better there, and it starts with myself.”
On the mood in the locker room:
“Disappointed. More than anything, you lose to the Falcons like that, especially on a Monday night game, and it sucks. You can't say, ‘Oh, man that doesn't suck.’ It definitely does.
“But I do know as a team that we're extremely close and that we're going to keep going and keep our eyes forward. We have really good leadership, and our leadership admits that we've got to get better. We have to get better, watch the film and evaluate that. There's no hiding that.
“But at the same time, it is a long season, and there are a lot of games yet to be played where we can do that. There's nothing set in stone. We know that, and that's the best part about this business is that we're going to keep climbing.”
On the disappointment of the loss:
“I hate that we had a slow start. We got punched in the mouth early and look at the response. It's one of those games where we weren't good on offense, defense or special teams. You look at the second half and are ready to fight back.
“When you play a division rival it's like playing two games. When you have the Falcons coming into our building, you have to be ready. They had an early score with Bijan [Robinson]. At that point with 60 yards on the ground, we have to figure something out.
“They had almost 200 yards rushing (205). That's on the defensive line. When you have a ground game like that, then you have to tell the defensive line to tighten up. Our secondary had to come down and try to focus on the run and then that's when they have their way. They had their way tonight. It's embarrassing.”
On why the Saints couldn't stop Atlanta's rushing attack:
“Without sounding redundant. A 60-yard (59) touchdown. We didn't shut down our run defense. Our run defense did not show up to play early on. A 60-yard touchdown.
“From there, they see that their zone schemes are working, so they relied on that. For whatever reason, we couldn't tighten up our gaps. Our gap integrity has to be at a premium, especially when you have a top-tier back like Bijan or any running back the way that we were playing. It just wasn't good enough.”
On what the Saints should expect moving forward:
“Football is not always what you expect it to be. It is a good thing that we have 17 weeks. We have to stay encouraged. We have to have the mindset that this is not a defining moment.
“We can't take a step back because the rear view mirror is smaller than the front mirror. So, let's just keep it there.”
On whether someone needs to speak up after the loss:
“Nobody has to speak for it. Nobody says we have to step it up. Everyone knows that. Go make plays. Make this happen. We start with turnovers. We start with shooting ourselves in the foot. It's all obvious.
“We know that and we all have to be intentional about it. We play smarter ball and the results are different. These are all things that we can control. The outcome will be the outcome. We just have to control what we control and let the results speak for themselves.”
On whether Atlanta's play-action game surprised the Saints:
“We weren't surprised. We feel like we knew what they were going to do, but we just have to be better. Keep your eyes open and be ready to defend anything that you are going to get.”
On what hurt the Saints defensively:
“No, we just feel like we didn't play our best game and they played one of their best games. Congrats to them.”
On whether Atlanta's running game opened everything else up:
“I mean, we know that they are going to get some runs off. We just have to be better all across the board including the run game and pass game.”
On the offense's performance:
“There are a lot of things that we have to fix. We started out slow. We talk about starting fast and we didn't do that. We lost the ball as well. There are a lot of things here and there.
“There was a lot of emotions this game. Obviously, it was a tough…

title: Saints Humiliated by Rival Falcons in 45-24 Monday Night Rout
full_text:
In what was supposed to be a night of celebration for New Orleans and its resilience following Hurricane Katrina, with the game designated as the 20th anniversary of the Domecoming, the Atlanta Falcons made it a night of dread.
The Falcons defeated the New Orleans Saints 45-24, and it was not close from start to finish as the Falcons led the entire way . The Falcons outgained the Saints 410-320, but the margins really separated them in yards per play. Atlanta averaged 7.5 yards per play while New Orleans averaged 4.6.
While Atlanta quarterback Michael Penix threw efficiently, completing 15 of 20 passes for 220 yards and a touchdown, its rushing attack killed the Saints.
The Falcons rushed for 205 yards after Bijan Robinson and Brian Robinson ran roughshod over the Saints’ depleted defense.
Bijan Robinson had 19 carries for 145 yards and two touchdowns, while Brian Robinson had 14 carries for 62 yards and three touchdowns.
Tyler Shough did have a decent game, completing 30 of 48 passes for 288 yards and a touchdown. Chris Olave had a quiet but productive day, catching 8 for 114 yards, but it was overshadowed by the beatdown the Falcons put on the Saints.
Tyler Shough did have a decent game, completing 30 of 48 passes for 288 yards and a touchdown. Chris Olave had a quiet but productive day, catching 8 for 114 yards, but it was overshadowed by the beatdown the Falcons put on the Saints.
Otherwise, the Saints had no bright spots offensively, rushing the ball 15 times for 50 yards, an average of 2.6 yards per carry. Meanwhile, Atlanta averaged nearly 6 yards per carry.
The first half was another slow start for the Saints as they trailed 24-7 at halftime.
The Falcons had the ball on the first possession and needed only three plays to score.
After Penix found Drake London and tight end Austin Hooper for gains of 12 and 9 yards, Bijan Robinson got the handoff, bounced to the outside and proceeded to go 59 yards to the house untouched to take an early 7-0 lead with 13:43 left in the first quarter.
On its second drive, New Orleans looked as if it were finally going to get something going offensively. However, a third-down stop by Atlanta led to a 52-yard field goal attempt by Daniel Carlson that he hooked to the left.
Luckily, the Saints’ defense made up for it with a quick three-and-out. Then disaster struck.
Saints running back Kendre Miller coughed up the ball on the first play and the Falcons recovered it. Miller was originally ruled down before an official review reversed the decision.
A few plays later, Bijan Robinson scored his second touchdown rush of the game to give Atlanta a 14-0 lead with 52 seconds left in the first quarter.
The Saints responded quickly as Shough unloaded a 44-yard pass to Olave that put the Saints on the 10-yard line. Two plays later, Alvin Kamara scored his first rushing touchdown of the season from 3 yards out to cut Atlanta’s lead to seven points.
That’s where the fun stopped.
Atlanta scored on the ensuing possession as Brian Robinson reached paydirt on a 4-yard touchdown run to finish off a 10-play, 65-yard drive to take a 21-7 lead.
The Falcons scored the final points of the half on a 29-yard field goal from Nick Folk .
The Saints entered the second half needing something close to a complete reversal after Atlanta built a 24-7 halftime lead. Instead, the Falcons continued to control the game and never allowed New Orleans to seriously threaten their advantage.
New Orleans opened the third quarter with one of its better sustained drives of the night. Tyler Shough moved the offense downfield with completions to Olave, Juwan Johnson and Kamara, but the Saints stalled before reaching the end zone and settled for a Carlson field goal to cut Atlanta's lead to 24-10.
Atlanta immediately answered.
Penix connected with Jahan Dotson for a chunk gain before Bijan Robinson continued to punish the Saints on the ground. London later moved the chains through the air, and Brian Robinson Jr. finished the possession with his second rushing touchdown of the night, stretching Atlanta's advantage to 31-10.
The Saints finally found the end zone again early in the fourth quarter. Shough connected with Devaughn Vele and Kamara during the drive before Kamara powered into the end zone for his second touchdown, trimming the deficit to 31-17.
Any hope of a comeback disappeared almost immediately.
Atlanta responded with another explosive scoring drive, highlighted by a 28-yard catch-and-run from Kyle Pitts and Penix's 31-yard touchdown pass to Dotson. After the Falcons' defense stopped New Orleans on downs, Brian Robinson broke loose for his third touchdown of the game to make it 45-17.
New Orleans added a late touchdown when Shough found Vele in the back of the end zone, but by then the outcome had long been decided.
Vele finished with six catches for 54 yards
The Saints were able to move the football more effectively after halftime, but nearly every positive stretch was answered by Atlanta. The Falcons scored 21 second-half points and consistently prevented New Orleans from turning the game into a legitimate comeback, finishing off a 45-24 victory.

title: Saints vs. Falcons: 3 Keys to Victory for New Orleans on Monday Night
full_text:
Sign up for the daily Saints Newsletter by clicking here .
As NFC South action kicks off on Monday Night Football, the spotlight turns to the Crescent City for one of the NFL's most heated rivalries.
At the Caesars Superdome, the New Orleans Saints welcome the Atlanta Falcons . Both teams hold 1-2 records, making this divisional showdown a key chance to get back to .500 and seize early momentum in the division.
The Saints are eager to recover from a disappointing 35-27 loss to the Las Vegas Raiders , a game in which four consecutive second-half giveaways squandered a double-digit lead. The Falcons, meanwhile, arrive in New Orleans buoyed by a convincing 35-14 victory over the Green Bay Packers .
Monday's contest represents the Saints' initial Monday Night Football home game since hosting the Tampa Bay Buccaneers in 2022. It also marks their first night game overall since an Oct. 17, 2024, clash against the Denver Broncos —a pair of games that both ended in New Orleans losses.
If the Saints want bragging rights and to stay on the right path, here are three keys to victory against the Dirty Birds.
While Atlanta boasts the league's top-ranked run defense—yielding only 47.7 yards per game without allowing a single rushing touchdown—their secondary has proven to be a major vulnerability.
With the Falcons surrendering 263 passing yards per game (29th in the NFL), New Orleans has a strong tactical edge. The Saints enter averaging 281.3 yards through the air, ranking third overall.
This presents a clear opening for quarterback Tyler Shough . Instead of stubbornly challenging Atlanta's stout front line, New Orleans should capitalize on Shough, Chris Olave , and the aerial attack to generate downfield shots against a struggling Atlanta secondary.
And with Travis Etienne Jr . out for the foreseeable future, the Saints’ rushing attack will take a hit, so they might just need to throw the rock around.
Atlanta running back Bijan Robinson enters the NFC South matchup as one of the NFL's most productive offensive players. Through three games, the Falcons running back has rushed for 349 yards and two touchdowns on 66 carries, averaging 5.3 yards per attempt. Add his 13 receptions for 118 yards and a touchdown, and Robinson leads the NFL with 467 yards from scrimmage.
The Saints also will be dealing with a player coming off his best performance of the season. Robinson shredded Green Bay for 194 yards and two touchdowns on 29 carries, including a 55-yard run, while adding two catches for 19 yards. Atlanta finished with 242 rushing yards and controlled possession for more than 37 minutes in its 35-14 victory. Robinson was subsequently named NFC Offensive Player of the Week.
This one should be straightforward after what happened against Las Vegas.
New Orleans committed four consecutive turnovers in the second half of its 35-27 loss to the Raiders, turning what had been a double-digit Saints advantage into a frustrating defeat. The Saints enter Monday with a minus-4 turnover differential, ranking near the bottom of the NFL.
Atlanta has its own turnover problems — the Falcons enter at an NFL-worst minus-6 — making possession potentially one of the biggest deciding factors Monday night.
The Saints have shown they can move the football and score. They simply cannot give Atlanta extra possessions, especially in a rivalry game that could come down to one or two critical mistakes.

title: Giants OC Matt Nagy Welcomes Malik Nabers’ Demand for the Ball
full_text:
To quote the fictional yet legendary Washington Sentinels coach Jimmy McGinty, “Winners always want the ball when the game is on the line.”
So when New York Giants receiver Malik Nabers openly asks for a bigger role in the team’s passing game, offensive coordinator Matt Nagy is more than willing to let life imitate some of “The Replacements” art.
“I do really like it as long as it’s done the right way,” Nagy said of Nabers’ recent remarks. “Malik is without a doubt one of the most talented players that I’ve ever been around. And he’s one of the most competitive too. So, you morph those two together.”
Despite his standout performance in New York’s Week 4 victory over the Arizona Cardinals, a game in which he compiled 112 receiving yards and one touchdown, Nabers was quite vocal about his desire to be used in the deep passing game during the second half.
In fact, the sixth overall pick in the 2024 NFL Draft was spotted expressing his frustrations on the sidelines.
“I felt like I didn’t get targeted much after halftime,” Nabers told reporters on Wednesday. “I felt like creating explosive plays down the field was just helping us get in a better position to score touchdowns. Some of those plays didn’t come my way, so I’m just trying to figure out why.
“During the first half when we did that, it kind of led us in the right direction, and we scored touchdowns in the red zone,” he added. “After that, we just couldn’t get going. So, I felt like the offense was needing a spark and I wanted to be that spark.”
While some have tried to label Nabers’ actions as disruptive, Nagy understands his intentions were purely helpful. Nagy is best known for using pre-snap motion to create misdirection for opposing defenses, but the deep passing game can succeed under his watch.
If Nabers believes he can be even more effective as the driving force of an offense that showcases quarterback Jameis Winston’s arm strength, Nagy is certainly going to encourage his young star receiver to demand the ball, as long as it is done respectfully.
“You’re crazy if you take that away from somebody,” Nagy said. “We want to get him the football. So, he knows that. But you’ve got to make sure that probably the best way to think of it is that it’s constructive and not destructive in how that happens.”
Fortunately for both Nagy and the Giants, Nabers appeared eager and able to play against the Washington Commanders in the upcoming Week 5 matchup at Northwest Stadium. As he continues to deal with lingering knee and shoulder injuries , the 23-year-old remains intent on adding to the 18 catches for 208 yards and one touchdown he has compiled in New York’s first four games.
If Nabers wants to help the Giants improve to 4-1 on the season, he’ll want the ball with the game on the line. Nagy’s task, should he choose to accept it, will be not only to scheme up situations where his top receiver can be effective, but also to channel his inner “McGinty” by realizing that “winners always do.”
“That’s important, and he’s still young,” Nagy said. “We’re still going through that process. We’re four games into it together … I’ve got thick skin. I can handle it. But we want to make sure that it’s for us and it doesn’t cross the line.
“We had a great conversation, and he’s in a great spot,” he concluded. “We definitely want to get him the ball a lot.”

title: Giants RB Cam Skattebo Good to Go for Sunday; Can't Wait to Get the Ball
full_text:
After missing most of last season with a dislocated ankle, not much is going to keep New York Giants running back Cam Skattebo off the bench.
That includes the shoulder ailment that landed him on the injury report this week and resulted in him being told to wear a red no-contact jersey during Wednesday’s practice.
“My shoulder's okay,” Skattebo said on Friday after the team wrapped up its practice. “I literally had a little bit of muscle tightness in my back, and over the last couple of days I've worked it out, and I feel great.”
Skattebo finished the week limited but did not receive an injury designation for this weekend’s game at Washington, and that’s a good thing for the Giants, who will more than likely lean heavily (again) into their running game if the miserable,  wet conditions forecast for Sunday hold.
“I already told Coach Nags (Offensive Coordinator Matt Nagy), ‘Just give me the ball, we'll be fine,’” Skattebo said with a grin.
In other injury-related news, safety Jason Pinnock (concussion) is not expected to clear the concussion protocol in time for this week’s game, so he’s been declared out. Also, defensive lineman Chauncey Golston, who has been dealing with a neck injury that he suffered last week, is expected to land on IR by Saturday, so he too has been declared out.
Additional positive news includes left tackle Andrew Thomas (groin), tight end Isaiah Likely (knee/groin), tight end Chris Manhertz (shoulder), and Skattebo all being upgraded to full practice participants.

title: How the Giants Can Attack Washington’s Vulnerable Pass Defense
full_text:
Entering Week 5 of the 2026 NFL season, the New York Giants sit atop the NFC East. This week, they head to Landover, Maryland, to take on the Commanders in their second divisional matchup.
Whatever people think, this Washington squad will be difficult to beat largely due to its defense. They are formidable against the run but leave openings in their pass coverage. They do surrender a lot of points, and the Giants will look to follow suit.
Let’s take a look at the Commanders’ defense.
The Commanders spend a majority of their time in a 4-2-5-based defense. When they want to be more robust against the run, they will adjust to a 4-3 over/under front.
They want to keep four down linemen on the field at all times to combat the run and use varying packages to try to rush the quarterback with four guys.
With their two primary linebackers holding down the inside, they need linebackers who can run sideline to sideline.
Rookie linebacker Sonny Styles has been playing well while moving all over the field. He has 20 tackles, including two tackles for loss, a forced fumble, and a sack.
In pass coverage, he has two passes defensed and an interception.
The Commanders' primary coverage is a Cover 3 shell, which is one high safety manning the middle of the field.
The two corners usually stay deep, and each takes a third of the field, along with the free safety.
In a traditional Cover 3, four defenders take away the primary and intermediate areas, which are the quarterback's normal passing lanes.
The Commanders' pass defense ranks 29th in DVOA and 23rd in passing yards allowed, averaging 242.5 yards per game through the air. This is clearly not one of their strongest areas on defense, and the Giants should look to take advantage of it.
Nickel back Mike Sainristil handles most of the work in the slot, covering any elite pass receivers who line up there. He will definitely need to be monitored, as he is a solid pass defender and will make plays if the quarterback gets lazy or careless with his passes.
Frankie Luvu and Odafe Oweh pair with Daron Payne on the inside to give Washington a formidable interior/exterior/blitzer pass rush.
Despite ranking seventh in run defense DVOA, the Commanders still give up over 100 yards a game on the ground. They rank 11th overall in rush defense, surrendering just under 104 rushing yards per game.
Payne is the Commanders' best interior run defender on the defensive line. He provides the physicality and knockback ability to reset the offensive line in the negative, and he has the athleticism to chase down rushers.
Luvu and the rookie Styles can run anything produced by the opposing rushing attack down, regardless of where it's designed to hit.
Luvu is a quick downhill-trigger linebacker who will thump you, and Styles provides elite-level athleticism at the position.
Together, they can wreak havoc and give the defense the flexibility to avoid having a third stand-up linebacker on the field.
Former Kansas City Chiefs linebacker Leo Chenal is out for the season, which dramatically hurts the Commanders' depth at the position. Luvu and Styles have also dealt with injuries that have kept them out of practice.
Safeties Percy Butler and Tyler Owens have also dealt with injuries that have kept them out of practice, along with defensive end Charles Omenihu, who has been on the injury report.
The Giants will need to soften up the Washington run defense by keeping them off balance with early-down throwing opportunities. It can't just be run on first down, run on second down, and then put it in Jameis Winston's hands and expect him to pick up a first down.
They need to invest in early-down throws that put them in second-and-short and short, where the entire playbook opens up, and they can be less predictable.
If pass coverage is Washington's weakness, the Giants need to be strongest there, even if the weather isn't likely to be ideal.

title: Giants Rookie Arvell Reese Is Just Getting Started, Says Dennard Wilson
full_text:
New York Giants defensive coordinator Dennard Wilson never doubted that rookie defender Arvell Reese was meant to be an NFL linebacker.
Since his days as an Ohio State standout, the 6-foot-4, 243-pounder has had a triple-threat skill set that lets him stop the run, drop into coverage, and rush the passer. As a result, Reese has found comfort playing all over the field.
Still, Wilson believes the No. 5 overall pick in the 2026 NFL Draft is at his best when aligned inside.
“When you watched him play at Ohio State, when he was off the ball, he made a huge impact,” Wilson said. “He can read. He can dissect. He's just a natural linebacker.
“We always thought that the subset was him to go forward as a defensive lineman. We thought that it would have been harder to teach him to go forward than him playing off the ball first because it was a new world for him. So, when we saw him, there was no question from day one that he was a linebacker, and that's how we always viewed him.”
After a stellar performance throughout training camp and into the preseason, Reese earned the starting spot on the weak side of head coach John Harbaugh's defense. Through the first four games of the season, he leads the team in total tackles with 34.
In New York’s Week 4 victory over the Arizona Cardinals, Reese turned in a defensive masterpiece, logging nine solo tackles, one tackle for loss, three passes defensed, one quarterback hit, and one interception.
He also became the fifth Giants rookie with three or more passes defensed and an interception in a game, and the only Giants rookie since 1994 with nine or more tackles, three or more passes defensed and at least one interception in a game. For his efforts, Reese earned Pepsi NFL Rookie of the Week honors.
As he continues to grow in prowess, Reese will be asked to take on a more prominent role within the Giants’ defense — a point that Wilson readily acknowledges. With New York’s Week 5 showdown against the Washington Commanders at Northwest Stadium fast approaching, the 21-year-old is likely to play an integral part in the  defensive game plan.
Fortunately for both him and the Giants, Wilson believes that Reese’s best is yet to come.
“You're starting to see it. Game four of his rookie year, you see the maturation already,” Wilson said. “You see the impact that he's had on his defense. He's a guy that loves football. He's tenacious about it. He doesn't want to be wrong. He's had some plays he wishes he could get back, but he doesn't make those mistakes again.
“When you see him, he is a force of nature when he's on the football field,” he further stated. “We expect him to keep getting better and better.”

title: Giants’ QB Jameis Winston Reveals His One Goal
full_text:
New York Giants quarterback Jameis Winston isn’t worried about what may or may not happen regarding his status as the team’s starting quarterback. Instead, he is taking nothing for granted heading into Week 5 of the 2026 NFL season.
With Big Blue in sole possession of first place in the NFC East for the first time since 2022, Winston knows that it will take his best performance to bring the 3-1 Giants to victory over the Washington Commanders this weekend at Northwest Stadium.
Despite having led New York to a 36-24 victory over the Arizona Cardinals in Week 4 — a game in which he completed 18 passes for 250 yards and three touchdowns — the 12-year veteran is already hard at work to ensure that his team takes home its fourth win of the season.
“My desire is still to get better and better,” Winston said. “It felt good to get a win (against Arizona), but I desire to be so much better for this team and to play faster, to play more precisely, to really be my very best, and I just want to keep getting one percent better every day.”
Though he began the year behind incumbent starter Jaxson Dart, Winston was thrust into the top spot on the depth chart after Dart suffered a season-ending knee injury in the first quarter of their Week 2 loss to the Los Angeles Rams.
Because of his arm strength and greater comfort within the pocket, many questioned whether the 32-year-old was the right fit for coordinator Matt Nagy’s run-centric, motion-based offense.
Still, Winston endured. Having accounted for zero touchdowns in Weeks 2 and 3, the former Florida State quarterback connected with his receivers on three scoring opportunities — ridding himself of a considerable burden in the process.
It should also be noted that Winston’s performance against the Cardinals was far from perfect. At times, questionable decision-making and red-zone struggles led to two interceptions and a roller-coaster feel for much of the game.
For this week’s contest, Winston must live up to the elevated expectations that now surround his team. Fortunately for him and the Giants, Washington’s defense has yet to allow fewer than 24 points in a single game this season.
In fact, they have yielded at least 30 points in each of their last three games. Given Winston’s penchant for explosive plays, New York could be poised to exploit the Commanders’ defensive woes in Week 5.
Of course, even the best of intentions will not matter if Big Blue does not pour every bit of its efforts into playing smart, fundamentally sound football — a process that must begin this week in practice.
Perhaps no one knows this better than Winston.
“We're grateful for where we're at, but at the end of the day, we're playing against a great division opponent, so today we had a pretty good practice,” Winston said.
“But, every single day that we are here preparing, we're getting one percent better to give ourselves a chance to be our very best on Sunday, when it matters most.”

title: Giants WR Malik Nabers' Practice Participation Status Upgraded
full_text:
The New York Giants ' Thursday injury report looked much better than the day prior, as two key offensive starters are trending in the right direction.
Those two starters are offensive tackle Andrew Thomas and receiver Malik Nabers. Thomas has been dealing with a groin injury for the last two weeks, and after sitting out Wednesday’s practice, he was listed as limited on Thursday.
Thomas, the team’s starting left tackle, is clearly having his practice reps managed during the week to keep him fresh and ready to go each week. He appears to be on track for Sunday’s Week 5 game against the Washington Commanders.
Nabers told reporters he felt soreness on Wednesday, which kept him out of practice, and he has been listed with a knee ailment. He participated in Thursday’s practice on a limited basis and appears to be trending in the right direction for Sunday’s game as well.
In even more positive news, running back Cam Skattbo, who has been listed as a limited participant the last two days due to a shoulder injury, was out of the red no-contact jersey that he wore on Wednesday, suggesting that he too is trending in the right direction.
Meanwhile, the Commanders had a mixed bag on their nearly two-dozen-strong injury report this week. Interior offensive lineman Nick Allegretti (hip/achilles) was downgraded from limited to did not participate. Safety Nick Cross (illness) was also downgraded from full to limited.
Three Commanders – guard Sam Cosmi (concussion/throat), tight end Ben Sinnott (rib), and linebacker Sonny Styles (groin) were all upgraded from limited to full.
But Washington's top two receivers, Terry McLaurin (hamstring) and Sefon Diggs (hamstring), missed their second day of practice this week, putting their statuses for Sunday’s game in jeopardy.

title: Greg Newsome II Isn’t Surprised by the Giants’ Defensive Turnaround
full_text:
New York Giants cornerback Greg Newsome II isn't surprised by the team’s defensive resurgence this season.
Despite preseason prognostications of doom — in which one major outlet ranked their secondary 27th in the NFL — the Giants are among the league’s best at forcing turnovers. In fact, New York has eight takeaways through the first four games of 2026.
Though many have been surprised by New York’s recent prowess on the preventive side of the ball,  Newsome believes that their success is simply a byproduct of organizational hard work.
“I think it’s attributed to a lot of things,” Newsome said. “First, our coaches. How we structure practice. We're always doing takeaway things before we get into team activities and things like that.
“Obviously, I think our d-line, our front seven, the guys that are blitzing,” he added. “I think they're doing a great job of just pressuring the quarterback, affecting the quarterback, and just giving us a chance to make plays out there. It's a credit to a lot of things.”
Having ended the 2025 season ranked 27th in total defense, the Giants are currently enjoying a renaissance of sorts.
New York’s defensive unit ranks eighth in scoring defense (allowing 19.8 points per game) and ninth in total defense (314.2 yards per game) — a performance that has the team off to its first 3-1 start since 2022.
While the Giants have improved at all three levels of defense, the secondary has been particularly impressive. Newsome, who signed a one-year deal with New York this offseason, has been a key component in the team’s revival.
The Northwestern product has compiled 18 total tackles, five passes defended, and one interception — a takeaway that came in the second quarter of the team’s 36-24 victory over the Arizona Cardinals in Week 3 at MetLife Stadium.
To keep Big Blue on the right trajectory, coach John Harbaugh is narrowing the team’s collective focus to their next opponent. Rather than entertaining the idea of going 4-1, Harbaugh has adopted a 1-0 mantra for the team’s upcoming Week 5 matchup against the Washington Commanders .
How might the Giants accomplish that goal?
For Newsome, it is simply a matter of his team staying humble and staying the course.
“I mean, we're always humble. We're underdogs every week, so that's enough humbling for us,” Newsome said. “We've got to continue to keep going 1-0 each week. We don't get too high, we don't get too low. It's a long season, so it's great to be 3-1, but we have a lot of football left to play.
“I think we have a lot of vets here that have played meaningful football and know how much each win matters,” he added. “So, we just focus on the next opponent. We don't really care too much about the last game. It's in the past, and now we've got to find a way to go 1-0 this week.”

title: Giants Quarter-Season Report Card: Biggest Surprises and Disappointments Through Four Games
full_text:
The first four games of the New York Giants ' 2026 season have come and gone in a flash, but they've provided a sample size big enough to start evaluating which players on John Harbaugh's roster are making the biggest or smallest impact in their 3-1 start.
Despite many football analysts considering them outsiders in the NFC East race, the Giants have taken the division lead after the first quarter of the season, led by an impressive season-opening win against the pesky Cowboys and two gritty defensive finishes over the Titans and Cardinals.
Not every win has come the same way, but each has come from Harbaugh's players adopting the "1-0" mindset and not letting one play's failure dictate the next.
A select handful of Giants have exemplified that best through one month of action, while a few others have been very disappointing.
One year ago, Deonte Banks was walking the plank out of the Giants organization in the eyes of the fanbase after his worst NFL season in coverage, when he was picked apart and allowed a career-high 81.3% of his targets to be completed.
Banks entered a "prove it" year after the Giants declined his rookie fifth-year option, needing to show he could fix his poor coverage and penalties to perform at the level of a first-round pick. The answer might be the coaching around him, but it's clear the new defensive system is starting to salvage his career.
Banks made his first statement by winning the starting job opposite Greg Newsome II in training camp, and has since been the team's best-graded cornerback in the deep field, with just seven receptions on 16 targets for 42 yards, three pass deflections and an interception despite having missed two games with a calf injury.
For the second time in 10 months, Banks had his handprints all over a huge scoring play for the Giants with the aforementioned interception on the last play of their Week 4 contest with the Arizona Cardinals, which went back 98 yards for the touchdown and highlighted a commanding day for the defense and the team's win.
Penalties haven't been the same issue either, with Banks (No. 2) flagged just once in four games, helping his case to earn a new contract before he hits free agency.
The arrival of undrafted rookie Dominic Zvada has ended the Giants' constant kicking carousel that hurt them in recent seasons and left the position a concern heading into game days.
However, signing a novice specialist rarely comes without early growing pains. That hasn't been the case with Zvada, who has not recorded a single stain on his kicking résumé, converting all nine field goals, including three from 50 yards or more, and all five extra-point attempts.
That puts him in the company of seven kickers who have yet to miss a field goal, and another five who have been perfect from 50-plus yards on at least three attempts.
Zvada was a prospect many doubted would succeed at the next level, especially after his efficiency flunked in his senior season at Michigan, when he converted only 68.2% of his field goals and struggled from longer distances.
Special teams coordinator Chris Horton saw something different in the rookie's potential, and so far that hunch has been validated, with Zvada serving as a huge scoring option over the past couple of games.
Likely was expected to be a top weapon for quarterback Jaxson Dart upon rejoining Harbaugh in New York. With Malik Nabers returning from his 2025 ACL tear, uncertainty remained about which pass catcher the Ole Miss gunslinger would jibe with first.
Until Dart suffered a season-ending meniscus injury, the answer was undoubtedly Likely, who, according to Pro Football Focus, held the highest expected points added (EPA) per play in the league among all quarterback-receiver pairings after Week 3 (+1.66).
Likely's Giants debut saw him lead the team in targets and receptions while tallying 80 yards and two touchdowns to help New York stun its NFC East rival. Since then, opponents have keyed on him more, but he still sits second on the team in receiving production, behind Nabers, with 22 catches for 190 yards.
As the season continues, the Giants hope to get Likely more involved in the offensive attack.
Carter's rookie season picked up steam late in the year, but the other story was the Penn State product's disciplinary run-ins, which stemmed from a lack of maturity and limited his time on the field.
With Harbaugh in command, the No. 3 pick has been performing at a completely different level, matching the potential he showed in college, where he led the nation in sacks in his final season.
Carter has stepped up admirably after the loss of Brian Burns, leading the defense in pass-rush grade (84.7) with 11 pressures, one sack, four hits, and a 28.3% win rate in true pass sets .
Without Brian Burns in the lineup against the Cardinals, Abdul Carter led the Giants with nine pressures, including eight coming in less than 2.5 seconds. No other Giants pass rusher had more than two pressures on the day. #AZvsNYG | #BigBlue pic.twitter.com/Q0rNXiMXwT
Carter dominated in the Giants' latest win over the Arizona Cardinals, recording nine pressures, including eight in under 2.5 seconds, per Next Gen Stats. That's the kind of pass-rushing impact that made the franchise wager a top-three pick on him, and a trend he must continue if he wants to become the next legend.
The Giants were stunned when Arvell Reese fell right into their laps at the fifth pick in the draft, and it's obvious why: He's been one of the league's most productive players through his first four games as a pro.
Not only does he lead the NFL in solo tackles (27), but Reese also ranks 14th among linebackers in defensive grade (77.1), with three pressures, one pass deflection, one interception, and 13 run stops with only one missed tackle, all of which rank him third among his draft class.
Rather than try him out as an extra edge rusher, the Giants wanted to see how Reese would fare as the starting inside linebacker opposite Tremaine Edmunds. He has improved with each game leading into his best outing against the Cardinals, where he posted his lowest passer rating allowed when targeted (52.1) and intercepted a Jacoby Brissett pass attempt.
His lone deficiency has been disrupting passes in coverage. Still, if he improves there, he is an absolute bulldozer on the field, and all signs point to Reese being something special for the Giants defense.
Greg Newsome has been another free-agent signing that has paid dividends for the Giants, who gave him the third-highest average annual value ($8 million) on defense to bolster the man-coverage strengths of their young secondary.
Newsome has provided that as the team's No. 1 corner, allowing a catch on 56.5% of targets for 151 yards and zero touchdowns.
While rare zone coverage looks have dragged his grade (61.6) down a bit, he has excelled in press man, limiting opposing receivers to 39 yards after the catch and tying Banks for the team lead in deflected balls (three).
The 26-year-old veteran came up big on Sunday against the Cardinals, intercepting a deep pass intended for Marvin Harrison Jr. as he and Reese converged on the receiver. It was a huge turnover that likely stopped what could have been Arizona's third straight scoring drive to open the game.
Newsome brings feisty energy on and off the field, and that can't go unnoticed as the Giants defense looks to finally find answers for slowing down elite opposing receivers who typically torment the secondary.
Amid all the constant trade chatter surrounding him, Thibodeaux has once again gotten off to a very slow start in a contract year.
The former fifth overall pick dealt with injuries over the previous two seasons, but now his biggest issue has been a lack of production in the pass rush. Thibodeaux has the worst pass-rush grade in the front seven (49.4), with just four pressures and one hit in 91 pass-rush snaps.

title: Can More Play Action Fix the Giants' Stalled Run Game?
full_text:
The New York Giants' offensive identity is built on a power rushing game designed to wear down opponents.
But after four games, the Giants' rushing offense ranks 12th in total yards (442), 23rd in average yards per rush (3.7) and tied for 28th in rushing touchdowns (one), and it is 19th in explosive runs of 10 or more yards (eight).
That’s probably not what head coach John Harbaugh was imagining when he took the job in January and began building the roster.
“Yeah, I mean, we're just not good enough yet. Defenses are playing us pretty well,” he said when asked specifically about the lack of explosive runs, which would boost the total yards and average yards per carry.
The Giants’ running backs are who they are. Cam Skattebo and Najee Harris, who have handled most of the rushing attempts over the last three weeks, are power backs who sometimes work behind fullback Patrick Ricard.
On the flip side, Devin Singletary and Tyrone Tracy Jr., both of whom can provide a semblance of explosiveness, have been seldom used on offense. Tracy has mainly been used on special teams, and Singletary has been inactive the last two weeks.
For now, the Giants will roll with what they have, though there is a growing public sentiment that they might look to add an explosive back like Cardinals rookie Jeremiyah Love, whom the Giants were heavily linked to in this year’s draft.
“As we get better, we'll probably have more longer runs,” Harbaugh said. “Also, if we make them pay a little more with play action, I think that'll loosen (defenses) up a little bit, probably. But we just got to keep getting better.”
To his point, the Giants have run play action just 33 times through four games, which ranks 24th in the league. And when they have run play action, they have averaged 10.3 yards per play.
Until they can address that, Harbaugh believes all they can do is keep making strides toward improvement every week.
“I think the guys are working hard at it. We're playing very hard. We're trying to play very physically. So, all the elements are there. We have to keep getting better,” he said.

title: Malik Nabers Dismisses "Breakout" Label After 112-Yard Game
full_text:
New York Giants receiver Malik Nabers finished last week with his first 100-yard receiving game since returning from a torn ACL.
But for him, catching six of seven passes for 112 yards and one touchdown is far from what he considers a "breakout" showing.
"I think everybody's saying it's a breakout because I scored and got 100 yards," Nabers said Wednesday.
"I could have done that in game one, but I just slipped a couple times, and the ball just didn't come my way, or we just didn't complete on some routes.
"So, I don't know why everybody's saying it's a breakout game. I feel like that was a basic game. I could have done more."
Nabers, who caught five of five targets for 84 yards and a touchdown in the first half, said he wanted more opportunities to help the offense.
"I felt like I didn't get targeted much after halftime," he said. "I felt like creating explosives down the field was just helping us get in a better position to score touchdowns. Some of those plays didn't come my way, so I'm just trying to figure out why."
The receiver, who landed on this week's injury report with a knee issue and said he's "a little sore," shared his feedback with head coach John Harbaugh.
"I think we need to implement more things after halftime. Just also trying to give me the ball down the field to create some of those opportunities for us to gain more points," Nabers said.
"It felt like during the first half when we did that, it led us in the right direction with scoring touchdowns in the red zone. And after that, we couldn't get going.
"So, I felt like the offense was needing a spark and I wanted to be that spark."
Nabers did not practice Wednesday; the reason listed was his knee, though it’snot known if the knee issue involves the same knee where he suffered the torn ACL last year.
Nabers, who repeatedly said he was sore, would not commit to Sunday.
"We'll see how the next day goes, but through the week I'd usually be sore," he said. "But this one was kind of a little bit more sore, but I always continue to fight through it."

title: 3 Matchups That Will Decide Jets’ Week 5 Game Against Browns (All Eyes on Thomas-Stephens Tandem)
full_text:
The Jets hope to get back on track in Week 5 after dropping their last three games. However, it will be no easy task for Gang Green, as the Browns come into town riding a three-game winning streak. Both teams are dealing with their share of injuries , but that’s part of the challenge every team faces over a season.
For the Jets, Sunday’s game could be a turning point in the season.
A loss would drop the Jets to 1-4 and put even more pressure on head coach Aaron Glenn’s future , especially with three of the team’s next five opponents having a winning record. That’s why coming away with a win is critical for New York.
With that said, here are the three matchups that will determine whether Gang Green gets back on track.
Several factors have contributed to the Browns’ hot start. Watson has played well, the defense has been great, and head coach Todd Monken has had a big impact.
One area that’s been almost been a non-factor, however, is Cleveland’s run game. Through four games, the Browns rank 23rd in rushing yards per game (93.8) and yards per carry (3.7). Star running back Quinshon Judkins just hasn’t been able to get things going, recording 177 rushing yards and averaging an abysmal three yards per carry.
The unit has been better, combining for 244 yards in the last two games, but it’ll need to step it up to keep the win streak going. Shutting down their run game should be among the Jets’ top priorities heading into this matchup.
New York emphasized improving its run defense by getting bigger up front in the offseason. The unit looked significantly better in the first two games, allowing just 131 rushing yards. However, they’ve regressed over the last two weeks.
In their losses to the Lions and the Bears, the Jets have been dominated at the line of scrimmage, giving up 363 rushing yards and eight rushes of 10 yards or more.
They’ll need to bounce back against the Browns.
Luckily for New York, Cleveland isn’t as explosive on the ground, with just nine runs of at least 10 yards through four weeks. Their offensive line hasn’t helped, as the unit ranks 24th with a 57.9 run-blocking grade , per Pro Football Focus .
To beat the Browns, the Jets’ defensive line must maintain outside leverage, clog the gaps, and prevent Judkins from reaching the second level. Forcing Cleveland into obvious passing situations would put the game in Watson’s hands and give New York’s defense more opportunities to generate pressure.
Watson has already had to bail them out of multiple games this season, with some victories coming down to the final whistle. If they can force Watson to do it all himself, they’ll have a chance to capitalize on his mistakes.
Although KC Concepcion Jr. and Harold Fanin Jr. lead the Browns’ pass catchers in targets with 17 apiece, it’s Denzel Boston who’s been Deshaun Watson’s go-to receiver .
That shouldn’t surprise anyone.
Standing at 6'4" and 215 lbs, Boston excelled at the University of Washington at moving the chains with his contested-catch ability and was an elite red zone threat, with 14 of his 20 touchdowns coming in the red zone. Those traits have quickly translated to the NFL, where he’s become Watson’s most trusted target.
Over four games, Boston leads the team in receiving yards with 284, while hauling in 13 catches for two touchdowns. Of his 22 targets, eight are on passes of at least 20 yards downfield , according to NFL Next Gen Stats.
Last week against the Steelers, Watson connected with Boston for a 60-yard completion, setting the Browns up for a touchdown three plays later. Boston has primarily run go routes, outs and comebacks, with some slants over the middle, giving him opportunities to use his size and playmaking ability at different levels of the field.
“(Boston is) only going to get better because he’s tough physically and mentally , he’s diligent, he’s got an excellent catch radius and plays strong to the ball,” head coach Todd Monken told reporters.
Limiting Boston from making explosive plays will be the top priority for the Jets. Outside corners Brandon Stephens and AZ Thomas will be tasked with neutralizing Boston’s big-play ability.
At 6-foot-1 and 6-foot-2, respectively, Stephens and Thomas have the size and the physical play style to match up with Boston. So far, the two have stood out in coverage.
Stephens has allowed just 11 receptions (18 targets) for 141 yards, while Thomas has given up 17 catches (21 targets) for 123 yards and two touchdowns. According to PFF, Stephens has posted a 74.4 coverage grade and Thomas a 70.2 , with both ranking among the top 20 cornerbacks in coverage among 103 qualifying players.
This matchup comes down to whether Stephens and Thomas can prevent Boston from creating explosive plays. They have the length and size to challenge him on any deep shot, but they’ll also have to limit his yards after the catch.
The Jets did a good job limiting downfield targets to Rome Odunze last week, but he was still making plays at the intermediate levels. They’ll need to avoid a similar outcome with Boston, who can hurt them with any room they give him.
Even after trading away superstar pass rusher Myles Garrett, the Browns’ pass rush has remained highly effective at generating pressure.
Cleveland has proven it can get after the quarterback with its front four, as the unit is tied for fifth in sacks (12) and sixth in quarterback pressure percentage (40.4%), despite blitzing at just a 27.3% rate.
This has allowed them to drop more defenders into coverage, where they’ve recorded four interceptions.
However, the Browns’ defensive line is banged up . Mason Graham, who leads the team in sacks with four, Kalia Davis, and Mike Hall Jr. all missed practice on Thursday, while Derek Barnett was limited. Their availability for Sunday is uncertain.
Even if some of those players miss Sunday’s game, Cleveland can still cause problems for New York, as they still have Isaiah McGuire, Maliek Collins and Jared Verse.
The Jets’ offensive line has been inconsistent through the first four weeks.
Starting left guard Dylan Parham has been the team’s best pass-blocker , per PFF , earning a 75.9 grade. However, he’s unlikely to play after missing the first two practices. Jordan Meredith has filled in over the past two weeks, but the five-year veteran has struggled, allowing two sacks and seven pressures across 40 pass-blocking snaps.
Left tackle Olu Fashanu hasn’t been any better, allowing five sacks and 11 pressures. If the Jets can’t improve their protection against Cleveland, then it could be another long day for quarterback Geno Smith.
To limit Cleveland’s pass rush, offensive coordinator Frank Reich must give Fashanu extra help on the left side, using a tight end, like Jelani Woods, or a running back to chip the edge rushers.
New York could also make life easier by establishing the run after struggling to do so over the last few weeks. This would keep the offense balanced, prevent predictable passing situations, and take the pressure off Smith.
Reich also needs to get the ball out of Smith’s hands faster. A mix of quick passes, screens, and play-actions would make life easier on the offensive line and create opportunities to attack downfield.

title: 3 Changes Frank Reich Must Make to Turn Jets' Offense Around Before It's Too Late
full_text:
FLORHAM PARK, N.J. — Inconsistent. That's probably the best word to describe the Jets' offense through the first four games of the season. In some games, like Week 3 against the Lions, the offense looks solid. In other contests, like last week against the Bears, the offense failed to produce much of everything.
For offensive coordinator Frank Reich, the stats highlight a poor overall group.
New York ranks as the 25th-best offense in the league and the sixth-worst rushing attack in the game. The Jets' passing unit is ranked in the top 10, but failing to pick up a third-down conversion last week was another example of the recent frustration.
If the numbers show a struggling team, the tape only enhances those same issues.
For Reich and the offense, there are three things that the unit needs to fix going into Week 5's clash with the Browns. Otherwise, it will be another year in which the Jets fail to put up an offense inside the top 20.
After last week's abysmal performance , the Jets' offense dropped to fourth-worst in the NFL on third down. They saw many third-and-short opportunities against the Bears but even failed to pick those up.
For Reich, the reason for it is simple, he has to be better as a play-caller.
"I'm ultimately responsible for that," Reich said. "We had two short fields that yielded six points, and I think if that yields more than that, it allows us to apply a little bit more pressure than we did."
There are different reasons why a team fails to convert on third down. Some plays could start with a breakdown in blocks along the offensive line. A bad pass here, a missed read there and everyone always tends to have a hand in third-down struggles.
But when everyone is at fault, then it becomes a coaching issue. Reich needs to make sure his guys are more buttoned-up going forward.
The Jets have loved Braelon Allen for years now . His size as a 6'2", 250-pound running back makes him an intriguing weapon for any offense. The problem for him is that he hasn't been productive.
Sunday's loss in Chicago was his best game, rushing 14 times for 59 yards and a 4.2-yard-per-carry average. Meanwhile, Isaiah Davis didn't receive a touch on Sunday .
New York's fascination with Allen or Davis has never truly made sense, especially when production between the two couldn't be further apart. While Allen has recorded a career yard-per-carry average of 3.7, Davis has averaged over 5.6 per opportunity.
In short, Davis is more efficient and more productive, even if the Jets won't play him.
With Breece Hall still dealing with a quad injury, the Jets must give up this idea of Allen being the team's lead back. He isn't efficient enough to do it. Davis must receive touches going forward.
New York is without Hall, AD Mitchell and Omar Cooper Jr. Four of the team's top six targets have missed games over the last few weeks .
The easiest way to put up points is to get the ball to the other top targets: Garrett Wilson and Kenyon Sadiq. Getting the ball to your better players is an excellent way of keeping teams that may have more talent than you in bind.
Instead, Reich chose to focus his efforts last week on getting the ball to Allen, who, as we've mentioned, has never shown an ability to carry an offense on his own. Allen saw 16 touches in last week's game. Wilson and Sadiq combined for eight.
Inexcusable, yet Reich tried to do it.
Was that the problem? Just not converting on third down? Or was featuring a backup running back at all a bigger issue?
Good teams stay good because they get the ball to their best players and let them use their talent to succeed. Bad teams try to outsmart the good teams and, in turn, end up costing themselves.
The Jets are a bad team right now, and they will stay bad as long as Reich thinks he can outsmart other coaches.

title: Jets Friday Notebook Week 5: Key Injury Updates, Nahshon Wright's Outlook & More
full_text:
FLORHAM PARK, N.J. — The Jets need a win, and fast.
At 1-3, the organization has little wiggle room to remain competitive this season. They also happen to be walking into a home contest this weekend against the 3-1 Browns in what is expected to be rainy weather. According to AccuWeather, there is a 94% chance that rain from Tropical Rainstorm Isaias will impact the East Rutherford weather on Sunday.
At practice on Friday, the Jets shifted their focus to the Browns with some key notes along the way.
So let's open up the notebook and see what fans should know heading into the weekend.
There's good news and bad news when it comes to the Jets' injury front.
The good news is that starting tight end Mason Taylor is expected to play on Sunday after missing the last two games with an injury. He will be a welcome addition to the offense heading into Week 5. Jarvis Brownlee and Kingsley Enagbare are also expected to practice today and could be in line to start on Sunday.
In the case of Adonai Mitchell, the team also believes he could eventually get back to practice next week with a finger injury that did not require surgery, according to Jets head coach Aaron Glenn.
But is the finger broken? A sprain? No one seems to know . All Glenn will say is that no procedure was done.
"(Adonai is) progressing faster than we thought that he would," Glenn said. "Once we got to the end of it of knowing exactly what the prognosis was when it comes to his finger."
That said, the likes of running back Breece Hall, Mitchel, and left guard Dylan Parham will all miss Sunday's action against the Browns due to their slate of injuries. Glenn did seem hopeful they could also return to the practice field next week, but they are not making any promises or clear expectations.
The Jets signed Nahshon Wright this past offseason to help fix a secondary that was one of the worst in the league last year. Wright was coming off a Pro Bowl season in Chicago, and his ball-hawking abilities were seen as a positive for a Jets team that failed to record an interception the previous year.
So far this season, though, Wright hasn't played . In fact, New York has made him a healthy scratch in the last two weeks, leaving some to wonder whether his time in Gotham is already nearing its end .
On Friday, Glenn broke down exactly why Wright has been on the outside looking in. While the Jets brought him in to help fix the defense, the cornerback room has played a lot better than anyone could have previously predicted.
Glenn is correct. Stephens and Thomas are both ranked as top-20 cornerbacks in the league in pass coverage. Stephens, specifically, is in the top 15. The development of their outside corners has been a small positive for the 1-3 Jets.
While Glenn did say Wright will eventually see the field, barring injury or poor play, it's hard to pinpoint exactly where at this time.
Every coach looks at the NFL season in quarters. The first four games of the year are the "first quarter" of a season, and so on. Glenn confirmed that's exactly how he looks at where the Jets are going forward.
Even if they were bad in the "first quarter" of the year.
"I think it helps to look at it in that aspect," Glenn said. "Knowing that we're 1-3 this quarter, we have another quarter to be able to see how we improve on that. I think sometimes it makes it easy to just condense the season into that, so guys can stay just pinpointed and focused on it. Also, I think it's important you just look at each game and just go from there."
As the Jets prepare for the second quarter of the season, they will have three games against teams that didn't make the playoffs last season. The Browns, Dolphins and Raiders are all teams that the Jets need to beat in order to keep their season alive.
And at the end of the day, if they can win the second and third quarter of the year, it may put them in better standing moving forward.
Part of that switch, though, is getting the team to start fast. New York has found themselves in offensive holes over the last few weeks, and it's something the team is working to correct.
"Just for the psyche of your team, just for the fans and all that, it's obviously pretty good to be able to do that," Glenn said.
While Gang Green's psyche is poor right now, it's even worse for the fans. If the Jets want to show they have grown as an organization, Sunday is as much of a must-win as ever .

title: Jets Share Another Cryptic Adonai Mitchell Injury Update: What Exactly Is Going On?
full_text:
The Jets are working hard as they prepare for a Week 5 clash with the Browns , hoping to end their losing streak at three games. Head coach Aaron Glenn will need all hands on deck to overcome a 3-1 Cleveland team that has exceeded expectations, which is why No. 2 wide receiver Adonai Mitchell's health has been a hot topic among New York fans in the lead-up to Sunday.
After all, Mitchell missed Weeks 3 and 4 with a mysterious hand injury the Jets have bizarrely been cryptic about—even after he was spotted in practice last month with a heavily taped hand (h/t Sleeper NFL). All Glenn told fans was that Mitchell's finger got caught in a teammate's jersey during practice and that it wasn't broken, opting not to detail an official diagnosis.
Fast-forward to Week 5, and the mystery continues: Mitchell will miss Sunday's contest against the Browns, according to ESPN 's Rich Cimini on Friday. The situation became even more frustrating when Glenn seemingly admitted to not knowing "if it’s a sprain or fracture," per Cimini, and that surgery wasn't required.
Aaron Glenn continues to be evasive with regard to AD Mitchell’s finger injury. Wouldn’t say if it’s a sprain or fracture, suggesting he doesn’t know. Says there was no surgical procedure. Adds, “He’s progressing faster than we thought.” This will be Mitchell’s third missed game.…
Even though Glenn added that Mitchell is "progressing faster than we thought," that kind of update doesn't exactly mean much when the Jets have been considerably mum on the situation.
Injuries happen, and some are harder to diagnose than others. That said, the Jets have had over two weeks to explain exactly what's going on with Mitchell, yet nothing concrete has come out. It especially isn't encouraging when Glenn sounds like not even he knows what's happening. You'd think that enough imaging would be done by now to determine what's going on.
Did Mitchell's injury look like it'd heal quickly only for him to suffer a setback? Are the Jets worried that the situation is worse than it is? Do they regret not putting him on injured reserve as soon as the issue popped up?
Those are all pressing (and valid) questions stewing in the minds of Jets fans, making it clear that Glenn & Co.'s cryptic ways aren't doing anyone any favors.
Earlier in the week, Cimini discussed Mitchell's injury on Monday's edition of the "Jets Collective" podcast, saying he "would not shock me if we find out that (Adonai) had surgery." Obviously, Glenn said that wasn't the case on Friday, but the fact that the ESPN insider hasn't even seen Mitchell around team facilities only adds to the fear about how severe his injury is.
Sports fans need transparency from the front office and coaching staff, no matter how unfortunate a player's injury situation is. The Jets' faithful especially deserve that, after all they've been through over the last decade and a half. If Glenn and general manager Darren Mougey want to be seen as the right people to turn Gang Green around, they can't let situations like Mitchell's injury snowball into an avoidable avalanche.
Regardless of the sparse details regarding Mitchell's injury, the fact is that—no matter why—the Jets will be without their No. 2 WR on Sunday afternoon.
Naturally, that means Garrett Wilson should see more volume than the four targets he saw last week, after commanding 13 in the previous game. Isaiah Williams also has some momentum after scoring his first touchdown on a 58-yard reception last week, and Tim Patrick could be coming off IR after his practice window opened on Wednesday .
The Jets are still waiting to see more production from former taxi squad wideouts Malik McClain and Jamaal Pritchett, who haven't been targeted yet. There's also a good chance that Sterling Shepard will be elevated from the practice squad for the third time, with Tyler Johnson as another option waiting in the wings. That's without even mentioning the expanded action the tight end room could see, especially with Mason Taylor potentially returning to reform New York's talented 1-2 punch at TE with Kenyon Sadiq.
The Browns are off to a strong start, but their defense hasn't been perfect, and a 55.7 grade on PFF (T-26th) drives that home. Despite being shorthanded, the Jets' offense must capitalize on every chance it gets to put up points, or else any hope of looking like a competitive team this year could slip through their grasp.
In the meantime, let's hope the next update on Adonai Mitchell's status isn't as cryptic and makes it clear what New York fans can expect next for the 24-year-old receiver.

title: 3 Most Likely Will McDonald IV Trade Destination as His Jets Outlook Remains Unclear
full_text:
Through the first four games of the 2026 NFL season, Jets edge rusher Will McDonald IV has been a clear disappointment . He has tallied one sack but has been nonexistent for a majority of the year, both in run defense and in getting after the quarterback. He went from having five pressures and a sack in the season opener to four sackless pressures in the last three games.
Not good for a first-round pick in need of a new deal.
If the Jets continue to keep losing, they will seemingly need to give away some of their talent on expiring contracts in order to accumulate more draft capital. McDonald may have an additional year of team control, but it's clear he's not in New York's long-term plans , potentially putting him on the move before the 2026 NFL trade deadline on Tuesday, Nov. 10.
And that could make McDonald attractive to at least three times around the league.
The Panthers have been ravaged by injuries, but they remain the one team that seemingly is competent enough on offense to win the NFC South again. In order to do so, they'll need to address some key areas along the defensive line.
Currently, Carolina ranks third worst in the league in pressure rate. Their eight sacks are also among the lowest in the league as well. If the Panthers want not only to get to the playoffs but also to find a way to win, they'll need to provide some semblance of a pass rush.
The potential acquisition of McDonald may put the team closer to some of the other playoff contenders in the NFC than people realize. The Panthers are good this year. They need a pass rusher like McDonald to put them over the hump.
With the NFC East in a state of flux, the Cowboys seem like the one team that actually has the pieces to win the division by default now, even if they fell to the then-winless Buccaneers on Thursday Night Football. Dallas still needs help on defense, though, especially when it comes to getting after the passer, currently owning the eighth-worst pass-rush grade (61.5) on Pro Football Focus .
The Cowboys have some concerns about stopping the run, but since trading Micah Parsons , they have clearly taken a step back when it comes to getting after the quarterback. McDonald is no Parsons, but he could provide an immediate boost to the group going into the later parts of the season.
Don't let their 4-0 record fool you: the 49ers are banged up across the roster. Despite that, the team is undefeated and playing inspired football. They do need some extra edge-rusher help as they go for a run at the championship.
McDonald has struggled so far this season, but he should be someone who can get after the quarterback at a consistent level. Outside of Nick Bosa, the 49ers could use extra players to aid in their defense when going against the Cowboys or Rams.
This seems like a fair deal for both sides as New York would want fair compensation in the draft.

title: 4 Biggest Jets Concerns Heading Into Week 5 (Mounting Injuries Remain a Problem)
full_text:
As the Jets continue to search for answers following a disappointing 23-12 loss to the Bears last Sunday, a home game against the surprisingly successful Browns looms in Week 5.
After the uninspiring loss to the Bears , that next kickoff cannot come soon enough for Gang Green, after a three-game losing streak wiped away the encouraging start to the season. While it is easy to overreact to some of the things that have transpired throughout the first month of the season, there are some obvious areas of concern in Gotham as the Jets find themselves at 1-3 and staring down another potentially lost season if they can't reverse course.
Some players are already on thin ice after just four games, and patience will eventually run out if the ship doesn't get righted soon. As the Browns come to town on a three-game win streak and with a much different look overall, here are the four biggest concerns the Jets face heading into Week 5.
The Jets were without nearly half of their offensive starters against Chicago, which continued a worrisome trend to begin the season as the injuries have completely taken over this roster. Those concerns were still evident on Wednesday's injury report , which did not offer a lot of optimism regarding the status of key players like Adonai Mitchell (right finger), Breece Hall (groin), Dylan Parham (knee) and Jarvis Brownlee Jr. (concussion), while Kingsley Enagbare (knee) and Mason Taylor (thumb) seemed to be trending in the right direction.
Fast forward to Thursday, and it was more of the same a s ESPN Jets reporter Rich Cimini noted that there was " no sign" of Hall and Mitchell at the latest practice . Brownlee, meanwhile, was "in positional drills."
No surprise here, but no sign of Breece Hall and AD Mitchell at practice. Jarvis Brownlee Jr in positional drills. #Jets
While the absence of each of these players has certainly been felt, rookie D'Angelo Ponds filled in admirably when Brownlee went down in the Windy City. Although it would be a blow if Brownlee remains out of action, Ponds possesses the versatility to play in the slot and on the perimeter and could be staring at a bigger role moving forward , especially if he plays well.
Still, that doesn't apply to the other setbacks on the team, and the potential voids that will still be there if the offense is without some of its top players for another week. It proved costly in all phases of the Week 4 loss to the Bears, and it could be again if the correct adjustments are not made to account for the lack of depth.
Arguably the most frustrating aspect about the 2026 Jets has been the disastrous play from the defense , which only sacked backup quarterback Tyson Bagent one time and allowed him to pass for a career-high 268 yards. They also had no answer for Chicago's league-leading rushing attack, giving up 232 yards on the ground and allowing the Bears to amass more first downs (34) than the total plays the Jets offense ran (32).
An interception from safety Minkah Fitzpatrick— the first in 636 pass attempts for Gang Green (h/t NFL)—offered a bright spot, as did the play from the team's best offseason addition , safety Dane Belton.
Minkah Fitzpatrick gives the Jets their first INT in 636 pass attempts NYJvsCHI on FOX/FOX One Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/CQUCl4JVnt
Still, the Jets' defense had three potential interceptions off Bagent that were negated by penalties and struggled to get off the field despite numerous chances.
The Browns are only scoring the 22nd-most points per game (20.3 ppg) this season and should present an opportunity at first glance. That said, the Jets couldn't slow down a backup QB last week and could be in trouble again if they keep beating themselves and lack a consistent pass rush, which has plagued them so far.
Dylan Parham's knee injury and his uncertain status moving forward have only added to the woes this O-line has experienced so far. Armand Membou and Joe Tippmann have done their part on the right side, but the subpar play from Olu Fashanu and the low ceiling that Josh Myers offers have created some adversity up front for the Jets.
Smith has taken 12 sacks this season, eight of which have come in the last two games. Some of that has been due to Smith's tendency to hold onto the ball too long, but that is still concerning. Additionally, the run game has failed to deliver a consistent balance on offense, and WR1 Garrett Wilson has fallen victim to the same Jets mistake , recording only three receptions for 27 yards in Week 4.
While some of that is due to a lack of explosiveness in the ground game and a poor game plan coming into each week in terms of not getting the top targets more involved, a lot of it comes back to the Jets' O-line and its inability to set the tone up front to give the offense enough time to operate when it is on the field.
Much has been made of New York's struggles in the two-minute offense and head coach Aaron Glenn's tendency to mismanage timeouts and end-of-game situations. This team has constantly played from behind this season due to slow starts out of the gate.
The Jets have 17 total first-half points over the last three weeks and have not scored in the first quarter in any of those games. Their 5.7 points per first half rank third-worst in the NFl during that stretch.
In last Sunday's Week 4 loss alone, the Jets punted on three of their four first-half drives and allowed the Bears to run 26 plays in the first quarter.
While much of the blame goes to disciplinary issues and  Glenn's defense struggling to slow down Chicago's stout run game, these slow starts simply cannot happen. The injuries are one thing, but if the Jets continue to put themselves behind so early in each game, this losing skid may not end anytime soon.
