title: Staff Predictions for Titans vs. Ravens: Tennessee Comes Out on Top for 1 Main Reason
full_text:
Last week, the Titans On SI staff predicted a Tennessee loss across the board against the Baltimore Ravens. Unfortunately, we turned out to be correct. The Titans fell in Week 4 to a score of 24-18, in a game that saw Brian Daboll's offense progress just below a breakthrough.
This week, our two picks tell a different story. In a pivotal AFC South matchup that will see one of the Titans and Texans secure your first win, we're predicting Tennessee's offense to tick in the right direction at the exact right time.
Robert Saleh just expressed his confidence that this Titans season is not over yet. "I feel if we can win one, we can build momentum," Saleh said. We expect Tennessee to finally make good on that opportunity this week.
I don't know why, but I've got a good feeling about this one. On paper, Tennessee winning their first game in Week 5 last year - after an 0-4 start - feels like a good omen. The Titans and Texans are also 24-24 all-time. For semantic reasons, Tennessee holding on to the series at home would be huge.
But Week 5 also looks to offer a few advantages for Tennessee. The Texans' passing defense has been among the least efficient in the league this season, and head coach DeMeco Ryans taking over play-calling duties could lead to a rough transitional period for Houston.
On the other hand, Cam Ward is coming off his best game of the season. With Carnell Tate good to go and the Titans playing their first game in Nashville in three weeks, the cards are quietly stacked up for a revenge game here.
The divisional stakes make it all the more important. Call me crazy, but I have the Titans in a narrow, offense-leading victory.
Although the Titans' offense is yet to crack 20 points, they have been forced to play in either extraordinary heat or rain in each of their four games this season. The weather in Nashville is expected to be 60s with a chance of sprinkles on Sunday, a welcomed change for the home team.
Houston's defense has been disappointing, giving up the sixth most points despite an elite pass rush. I anticipate big outings from WR Wan'Dale Robinson and WR Carnell Tate, as the Titans seek, and secure, their first victory of the season.

title: Titans Red Zone Report: Tennessee's Major Key to Scoring When it Matters vs. Texans
full_text:
So long as the Tennessee Titans continue to be one of the NFL's least efficient offenses, these red zone reports will continue to feel more like futuristic wishful thinking than anything else. Brian Daboll and Cam Ward have to find a way to get on the same page, and fast.
However, Week 4's loss at the hands of the Baltimore Ravens provided us with a one-drive sample size to properly diagnose the team's problems. The Titans found momentum in the second half, but Robert Saleh could have had his first win had one series of plays gone Tennessee's way.
Down 14-7 in the second quarter, the Titans were facing a first and goal in the red zone. We've already hit this issue numerous times, so I'll keep it short: Daboll ran Tony Pollard four straight times, Tennessee got stuffed on the goal line, and Baltimore scored in the other direction prior to halftime.
The Titans ultimately closed the gap to six points by the game's end - the difference between the team finding a way in on that pivotal drive in the second. In Week 5, it's all about trusting Ward's progression and betting on the guy under center.
Pollard is effective as a consistent, early-down veteran in an offense otherwise filled with rising young assets. Daboll using him as a four-down workhorse, however, is both predictable and terrible ineffective.
Daboll confirmed this week that he "felt good" about the looks for Pollard, refusing to express any outward regret on the plane ride home looking back on the incident. Again, though, the offense gave Ward the keys to open things up downfield after that.
Tennessee's comeback effort may have fallen short, but Ward would find Wan'Dale Robinson for a passing score in the first quarter. He'd then hit Carnell Tate in the end zone for a successful two-point conversion, too.
Of the Titans' four red-zone touchdowns this year, three have come through the air. If the Titans are set on allowing Ward to have this season to hash out his issues - as expected - he'll need to be given a chance to do so in important situations.
In a contest with the Texans likely to yield opportunities for both offenses, the 0-4 Titans could ask for no better reason to open things up. In red-zone looks, the Titans can't hope for the best on the ground. In Week 5, Daboll and Tennessee have no choice but to scheme for Ward and his weapons if they want to keep up with high-scoring Houston.

title: The Titans Score Less Than Any Team in NFL — But Week 5 Looks Like a Breakthrough
full_text:
The Tennessee Titans are facing a high-powered, veteran-led Housto Texans offense in Week 5. Despite being in front of their home crowd, the lowly Titans aren't being given the benefit of the doubt by pretty much anyone in the space. It's another underdog opportunity for Robert Saleh's team.
This matchup, while not a nightmare for Tennessee, does present a great challenge for Brian Daboll's offense. To keep pace with C.J. Stroud, that unit will likely have to have their best game of the season.
Per PFF, the Titans have the lowest percentage of drives ending in a score this season, at 26.3%. Tennessee has only reached 20 points one time, and has scored 10 or less on two occasions. Last week's 18-point outing against the Ravens bore improvement across the board, but it still wasn't enough to dig the Titans out of the hole they're in.
Lowest % of drives ending in a score this season Titans           26.3% Patriots        26.8% Dolphins      27.0% Chargers      27.7% Steelers       29.8% pic.twitter.com/ZQ9g58vLmQ
Yet, the Texans' defense may promise a real chance for Tennessee to break through on that front. DeMeco Ryans is taking over play-calling starting in Week 5 due to the defense's struggles. The pieces are there for Houston, but the execution has been well beyond.
Cam Ward and Daboll have to jump on that. This could be the leap Titans fans have been waiting for.
The Texans' secondary has only picked the ball off one time this year. They've allowed 20+ points in every game but one, and that game saw the Indianapolis Colts put up 19. In two of those contests, Houston allowed 30 or more.
Of course, the Texans are also 0-4. Experts may be favoring Houston, but the gap between Tennessee and the visiting team isn't as big as some people may be anticipating.
That is especially apparent on defense. With Ward coming off a season-high 222 yards vs. Baltimore, and rookie WR Carnell Tate accounting for 145 of those yards in his own season-best showing, Daboll finally seems to be working out the kinks.
We've got every reason to think the Titans continue to find ways to score here. That doesn't mean Tennessee wins. Stopping the aforementioned Stroud will be a challenge that Saleh's defense must embrace, and at least partially succeed in.
Week 5 simply feels like a cross between positive momentum for the Titans' offense and a matchup vs. a defense that's already in a corner. If there's anything about Sunday to get your hopes up for, Titans fans, it's for Daboll's scoring unit to finally find their footing before it's too late.

title: Titans Need Alontae Taylor to Turn a Corner With Tennessee Staring at a Possible 0-5 Start
full_text:
One of the Tennessee Titans' prized free-agent additions was cornerback Alontae Taylor, who signed a three-year, $60 million deal with the team after spending his first four seasons with the New Orleans Saints.
Taylor, a second-round pick in the 2022 NFL Draft, established himself as a durable starting corner during his time in New Orleans. The 27-year-old's ability to play on the outside and in the slot is also a valuable asset he brings to the table.
Entering his debut campaign with Tennessee, Taylor was expected to be a solid No. 1 boundary corner for Robert Saleh's defense. Through four games, that expectation hasn't come to fruition.
It's been a rough start to 2026 for Taylor. The Tennessee product has allowed an 83.3% completion rate (15/18) when targeted, 149 passing yards, and a 101.2 passer rating. Taylor has also posted an abysmal 39.5 Pro Football Focus defensive grade, including a 31.5 coverage grade.
From Weeks 2 to 4 alone, Taylor surrendered 14 of 16 passes in coverage and over a 100 passer rating when targeted in Weeks 3 and 4.
The Titans' defense hasn't gotten much help from their offense this year, as the unit is constantly on the field because of offensive failures. However, the defense has also been incredibly inconsistent, and the secondary has struggled at times. Taylor can be blamed for some of those troubles, though nobody in the back end is playing at a high level right now.
Taylor has never been an elite cover corner or ball hawk, but Tennessee paid him way too much money for him to be a complete liability in the secondary. Taylor's entire 2027 salary of $20.5 million is guaranteed, and that is a scary sight for the Titans if the veteran defensive back is playing more like a backup than a quality starter.
Regardless, Tennessee needs Taylor to find his footing and play like a CB1. The Titans are staring at their first 0-5 start since 2009 if they fall to the fellow winless Houston Texans at home this week. For multiple individuals and the team as a whole, it's a make or break week in front of a desperate home crowd in Nashville.
If Taylor continues to struggle as he is matched up against Texans star wide receiver Nico Collins , it's going to be a long day for the Titans.

title: Week 5 Injury: Examining Titans’ Chances if Carnell Tate Can’t Play vs. Texans
full_text:
The Tennessee Titans were hit with some concerning news ahead of their Week 5 AFC South matchup against the Houston Texans.
According to ESPN’s Turron Davenport, rookie WR Carnell Tate appears to have tweaked his back during the individual portion of Thursday’s practice.
It’s unclear whether he returned, since media members are only allowed to watch certain parts of practice, but the Titans listed him as ‘limited’ on its official injury report.
The talented rookie is coming off a monster breakout performance against the Baltimore Ravens that saw him reel in nine catches for 145 yards. And those numbers would be inflated even further had some missed opportunities not gotten away from him.
Nonetheless, the former Buckeye has really started to come alive over the last two weeks, essentially becoming the focal point of Tennessee’s offense, totaling 21 targets and 15 grabs for 203 yards over that span.
If Tate can’t go, the Titans’ already lackluster offense could be without their most explosive and consistent weapon in a divisional game they desperately need to win as they try to avoid an 0-5 hole.
Tennessee may need to lean on the ground game spearheaded by RBs Tony Pollard and Tyjae Spears. But without Tate, it will be up to Tennessee’s other group of pass catchers to keep the passing game afloat. This would be a great moment for the Titans to get their money’s worth out of one of their prized free agent acquisitions, WR Wan’Dale Robinson.
The Kentucky product has only caught 16 passes this season, one more than Tennessee’s rookie has over the last two weeks alone. Outside of him second year pass catchers Elic Ayomanor has only contributed in spurts, while WR Chim Dike and TE Gunnar Helm have been non-existent through four games.
Because of this, Titans QB Cam Ward would undoubtedly take the biggest hit should Tate’s injury keep him out of Sunday’s action. The two former top five picks have a budding connection that needs all the reps they can get together.
It would be a real shame if Tate’s sudden back injury prevents them from building off last week’s success. Only time will tell how all this plays out, but for the Titans’ sake, let’s hope they’re just being overly cautious with one of their most important players.
However, this situation definitely bears watching as kickoff draws nearer.

title: The 3 Matchups Titans Have to Win to Beat Texans in Week 5: Can Tennessee Stop C.J. Stroud?
full_text:
The Tennessee Titans are widely doubted against the Houston Texans this Sunday, despite returning from a two-game road stint. Titans fans are used to that song and dance by now.
Tennessee remains in pursuit of their first win, and Week 5 is specifically important due to it being their AFC South debut. For reference, the Titans went 0-6 in the divison last season. It was the first time they hit that low bar since the division's inception in 2002.
To say that the pressure is high for the Titans to find a way this week would be putting it lightly. Here are three matchups Tennessee has to find a way to win in order to come out on top on the scoreboard.
JC Latham has sneakily developed into one of the best RTs in the NFL in his third year with the Titans. He's yet to allow a sack this season, and is finally looking every part of the elite player Tennessee needs him to be.
Facing off against DE Will Anderson Jr., Latham will face his most important matchup of the season - perhaps even of his young career. With RG Fernando Carmona's absence already impacting the o-line, Latham being pitted against a defender like Anderson could make or break Ward's ability to make plays in the pocket.
Latham called the face-off a "battle of respect" as he looks to limit the 4.5-sack defender this coming Sunday. This is Latham's chance to plant his flag in what appears to be real long-term growth.
This is the big one. The Texans may be 0-4, but C.J. Stroud's revenge tour after his four-interception performance in the playoffs last season is very much alive.
Stroud has five touchdowns to zero interceptions this season. He's led the Texans to 30+ points in two of their four games, and has thrown more than 340 yards twice this year. PFF statistics have him in the league's top 10 in overall grade, passing yards (1141), and passing scores.
An expectedly healthy Titans' secondary, which Saleh acknowledged today "hasn't been great" adjusting to his system this season, will have to counter one of the most explosive passing offenses in the NFL.
For an 0-4 team, it simply is no longer a matter of paced development and inch-by-inch progress. If the Titans want to salvage this season as Saleh believes they can, what is arguably their weakest defensive unit will have to play above the line.
With defensive-minded coach DeMeco Ryans taking over play-calling duties on that side of the ball in Week 5, it will be a battle between Saleh and Ryans on the sideline.
Saleh already lost a similar duel to Aaron Glenn and the New York Jets at the beginning of this season. The secondary stopping Stroud is one thing, but with a new play-caller in place for Houston, we'll get to see two specialized defenses in direct comparison.
The head coach dove into what he dubbed a "unique" zone system for Tennessee today, as compared to match or man coverage. It's a compelling conversation that hasn't yet translated to consistent success on the field, even with pivotal veterans like DE Jacob Martin and EDGE Jermaine Johnson finally beginning to show progress under Saleh.
It must translate in Week 5 if the Titans are to pull off what is being perceived as an upset.

title: Titans' Front Office Firings Can't Distract From Franchise's Broken State
full_text:
How long can a rebuild be deemed a rebuild? When does a team trying to reshape things from the ground up transition from a multi-year project to something deeper than that? The Tennessee Titans haven't had a winning season since 2021. Robert Saleh is 0-4 in his first go-around.
Yesterday, it was announced that the Titans were firing three executives in an effort to overhaul the front office. These include: senior VP and chief revenue officer Adam Nuse, VP of creative Charles Jensen, and senior VP of brand marketing Erin Swartz.
The latter spearheaded Tennessee's recent aesthetic rebrand, seemingly leading the team into a new era that fans have long awaited. Now, as a result of that new era being fully implemented, Swartz has been let go alongside two of her colleagues.
We have an address from the organization regarding this sudden move that was issued to the Tennesseean :
“As the Titans prepare for the opening of our new stadium and the future of Titans football, we are making changes to how we lead the business side of the organization. We will hire an Executive Vice President and Chief Business Officer to lead our revenue, marketing, and communications teams. As part of these changes, Adam Nuse, Erin Swartz, and Charles Jensen are leaving the organization. We are grateful for everything they have contributed to the Titans and wish them the best in future endeavors.”
Burke Nihill has been the Titans' president and CEO since 2020. Under Nihill, the franchise has cycled through three head coaches and four general managers. Just about every level of the Titans' organization has undergone a change throughout their half-decade downward spiral.
The lone exception is, of course, Nihill himself. Is this all just a legendary streak of bad luck, or is there something to be said about the person pulling the strings for Tennessee's unending rebuild?
There may not be a direct answer, but something more has to be going south when a team is constantly recycling front office and sideline names to no avail. There's a deeply broken decision-making process in there somewhere, the blame for which can't be deferred forever.
In a leaked internal memo, Nihill tied off this news by saying: "We adapt when it's for the good of the team. I'm confident this structure sets us up to do special things together as a business and as a culture in 2027 and beyond."
Coach Saleh is still extremely early in his tenure, and GM Mike Borgonzi has helped usher in more than a few draft hits since his hiring at the beginning of last year. "The future is bright" is a common sentiment being floated around this 0-4 Titans team.
But how many times have we heard that in the past five years? More importantly, how much longer will fans accept that sentiment before it loses meaning? That is, if fans haven't reached that point already.

title: Experts Picking Texans Over Titans Reveal Exactly How Tennessee Can Win
full_text:
It's become a minor tradition for our coverage of expert picks to report the worst possible news. Yet again, heading into Week 5, the NFL's Preview Picks are 10-0 in favor of the visiting Houston Texans. This is the second straight week that Tennessee doesn't have a single projected win in the preview.
Although, this time around, these picks have one expectation in common. The Texans score between 23-27 points, and the Titans score between 10-17. Six of the 10 picks fall within this fair range. While only two see Tennessee keeping this contest in the single digits, this board of predictions may reveal just how the Titans can find their first win this week.
It's clear that Houston is expected to win by the merits of their offense. C.J. Stroud is coming off his second game of the year throwing more than 340 yards, and the Texans their second game scoring 30 points as a unit. That came in a loss - like Tennessee, Houstin is 0-4.
Now, head coach DeMeco Ryans did just take up defensive play-calling duties to try and improve the Texans' defense. But no matter how you spin it, the offense is what has brought Houston within striking distance this year.
If Robert Saleh can outmatch Ryans and shut Stroud, Nico Collins, David Montgomery and company down, the Titans may actually have a favorable shot at home.
This isn't just a "score more points than the other team" sort of plea. Week 5 could serve as the perfect crossroads for the Titans. Cam Ward just had the best game of his season against the Baltimore Ravens last week, coming on late and feeding rookie Carnell Tate to no end.
Ward still has plenty of room to improve, but he took a few strides that we've been waiting to see. Another (even small) leap from the offense paired with a sturdy defensive showing could mix the right formula to serve the Texans a defeat.
Per PFF, Houston's 109 points allowed is tied for 26th in the NFL. Their 84 points scored are only good for 20th, but the Texans have scored 19 or more in three of their four games. There's a wide gap between offense and defense right now, and it's one Saleh has to try and exploit.
With both teams looking for their first divisional win, and win in general, the stakes will be boiling over in Nashville this Sunday. If Tennessee can keep Stroud's passing game in relative check, perhaps Ward and the offense have had enough time to make good on some of their potential.
Perhaps the Titans can finally grab a victory, even if Robert Saleh's playoff hopes remain in question.

title: How Titans' RT JC Latham Could Make a Decisive Statement Against Texans
full_text:
The Tennessee Titans are set to host the Houston Texans in a Week 5 battle between two winless teams out of the AFC South.
If either team wants even a sliver of hope going forward, they must find a way win this game. Odds of a playoff run aren’t good with a record of 1-4, regardless, but they become almost nonexistent at 0-5. Simply put, Tennessee needs this one badly.
But for that to happen, the Titans will have to do something that seems almost impossible right now — slow down the incredible Texans DE, Will Anderson Jr.
According to Pro Football Focus , Anderson enters Week 5 as the highest-graded defender in the NFL (92.8), receiving grades of 90+ in the run game (92.2) and as a pass rusher (90.2). Needless to say, Titans RT JC Latham will have his hands full on Sunday. Fortunately, it appears he’s both willing and able to take on the challenge this time around.
The former seventh overall pick in the 2024 NFL Draft is undoubtedly playing the best ball of his young career. Latham hasn’t allowed a single sack or quarterback hit over 145 pass-blocking snaps, earning a pass blocking grade of 71.5 — the highest of his career.
. @Titans @Ravens RT, JC Latham  has emerged this year as a lock down consistent player...Focus, consistency; power.  it's all there regardless of opponent. #titanup #BaldysBreakdowns pic.twitter.com/nO1lxMLACN
To take how impressive he’s Latham has been a step further, he’s also left on an island nearly 70% of his pass-blocking snaps, winning over 95% of those reps, both of which are among the highest in the league per PFF .
It appears that Latham's elite ability to anchor that he routinely displayed at Alabama has found its way back into his arsenal. He's also utilizing his natural length more efficiently and to his advantage than he has at any point in his professional career.
As for the run game, that’s an area where Latham has excelled dating back to last year (PFF grade was 71.3). The third-year tackle has natural power and length at his disposal, and when he’s playing with good footwork and hand placement, he’s able to displace defenders at the point of attack with ease.
The Titans’ tackle is also doing a much better job of correctly identifying his assignments pre-snap. Latham has rarely found himself out of position this season, and that’s because he has a genuine understanding of how the defense is trying to attack him on every play.
These developments have undoubtedly been encouraging, but a massive benchmark now awaits the young tackle on Sunday. Arguably the best edge defender in the NFL will be across from him throughout the contest, so we’re going to find out real fast just how much Latham has truly grown.
In previous years, these are the types of matchups that would ultimately expose Latham’s deficiencies. However, he now has the chance to start changing that narrative completely with a great game on Sunday.
A strong performance against an all-around elite defender like Anderson would do wonders for Latham’s budding confidence going forward. This is the type of individual matchup that can validate him as one of the better right tackles in the NFL. It can also quickly become a brutal reality check if not taken seriously.
Someone like Anderson should have his moments; he’s too good not to do so, but if Latham is able to hold is own for the majority of the game, then he’s undoubtedly going to start being discussed in an entirely different tier of tackles than ever before.
More importantly, it’ll give the Titans a real shot to get their offense going as they try to win their first game of the season. Because if Anderson starts to dominate the way he typically does, we'd be in for another very long afternoon in Nashville.

title: Week 5: Analyzing Robert Saleh's Playoff Hopes Heading Into a Must-Win Game vs. Texans
full_text:
The Tennessee Titans find themselves in the depths of the standings at 0-4, but they're not alone in the AFC South. Although Tennessee is winless, they've lost by less than a touchdown across the last three games. On Sunday, the Titans host their interdivisional rival, the winless Houston Texans, in a dire, must-win game.
"I think anything is achievable," head coach Robert Saleh told the media today, per Jim Wyatt. "I feel if we can win one, we can build momentum [towards a playoff push.]"
While the playoffs are improbable, the Titans aren't eliminated from contention. Hope remains alive in Nashville.
The 1992 San Diego Chargers are the only team in NFL history to start 0-4 and make the playoffs . San Diego finished its season with a 11-5 record and beat the Kansas City Chiefs in the Wild Card.
Tennessee and Houston are two of five teams to be winless through four weeks, the first time this has happened since the 2019 season. To sneak into the playoffs, the Titans would likely have to capture the AFC South.
Currently, the Jacksonville Jaguars have the top spot at 3-1; behind them is the 2-2 Indianapolis Colts. The Titans' Week 5 matchup with Houston will be their first AFC South opponent of the season.
"You got to learn how to stop losing first," Saleh said to media on Monday . "When you're trying to figure out how to win football games, you have to figure out how to stop losing. Right now, we're doing things every week (where) we're putting ourselves behind the eight ball."
While any win would make the Titans' season salvageable, Saleh believes that first the team must not beat themselves. According to the numbers, Tennessee isn't all that far off.
The Titans have only lost by a combined 15 points in their last three games. Currently, Tennessee's -28 scoring differential is better than the 2-2 Green Bay Packers.
"Life does not change," Saleh continued. "I know it's a results-oriented business, but the only chance you have to get the results you want is to have a good process on how you approach things... When you get to Sunday you have to play your absolute ass off; that's the only chance to get the result that you want (a win.)"
The Texans were AFC-contender hopefuls coming off a 12-5 campaign last season, behind a juggernaut of a defense. However, Houston has given up more than 20 points in three games this season, including 36 points to Buffalo and 34 to Dallas.
Tennessee's offense has yet to score more than 18 points in a single game this season. On Sunday, they will look to exploit a struggling Houston defense to escape a 0-5 start. Right or wrong, Saleh believes in his message, and that execution is the difference between wins and losses. That's what it will take to finally get a victory.

title: Commanders Rule Out Six Players, Leave Major Terry McLaurin Question Unanswered
full_text:
The Washington Commanders will enter Sunday's game without six players: WR Stefon Diggs (hamstring), Marcus Mariota (knee), Percy Butler (hamstring), Nick Cross (illness), Charles Omenihu (groin/ankle), and Tyler Owens (hamstring) will all be out after missing Friday's practice. Diggs is obviously the biggest name on the list, but four defensive players, including three safeties, will be out against the Giants . Since the first injury report came out on Wednesday , everyone has been worried that both Diggs and Terry McLaurin would miss this week's game. McLaurin is now officially listed as questionable after returning to limited participation in practice Friday. Commanders head coach Dan Quinn stopped short of confirming McLaurin would play Sunday when he spoke Friday afternoon: "Terry, I thought, looked really good today." Quinn added that the team would decide on McLaurin closer to game time. The Commanders will get Jayden Daniels , Sam Cosmi, and Rachaad White back this week. Daniels was a full participant in practice every day, clearing the checkpoint Quinn established last week . Cosmi started the week limited on Wednesday , but was a full go both Thursday and Friday; White was limited all three days but had no game designation on the final report. The final report listed four Commanders as questionable: McLaurin, Trey Amos (ankle), Jeremy McNichols (quad), and Deatrich Wise Jr. (quad). Of the four, McLaurin is the only player currently on the active roster: the other three had their 21-day practice windows open early this week and would need to be activated first. Friday brought the most encouraging injury news, with Nick Allegretti moving from not practicing to being a full go on Friday. Frankie Luvu, Jacory Croskey-Merritt, and Chig Okonkwo improved from limited to full. Sonny Styles , Ben Sinnott, Treylon Burks, Javon Kinlaw, Fabian Moreau, and Jeremy Reaves all finished the week as full participants.

title: Commanders Mailbag: The Bigger Concern With Jayden Daniels’ Return
full_text:
We want to hear from you! Each week, we invite you, the Burgundy and Gold faithful, to send in your Commanders' questions about everything going on in Ashburn/Landover. We want to make sure everyone gets a chance to have their take heard in the HTTR4LIFE Mailbag, so we'll answer questions on either Monday or Friday, depending on the volume of responses each week. You can send your Washington Commanders questions for the HTTR4LIFE Mailbag to hailbng+si@gmail.com . The Commanders will play host to the New York Giants this week at Northwest Stadium in Landover, Maryland. This week’s mailbag questions focus on protecting Jayden Daniels as he returns from his elbow injury and what Daronte Jones can change to fix Washington’s second-half defensive struggles.
Question via Stanley M on Facebook It's important to understand the difference between designed runs and scrambling when needed. Washington was already using less of the read option with Daniels than you saw with Marcus Mariota . What makes that hard to see is that when plays broke down, Daniels was moving around to extend the pocket, and yes, taking off when needed. But that's different from what Kliff Kingsbury was doing with Daniels in the shotgun and no-huddle. David Blough has him running a more traditional offense that allows for him to move once the play breaks down. With that in mind, he was running with the ball more than I would have liked before the injury, but he was also doing things to protect himself: mainly sliding, going out of bounds when necessary, and avoiding hits at all costs. He was injured on a freak no-contact play when he came from under center after guard Chris Paul stepped on his foot. He wasn't playing with no regard to getting injured; it just happened. What worries me more with Daniels is other teams targeting the arm as the pocket collapses. We already know he will leave the pocket, injury or not; the question is how well he can hold onto the ball and still protect himself outside the pocket. He looked a bit uncomfortable handing the ball off in practice with that brace on, but I don't think it will change much about how they use him otherwise. Blough said Thursday, " He’s full go ."
Jayden Daniels in action. Note: he did catch the ball with two hands later. Also took snaps again. As he has been doing since last week. pic.twitter.com/pQsD8Gm5L8
Question via Cindy C. on X Seems like a question we've been asking for years about several different defensive coordinators. Joe Gibbs mastered the second-half adjustment; Ron Rivera stunk at it. Let's hope Daronte Jones finds the end of the stick that doesn't get him fired , since there are multiple paths to fix issues depending on what team you're playing. First things first, that unit is giving up 17.8 second-half points per game, which is currently tied for worst in the league. Jones pointed to conditioning and focus when asked about the second-half struggles Thursday. He used the example of a player expecting to play 25 snaps and ending up playing 40. “We can't let things out of our control be a determining factor,” Jones said. He has his work cut out for him, with missed tackles and assignment mistakes plaguing the defense through the first four weeks. If an opponent keeps winning the same matchup after halftime, Jones needs to change the coverage or give that defender safety help. The players still have to execute those changes on the field . Even the right defensive call won't get Washington off the field if someone misses a tackle or blows an assignment. I expect Jones to send the house at Jameis Winston this weekend. The test comes when New York adjusts to that pressure. Jones has to give Winston a different look, and the players have to handle their assignments even if they're playing more snaps than expected. Making Winston uncomfortable early won't mean much if Washington falls apart after halftime. title: Commanders Scouting Report: How Washington Exploits Jameis Winston's Penchant for Mistakes
full_text:
The Washington Commanders have an old friend coming to town this week as the New York Football Giants will travel to Northwest Stadium on Sunday. Waiting for them there, the Giants will find a defense that is much improved over last year's version. Jameis Winston will find it harder to beat than the one he faced in Arizona in Week 4, which intercepted him twice and sacked him four times. Winston still produced 250 yards and three touchdown passes in New York's 36-24 win over the Cardinals. Commanders defensive coordinator Daronte Jones was asked about Winston's tendency to turn the ball over: "Well, that same guy is also prone to making big plays," Jones said, adding, "He can also put four or five touchdowns on you in a heartbeat." Winston is an old bird among a league of younglings, but he showed last weekend he still has some of that gunslinger mentality, going 18-of-29 for 250 yards and tossing three touchdowns and two interceptions; it brought back memories of his 30/30 season of 2019 in Tampa Bay. I couldn't get much out of his film in the Tennessee game; the matchup was played during a nor'easter, and the weather was a major factor. One constant: teams were able to get at him, as he was sacked seven times across his two starts.
Washington blitzes 44% of the time 2nd-most in NFL Jameis Winston when blitzed this season: 36.8 passer rating (28th) 9 of 18 (50% comp) 3.9 yards per attempt When pressured? 8 of 24 with 2 INTs https://t.co/SnRJmlGXDa
In his two starts, Winston has targeted TE Isaiah Likely the most (17); Likely caught seven of those for 66 yards last weekend, leading the Giants in receptions against Arizona. With opposing tight ends acting like a thorn in the franchise's side for what seems like forever, Likely is the name to watch on Sunday, especially if Malik Nabers doesn't play (he was limited Thursday). Nabers has done well with Winston, catching 11 passes (13 targets) for 138 yards and a touchdown. Winston isn't afraid to throw downfield, and he's had some success lately. Against Arizona, he cashed in on several chunk plays, including a 40-yarder to Malachi Fields and two plays of 25+ to Nabers, who caught six for 112 yards and a touchdown. Winston is constantly working to get better: "I've got to do a better job of making sure our best players are touching the ball consistently," Winston said. Daronte Jones is focused on Likely and stopping TEs in the red zone: "Continue to point it out to the players, make the corrections, show the awareness of where certain players are, certain looks, and got to be dialed in," Jones said. "You got to understand the situation of the game and how they’re going to attack and what we’ve put on tape. And so, you know, it’s a copycat league, and so once you put something on tape, you got to take it off. And so, that’s been the focus."
Every play of Jameis Winston v. Cardinals 18/29 250 yards 3 TD 2 INT 4 Sacks pic.twitter.com/VJT9k9Q4hp
Washington has to find a way to get after Winston, who is susceptible to the pass rush and makes mistakes often. If they don't, Winston could have a field day with the weapons New York brings to the table. Isaiah Likely is a nightmare in the red zone, and Washington is a train wreck trying to stop tight ends in that section of the field. The Commanders must find a way to eliminate the chance of it happening altogether, since stopping it seems futile. I'd show Winston pressure, then bring four and drop an apparent blitzer into a passing lane. Give him a different picture after the snap, when he has less time to sort it out. With Likely getting that much attention, Washington should crowd his throwing windows and make Winston find another answer. If the front can generate pressure without extra help, Jones can keep a safety over Nabers instead of leaving his corner on an island. The idea is to tempt Winston into a throw that looks better before the snap than it does after it. That's an opportunity to turn his aggressive approach into a possession for Washington. The Commanders can't assume an interception means they've figured out Winston. He'll throw the next one like the last one never happened, and Jones knows it. The Commanders have to keep getting after him without losing their assignments behind the rush. Otherwise, the same quarterback they just picked off could come right back and put six on the board. title: Sonny Styles vs Arvell Reese: Which is Better Positioned to Win NFL Defensive Rookie of the Year
full_text:
Sonny Styles and Arvell Reese shared a linebacker room at Ohio State. On Sunday, Oct. 11, the two rookies will meet for the first time as NFC East rivals when the Washington Commanders host the New York Giants at Northwest Stadium. Back in April, these two made NFL Draft history for being part of the first college program to have two linebackers selected in the top 10 of the same draft. The Giants selected Reese with the No. 5 pick, and two picks later, the Commanders selected Styles with the No. 7 pick. When they each chose their NFL numbers, they both picked No. 52. Sunday's game will be the first time the two can be compared on the same grass. Currently, NFL.com's Gennaro Filice ranks Styles first and Reese second among defensive rookies. While that is only one opinion, it's a strong one with some backing. Both were on Ohio State's 2024 national championship team. By 2025, Styles led the Buckeyes with 82 tackles; Reese followed with 69 tackles and 6.5 sacks. At a media event in August of 2025 , Reese specifically credited Styles with helping him understand preparation away from the field, saying, "I have learned a lot from Sonny, and it's more off the field. How you prepare for games, how he prepares practice to practice, and how intentional he is, Sonny is a great person." At that same event, Styles said Reese’s mental development is the place he's grown the most: "I would say mentally, just understanding the game." Styles explained that Reese had always possessed the physical tools, but a better understanding of the game was allowing him to play faster and use them.
Since joining the Commanders , Styles has 20 tackles (two for loss), one sack, one interception, one forced fumble, and two passes defensed. He had eight tackles against Indy this past weekend, one week after becoming the franchise’s first rookie linebacker to record an interception, a forced fumble, and multiple passes defensed in one game. He won NFC Defensive Player of the Week for that performance . Styles's play has put him in the conversation for rookie of the year , even if that conversation was had without words. He has demonstrated several ways to affect the passing game, which strengthens his case beyond his tackle total. PFF agrees, giving him an 85.2 coverage grade through four games, third among 74 qualifying linebackers.
Sonny Styles was EVERYWHERE in Washington’s win over Seattle. 4 TKL, 1 INT, 2 PD, 1 FF, 1 QBH vs Seahawks The rookie came away with his first career interception and forced a fumble against the defending champs. https://t.co/UMG5nOAliR pic.twitter.com/H3zRDCHDxE
Reese hasn't been a slouch himself: in four games, he has 34 tackles (three for loss), four passes defensed, one interception, and two quarterback hits. This past Sunday against Arizona, he had nine tackles, three passes defensed, and his first NFL interception. PFF also credits Reese with 13 defensive stops and just one missed tackle, compared with seven stops and four missed tackles for Styles. That gives Reese an early advantage in tackling production and reliability as both build their cases for Defensive Rookie of the Year. Their overall PFF grades are nearly identical through four games: 77.1 for Reese and 76.9 for Styles. Reese has also played 243 defensive snaps compared with Styles' 219, giving him more opportunities to add to his numbers.
Arvell Reese just gets better every week 9 tackles, 5 stops, 1 INT, 1 pressure, 1 batted pass in week 4 https://t.co/RGJ6tKfoco pic.twitter.com/t0oPdXp2zX
Both players look like problems for the NFC East for several years to come, and right now, I have them in a dead heat. Styles has the stronger coverage grade, a sack, and a forced fumble. Reese has more tackles, more defensive stops, and fewer missed tackles. I can make a Defensive Rookie of the Year case for either one. What's wild is that two guys from the same college, wearing the same number and respecting one another, are now building those cases on opposite sides of an NFC East rivalry. Their first meeting comes Sunday, with all of us watching No. 52 on both defenses for different reasons. title: Commanders Need More From Chig Okonkwo, but the Problem Goes Beyond Him
full_text:
The Washington Commanders, like most 1-3 operations in the first month of the NFL regular season, have produced numerous players and position groups who could contend for the distinction of their roster's most disappointing element.
Even if it entered the season with minimal hype, the offensive line has crumbled about as dramatically as anyone could have imagined, with their two best blockers presently down for the count. Other playmakers like Terry McLaurin and Jacory "Bill" Croskey-Merritt have fluctuated between exciting and inefficient, while someone like Mike Sainristil has completely careened from Washington's secondary rotation, with some of the lowest defensive metrics of anyone league-wide.
#Commanders CB Rasul Douglas' share of defensive snaps: Week 1: 32% Week 2: 43% Week 3: 67% Week 4: 85% Over the same stretch, Mike Sainristil went from 98% to 8%. 📊: NFL Pro | #RaiseHail pic.twitter.com/EJMWLYowfy
Some of those key Commanders have been loud in their letdowns, but Chig Okonkwo deserves a shout of his own, given how little he's factored into the group's equation through four weeks. His lingering hamstring injury has to be mentioned for keeping him out of Washington's Week 2 and 3 matchups- the first absence of his professional career- but 21 yards on four receptions and seven targets just can't go undiscussed.
It's important to note that Okonkwo isn't Zach Ertz , and that's more or less the tight-end archetype that fans have grown to anticipate within their offense.
Okonkwo more closely resembles a big receiver than Ertz, someone who could regularly find openings 10 yards out and nab easy first downs as Jayden Daniels ' go-to checkdown read before he shredded his knee last season. It wasn't exciting, but it required strong footwork and a veteran awareness that was easily taken for granted.
Ertz's replacement, meanwhile, is more likely to try beating coverages with his raw speed, and he's failed to beat the Philadelphia Eagles' or Indianapolis Colts' defenses in two outings. And with Washington’s quarterback situation having changed repeatedly over the last few weeks, that lack of a security blanket has been particularly glaring.
One example of how Chig Okonkwo hasn't gotten it going yet. I assume this is supposed to be a rub route by Diggs but #57 just ... goes around it and Chig is never freed up for a big gain. Instead, just two yards pic.twitter.com/jcuSor5jRc
Again, this is based purely on two games' worth of snaps. Okonkwo will benefit greatly from a more consistent passing game once Daniels returns and McLaurin and Diggs are healthy, because he's likely getting very little help from his positional understudies .
Even if Okonkwo was never a star with the Tennessee Titans, his stable average of 450-560 yards a season sounded pretty nice when the tight end room was left without its pass-catching starter for two games.
For all the good things we can say about John Bates' willingness to stay committed to blocking in an overtasked role, he'll never force a defense's hand when he drifts downfield into open space. That's to say nothing of reserves like Ben Sinnott and Colson Yankoff, who've fallen short of leveraging their respective talents into every-down roles; despite playing eight combined games to Okonkwo's two, they've each failed to eclipse the starter's paltry yardage total of 21.
The Commanders' TE production through four weeks (via @TruMediaSports ): Receptions — 10 (Tied for 31st/last) Targets — 17 (tied for 31st) Yards — 65 (32nd*) Rec. TDs — Zero (one of four teams without a TD) Air yards per target — 2.30 (28th) YAC — 42 (31st)
Prodigies like Brock Bowers and Trey McBride aren't walking through the Commanders' facility anytime soon, and the following draft is still 13 games away. If the team has any hope of getting anything out of its disappointing tight end rotation, it'll come down to freeing Okonkwo up by taking pressure off him with other receiving threats and giving the quarterback enough protection to find him. That means a cleaner pocket for the quarterback, more play-calling and route-running diversions, and ideally, enough health to return as many receiving threats to the starting lineup as possible.
David Blough has passed most of the adaptive tests thrown his way, so consider the Okonkwo dilemma just another schematic puzzle for the new offensive coordinator to solve with his makeshift remains.

title: Jayden Daniels’ Return Could Put Antonio Williams in a Much Bigger Role — Commanders Daily
full_text:
The Washington Commanders face an interesting situation this weekend against one of their oldest and most bitter rivals, the New York Giants. The team is expected to get quarterback Jayden Daniels back just two games after he dislocated his non-throwing elbow in a contact-less situation. Daniels practiced fully for the first time since the injury on Wednesday , the same day Terry McLaurin and Stefon Diggs missed practice with hamstring injuries. McLaurin already missed the London game . The potential of not having Diggs, who leads all receivers with 18 receptions for 170 yards and three touchdowns — and/or McLaurin is nightmare fuel for the weak-hearted. This is where having a dynamic player like Antonio Williams pays off. He can be that guy when and if needed. The great part is, he's already been ramped up, inadvertently, for this very opportunity. Williams has seen his snaps climb from 26 snaps (37%) in Week 1 to 44 snaps (69%) in Week 4, with 49% and 41% snap shares in Weeks 2 & 3, respectively. Over that time, he has 12 receptions for 124 yards and one touchdown. Last week against Indianapolis, he had eight targets and caught three for 21 yards, but an 87-yard touchdown was called back due to penalties. His usage shows he's grown quickly from a complementary rookie to being in on two-thirds of Washington's offensive plays with McLaurin out. Williams' most productive game as a pro came in Week 1 against the Philadelphia Eagles when he was targeted four times and caught four passes for 64 yards and a touchdown. In the three games since (two without Daniels), Williams has caught eight passes for 60 yards without another touchdown.
Antonio Williams (#14) All-22 on 10 routes vs Eagles • 4 recs on 4 tgts • 64 rec yds • 1 TD • 91.0 PFF overall grade (highest graded receiver in the game yesterday) #RaiseHail pic.twitter.com/fGojlpffxz
Back at the end of July, McLaurin saw that Williams had the ability to contribute early on: "He has a good feel for the receiver position, and I think he has a chance to really help us, especially in [OC David] Blough's offense, where guys will be able to move around," McLaurin said. While most think Williams is only a slot receiver, a trip through his game film from Clemson will show you that he played there his last year in college, but he had 317 snaps on the outside during the 2024 season and did well. Blough's offense is supposed to be designed for players to move around, so that should benefit Williams no matter if Diggs and McLaurin can't play or not. "I think he really excels in the slot, and I know he's gonna have a chance to move around, but I think it's just really important, especially when you're a young guy gaining that confidence," McLaurin said. As we all know, more opportunities don't always turn into more production; as against Indy, Williams only had 21 yards on eight targets. But that conversation needs a little context, with the offense having to shift to a rookie quarterback with a different skill set, who the rest of the offense was not completely comfortable with, having not practiced much together, if at all. Then again, the 87-yard play that was negated by the illegal shift/holding penalties is the missing yardage. Daniels' expected return changes the quarterback situation, but doesn't eliminate the challenges facing the receiving corps. The Commanders drafted Williams hoping he could become a meaningful part of Daniels' offense. Depending on how the next two days unfold, they might be asking him to prove that sooner than anyone expected. title: Commanders News: Jayden Daniels Takes a Big Step, But Injury Questions Grow | Burgundy Roundup
full_text:
Wednesday brought several Commanders storylines, including Jayden Daniels getting closer to starting this weekend , the first Week 5 injury report, three players beginning the return-to-practice process, and roster moves. Washington Commanders quarterback Jayden Daniels was a full participant in practice for the first time since his Week 2 elbow injury. Commanders HC Dan Quinn expects Daniels to start, barring any setbacks this week. Daniels said, "I'm gonna embrace the brace," today after practice. The team also had safety Nick Cross back as a full participant. Receivers Terry McLaurin and Stefon Diggs were both DNP with hamstring injuries. Marcus Mariota, Charles Omenihu, Percy Butler, and Tyler Owens also missed practice Wednesday. Trey Amos, Deatrich Wise Jr., and Jeremy McNichols were officially designated to return to practice, but were limited during Wednesday's activities. This officially opens their 21-day activation windows. The Commanders signed safety Darren Hall, WR Nick DeGennaro, and outside linebacker T.J. Maguranyanga to the practice squad. They also released defensive tackle Jeffrey M'Ba from the practice squad. The team worked out former UFL MVP quarterback Jack Plummer but did not sign him. Quinn later said that the team does not currently plan to place Mariota on injured reserve because of his knee injury. While Washington is figuring out its injury situation, the New York Giants have some injury concerns of their own heading into Sunday's game. Malik Nabers, Andrew Thomas, Najee Harris, Jason Pinnock, and Chauncey Golston missed practice Wednesday for the Giants, but that doesn't mean they will miss the game this weekend.
The Washington Commanders are four games into the season, which doesn't give us enough time to decide what this team ultimately will be, but it's certainly enough to start figuring out where some of those preseason expectations were right and where they weren't. Washington sits at 1-3 after its loss to the Indianapolis Colts , and a month of actual football has given us more than just wins and losses to judge. Roles have changed, young players have been asked to grow up quickly, and some position groups that were supposed to help carry this team haven't done nearly enough.
No WR Malik Nabers or LT Andrew Thomas at practice for the New York Giants. RB Cam Skattebo and TE Isaiah Likely were limited. pic.twitter.com/DGaErauayA
While the Washington Commanders aren't the most penalized team in the NFL, they keep finding new ways to shoot themselves in the foot at the worst time. More importantly, the problem the team keeps talking about controlling is actually getting worse over the last two games.
"A center-run bus rapid transit,” D.C. Councilmember Charles Allen said this week. “If we want to go make the same mistakes and put the bus just right there with streetcar track, we could do that. I wouldn't recommend it, ‘cause that's not going to be a great use of our tax dollars. But, as some of my ANC commissioners and businesses on H Street said, if we’re going to do this thing, let’s do this. It's not worth it to mess it up."
Jayden Daniels throwing again today. Expected to be a full participant in practice. pic.twitter.com/R21ZuYUXTp
Running back Austin Ekeler was set to join the Carolina Panthers ' practice squad in Week 4 when the Washington Commanders called. What's wild is that after being signed back to the roster just a few days earlier, Ekeler not only made the trip across the pond ; he played 17 offensive snaps (27%) against the Indianapolis Colts. That may not sound like much, but Jacory "Bill" Croskey-Merritt led the backs with 29 snaps (45%), Ekeler was next with 17 (27%), and rookie Kaytron Allen played 12 (19%).

title: 6 Winners, 5 Losers From the Commanders’ First Four Games
full_text:
The Washington Commanders are four games into the season, which doesn't give us enough time to decide what this team ultimately will be, but it's certainly enough to start figuring out where some of those preseason expectations were right and where they weren't. Washington sits at 1-3 after its loss to the Indianapolis Colts , and a month of actual football has given us more than just wins and losses to judge. Roles have changed, young players have been asked to grow up quickly, and some position groups that were supposed to help carry this team haven't done nearly enough. With that in mind, here are six winners and five losers from the Commanders' first four games.
Sonny Styles Washington clearly had high expectations for Styles when they used the No. 7 pick on him, but there is still a difference between drafting someone that high and immediately asking him to become a major part of an NFL defense. Styles hasn't needed much time . Through four games, he has 20 tackles, a sack, an interception, and a forced fumble, with his best performance coming against Seattle when he finished with five tackles, two passes defended, an interception, and a forced fumble. He has already played every defensive snap in multiple games, which may say more about how Washington views him than any individual statistic does. The rookie treatment is basically over at this point. Styles is being asked to play like someone Washington expects to be around for a long time, and so far he has looked ready for it.
Sonny Styles has been a PROBLEM for some of the NFL’s most dangerous RB’s. Styles has recorded 3 STOPS against both Jonathan Taylor and Saquon Barkley. The Commanders rookie LB is already one of the BEST run-stoppers in the NFL 😳😈 pic.twitter.com/qWDO9mzRLZ
Amik Robertson Robertson was brought in to give Washington another experienced option in a secondary that had plenty of moving parts coming into the season. Four games later, he has done more than simply give the Commanders another option. He has made it difficult to take him off the field. Robertson has 26 tackles through four games and has consistently found himself around the football, including four passes defended and a forced fumble against Seattle before following that with a team-high nine tackles against Indianapolis. The numbers are nice, but the biggest thing with Robertson continues to be how hard he plays regardless of what is happening around him. Washington has had its share of problems in the secondary, but figuring out whether Robertson should be on the field hasn't been one of them. Josh Conerly Jr. Young offensive tackles are going to have rough moments, and Josh Conerly Jr. has certainly had some of his own, but the fact that Washington's right tackle position hasn't become a weekly conversation is probably a pretty good sign. Conerly was handed the job immediately, struggled as a rookie last season, and has taken a step forward in Year 2 , earning a 70.1 pass-blocking grade from PFF through four games while allowing nine pressures over 169 pass-blocking snaps. There is obviously plenty for him to clean up, and nobody should be declaring the position solved after a month, but that's not really the point. Washington's offensive line has already dealt with injuries, different combinations, and plenty of problems elsewhere. Conerly has stepped into one of the hardest positions for a young player to handle and hasn't given the Commanders a reason to start looking for another answer. That's a win. Antonio Williams Williams was one of the better stories coming out of training camp, but we've seen plenty of players have good summers and disappear once the regular season starts. Williams hasn't. He has 12 catches for 124 yards and a touchdown through four games, while his role has grown as Washington has needed more from the receiver room. He played 37% of the offensive snaps in Week 1, 49% in Week 2, and then jumped to 69% against Indianapolis with Terry McLaurin unavailable. That last part matters. Williams isn't just getting developmental snaps anymore because Washington likes what it sees from a young receiver. Injuries have created a need for somebody else to become dependable, and Williams is starting to become one of those guys.
Antonio Williams all routes from his NFL debut 4/64/1 on just 10 routes… GET HIM ON THE FIELD MORE! pic.twitter.com/F9mfhB8yc6
Odafe Oweh Washington didn't add Odafe Oweh just to fill out the edge rotation . It needed somebody capable of creating problems for opposing quarterbacks, and we're starting to see exactly what that looks like. His pressure against Seattle helped create Kain Medrano's pick-six, and against Indianapolis he decided to handle everything himself. Oweh sacked Daniel Jones on the Colts' second offensive play , knocked the ball loose, and recovered it at the Indianapolis 21. It's hard to create a better defensive snap than that. There have been stretches where Washington's pass rush hasn't gotten home enough, but Oweh has consistently looked like one of the players capable of changing a possession when he does. That's exactly what the Commanders needed when they rebuilt the position this offseason. Marcus Mariota Nobody wanted Washington to find out this early whether signing an experienced backup quarterback was worth it, but Jayden Daniels' elbow injury made that question unavoidable. Mariota answered it pretty well. His best performance came against Seattle , when he completed 19 of 31 passes for 183 yards and three touchdowns without turning the ball over in Washington's only win of the season. He also showed the value of having someone with his experience at the line of scrimmage, helping Washington get into better looks when Seattle presented something the offense could take advantage of. Mariota wasn't brought to Washington to be Daniels. They brought him here so the offense wouldn't completely fall apart if Daniels couldn't play . Until Mariota injured his own knee against Indianapolis, that's pretty much what he gave them.
Mike Sainristil's Role This isn't about declaring Sainristil a bad player after four games . It's about where his role was expected to be when the season started compared to where it is now. That change has been pretty dramatic. Sainristil played 98% of Washington's defensive snaps in Week 1 and 82% in Week 2. That dropped to 39% against Seattle, and then just five defensive snaps against Indianapolis. Meanwhile, Robertson and Rasul Douglas have become major parts of Washington's secondary, while Fabian Moreau has also gotten work. Whatever the long-term plan is for Sainristil, his first month went the opposite direction from what almost anyone would've expected when the season started. Running Backs Washington's overall rushing numbers don't look terrible until you start separating the quarterbacks from the running backs. That's where the problem shows up. The Commanders' backs have combined for 331 yards on 96 carries through four games, or about 3.4 yards per attempt. Jacory Croskey-Merritt has 157 yards on 56 carries and hasn't broken a run longer than 11 yards, while against Indianapolis the entire running back room combined for 49 yards on 18 carries. Washington's quarterbacks account for 165 of the team's 496 rushing yards. That isn't exactly the formula the Commanders were looking for, especially during a stretch when Daniels wasn't available and the running game should've been helping whoever was playing quarterback. Instead, Washington has too often needed the quarterback to create rushing production. Tight Ends Washington has enough tight ends to throw a small party, but so far there's been little reason to celebrate what they've done in the passing game. Through four games, the group has combined for 10 catches, 65 yards, and no touchdowns. Chig Okonkwo missing time hasn't helped, but the Commanders still have Ben Sinnott, John Bates, and Colson Yankoff, and none of them have become much of a factor when…
